The greedy with a heap is exact (each split goes to the piece that is currently largest) but costs O(k log n) — fine as a checker, too slow when k is 10⁹. The binary search is O(n log(W/ε)) regardless of k.

Topic 6D — Hard binary searches

Unit 6.5 — Median of two sorted arrays

One-line summary: Partition both arrays so that the left parts together hold half the elements and every left element ≤ every right element; then the median comes from the four elements at the cut. Binary-search the cut position in the shorter array: O(log min(m, n)).

# file: median.py
from check import stress, rand_list

def median_two_sorted(a, b):
    if len(a) > len(b):
        a, b = b, a                                   # binary search over the shorter array
    m, n = len(a), len(b)
    half = (m + n + 1) // 2
    lo, hi = 0, m
    NEG, POS = float("-inf"), float("inf")
    while lo <= hi:
        i = (lo + hi) // 2                            # take i elements from a ...
        j = half - i                                  # ... and j from b for the left half
        a_left = a[i - 1] if i > 0 else NEG
        a_right = a[i] if i < m else POS
        b_left = b[j - 1] if j > 0 else NEG
        b_right = b[j] if j < n else POS
        if a_left <= b_right and b_left <= a_right:   # a valid partition
            if (m + n) % 2:
                return float(max(a_left, b_left))
            return (max(a_left, b_left) + min(a_right, b_right)) / 2
        if a_left > b_right:
            hi = i - 1                                # took too many from a
        else:
            lo = i + 1                                # took too few from a
    raise ValueError("inputs must be sorted")

def median_brute(a, b):
    c = sorted(a + b)
    n = len(c)
    return float(c[n // 2]) if n % 2 else (c[n // 2 - 1] + c[n // 2]) / 2

print(stress(median_two_sorted, median_brute, lambda rng: (sorted(rand_list(rng)), sorted(rand_list(rng))),
             valid=lambda a, b: len(a) + len(b) > 0))

Pattern

P-7. “Minimise the maximum” or “maximise the minimum” almost always means binary search on the answer with a greedy check. (Practice) Write can(x) first, convince yourself it is monotone, decide whether you want the first true or the last true, and set the range from obvious bounds (for capacities: max(item) to sum(items)). The total cost is O(log(range) × cost of can). Trade-off: binary search on the answer finds the optimal value; if the problem also wants the arrangement, run can once more at the optimum and record the choices.

Mastery check

  1. Predict. first_true(0, 10, lambda i: i * i > 50) returns what? And last_true(0, 10, lambda i: i * i <= 50)?
  2. Predict. In ship_within_days, why does the search start at max(weights) and not at 1?

Chapter 6 Project — The k-th smallest pair distance

Goal: given n integers, find the k-th smallest value of |a[i] − a[j]| over all pairs i < j. There are n(n−1)/2 pairs — 5·10⁹ for n = 10⁵ — so generating them is impossible. Combine three patterns: sort; binary search on the answer d (“are there at least k pairs with distance ≤ d?” is monotone in d); and a two-pointer count of pairs with distance ≤ d in O(n). Total O(n log n + n log(range)).

# file: kth/kth.py
import random
import time
from check import stress, rand_list
from template import first_true

def count_pairs_within(a, d):                       # a sorted: pairs i<j with a[j]-a[i] <= d
    count, i = 0, 0
    for j in range(len(a)):
        while a[j] - a[i] > d:
            i += 1
        count += j - i                              # a[j] pairs with every element in [i, j)
    return count

def kth_smallest_distance(nums, k):
    a = sorted(nums)
    return first_true(0, a[-1] - a[0] + 1, lambda d: count_pairs_within(a, d) >= k)

def kth_brute(nums, k):
    return sorted(abs(nums[i] - nums[j]) for i in range(len(nums)) for j in range(i + 1, len(nums)))[k - 1]

def gen(rng):
    a = rand_list(rng, 0, 15, 9, 2)
    return a, rng.randint(1, len(a) * (len(a) - 1) // 2)

print(stress(kth_smallest_distance, kth_brute, gen))
rng = random.Random(2)
a = [rng.randint(0, 10**6) for _ in range(100_000)]
for k in (1, 10**6, 2_500_000_000):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    d = kth_smallest_distance(a, k)
    print(f"n=100,000, k={k:>13,}: distance {d:>7,} in {(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000:.0f} ms")

Notice the answer must be an actual pair distance — and it is, automatically: first_true returns the smallest d with at least k pairs within d, and if d were not itself a distance, d − 1 would have the same count, contradicting minimality. This “the binary search lands on a real value” argument recurs whenever the answer must belong to a set (a distance, an element of a matrix) but the search runs over integers.

Review checklist

  • Why is the two-pointer count O(n), and why does it require sorting first?
  • How would you find the k-th smallest element of an n × m multiplication table with the same technique?
  • What is the k-th smallest sum of pairs from two sorted arrays? Which part of the solution changes?

Answers to the Chapter 6 prediction questions

6.5 Q1. first_true(0, 10, i*i > 50) is 8 (49 ≤ 50 < 64). last_true(0, 10, i*i <= 50) is 7.

6.5 Q2. No capacity below the heaviest package can ship it at all, so can would be false there for a reason the greedy check does not handle (it would put an overweight package alone on a “day” and report success). Starting at max(weights) keeps the predicate both correct and monotone.

Chapter 7 — Sorting

Goal: know the sorting algorithms well enough to choose, adapt, and break them — merge sort, quicksort with good partitioning, heap sort, counting and radix sort — use custom orders correctly, select the k-th element in linear expected time, and recognise “sort first” as the step that turns many hard problems into easy scans.

What you will be able to do after this chapter

  • Implement merge sort, three-way quicksort, heap sort, counting sort, and radix sort, and state their properties.
  • Explain the Ω(n log n) lower bound for comparison sorting, and when linear-time sorts escape it.
  • Write custom orders with keys and comparators (functools.cmp_to_key), and rely on stability.
  • Find the k-th smallest element with quickselect.
  • Recognise problems that become simple after sorting.

Topic 7A — Comparison sorts

Unit 7.1 — Merge sort, quicksort, heap sort

One-line summary: Merge sort splits in half, sorts both, merges: Θ(n log n) always, stable, Θ(n) extra memory. Quicksort partitions around a pivot and recurses: Θ(n log n) expected with a random pivot, Θ(n²) worst case, in place, not stable; three-way partitioning (< pivot, = pivot, > pivot) keeps it fast with many duplicates. Heap sort builds a max-heap and repeatedly extracts the maximum: Θ(n log n) worst case, in place, not stable, poor cache behaviour.

Algorithm Best Average Worst Extra memory Stable
Merge sort n log n n log n n log n n yes
Quicksort (random pivot) n log n n log n n² (unlikely) log n (stack) no
Heap sort n log n n log n n log n 1 no
Insertion sort n n² n² 1 yes
TimSort (Python’s sorted) n n log n n log n n yes
Counting sort (range k) n + k n + k n + k n + k yes
Radix sort (d digits, base b) d(n + b) d(n + b) d(n + b) n + b yes 
# file: sorts.py
import random
from check import stress, rand_list

def merge_sort(a):
    if len(a) <= 1:
        return list(a)
    mid = len(a) // 2
    left, right = merge_sort(a[:mid]), merge_sort(a[mid:])
    out, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:                   # <= keeps equal elements in original order: stable
            out.append(left[i]); i += 1
        else:
            out.append(right[j]); j += 1
    return out + left[i:] + right[j:]

def quicksort(a, rng=random.Random(0)):
    a = list(a)
    def sort(lo, hi):                             # sorts a[lo:hi+1]
        while lo < hi:
            p = a[rng.randint(lo, hi)]            # random pivot: expected O(n log n) on every input
            lt, i, gt = lo, lo, hi                # a[lo:lt] < p, a[lt:i] == p, a[gt+1:hi+1] > p
            while i <= gt:
                if a[i] < p:
                    a[lt], a[i] = a[i], a[lt]; lt += 1; i += 1
                elif a[i] > p:
                    a[i], a[gt] = a[gt], a[i]; gt -= 1
                else:
                    i += 1
            if lt - lo < hi - gt:                 # recurse on the smaller side, loop on the larger:
                sort(lo, lt - 1); lo = gt + 1     # stack depth O(log n) even in bad cases
            else:
                sort(gt + 1, hi); hi = lt - 1
    sort(0, len(a) - 1)
    return a

def heap_sort(a):
    a = list(a)
    n = len(a)
    def sift_down(i, size):
        while True:
            big, l, r = i, 2 * i + 1, 2 * i + 2
            if l < size and a[l] > a[big]: big = l
            if r < size and a[r] > a[big]: big = r
            if big == i:
                return
            a[i], a[big] = a[big], a[i]
            i = big
    for i in range(n // 2 - 1, -1, -1):           # build a max-heap bottom-up: O(n)
        sift_down(i, n)
    for end in range(n - 1, 0, -1):               # move the max to the end, restore the heap
        a[0], a[end] = a[end], a[0]
        sift_down(0, end)
    return a

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for f in (merge_sort, quicksort, heap_sort):
        print(f.__name__, stress(f, sorted, lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, -5, 5, 15),)))

Deep & Tricky

DT-13. Quicksort with a fixed pivot (first or last element) is Θ(n²) on sorted input — and with two-way partitioning, on arrays of equal elements too. (Algorithm analysis) A sorted array makes every partition maximally unbalanced: sizes n−1 and 0. Random pivots make that astronomically unlikely on any input, and three-way partitioning makes runs of equal keys free (they end in the middle band and are never recursed on). The chapter project measures all of these. Production sorts go further: introsort (C++ std::sort) switches to heap sort if recursion gets too deep, guaranteeing O(n log n).

Unit 7.2 — The lower bound, and sorts that beat it

One-line summary: Any algorithm that sorts only by comparing elements needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case: there are n! possible orders, each comparison has two outcomes, so a decision tree must have depth at least log₂(n!) ≈ n log₂ n. Counting sort and radix sort escape the bound by looking at the keys’ values — they need small integer keys or fixed-length digits.

Recognise it when: keys are integers in a small range (ages, scores 0–100, characters), or fixed-width (32-bit ints, dates, equal-length strings).

# file: linear_sorts.py
import random
import time
from check import stress, rand_list

def counting_sort(a, lo, hi):                     # values in [lo, hi]
    count = [0] * (hi - lo + 1)
    for x in a:
        count[x - lo] += 1
    out = []
    for v, c in enumerate(count):
        out.extend([v + lo] * c)
    return out

def radix_sort(a, base=256):                      # non-negative integers, LSD radix with stable buckets
    if not a:
        return []
    out, shift, biggest = list(a), 0, max(a)
    while biggest >> shift:
        buckets = [[] for _ in range(base)]
        for x in out:
            buckets[(x >> shift) & (base - 1)].append(x)   # stable: keeps the order of the previous pass
        out = [x for b in buckets for x in b]
        shift += base.bit_length() - 1
    return out

print(stress(lambda a: counting_sort(a, -5, 5), sorted, lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, -5, 5, 15),)))
print(stress(radix_sort, sorted, lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 100_000, 15),)))
rng = random.Random(1)
a = [rng.randrange(1 << 30) for _ in range(500_000)]
for name, f in [("sorted() (TimSort, in C)", sorted), ("radix_sort (pure Python)", radix_sort)]:
    t = time.perf_counter(); f(a); print(f"{name:<26} n=500,000: {(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000:.0f} ms")

Radix sort is O(n) per pass and needs only four passes for 30-bit keys in base 256, yet the pure-Python version loses to sorted() written in C (DT-1). In C++ or Java radix sort does beat comparison sorts for large integer arrays; in Python, use sorted and save linear sorts for when the counting itself is the algorithm (bucket by frequency, Chapter 3).

Topic 7B — Orders

Unit 7.3 — Custom orders and stability

One-line summary: Sort by a key whenever the order is “by some property”: sorted(people, key=lambda p: (-p.age, p.name)) — tuples compare lexicographically, and negating a number reverses it. When the order is genuinely pairwise (“a before b if a+b > b+a”), use a comparator with functools.cmp_to_key. Stability — equal keys keep their input order — lets you sort by several keys in successive passes (least important first).

# file: orders.py
from functools import cmp_to_key
from itertools import permutations
from check import stress

def largest_number(nums):
    """Arrange non-negative integers to form the largest number: '3' + '30' > '30' + '3'."""
    strs = [str(x) for x in nums]
    strs.sort(key=cmp_to_key(lambda a, b: -1 if a + b > b + a else (1 if a + b < b + a else 0)))
    s = "".join(strs)
    return "0" if s and s[0] == "0" else s       # [0, 0] -> "0", not "00"

def largest_number_brute(nums):
    best = max("".join(map(str, p)) for p in permutations(nums))
    return str(int(best))

def sort_by_freq_then_value_desc(a):
    from collections import Counter
    c = Counter(a)
    return sorted(a, key=lambda x: (c[x], -x))   # rarer first; among equal frequency, larger first

records = [("bob", 25), ("ann", 30), ("cy", 25), ("dee", 30), ("eve", 25)]
by_age_then_name = sorted(sorted(records, key=lambda r: r[0]), key=lambda r: r[1])   # two stable passes
print(by_age_then_name == sorted(records, key=lambda r: (r[1], r[0])), by_age_then_name)
print(stress(largest_number, largest_number_brute, lambda rng: ([rng.choice([0, 1, 3, 9, 10, 30, 34, 5, 98]) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 5))],)))

Deep & Tricky

DT-14. A comparator must define a consistent total order — transitive and antisymmetric — or sorting may produce garbage (or, in Java, throw “Comparison method violates its general contract!”). (Library behaviour: TimSort) The “largest number” comparator looks ad hoc, but it is transitive (a+b > b+a defines a total preorder on digit strings — provable by viewing each string as a repeating fraction), which is why it works. A comparator like “a before b if |a − b| > 1” is not transitive, and sorts with it return an order that depends on the algorithm’s internal sequence of comparisons. When designing a custom order, check transitivity on small cases with a brute force.

Unit 7.4 — Quickselect: the k-th smallest in O(n)

One-line summary: Partition as in quicksort, then recurse only into the side that contains position k. Expected time O(n) with a random pivot (n + n/2 + n/4 + … ≈ 2n). Python’s heapq.nsmallest/nlargest (O(n log k)) and plain sorting (O(n log n)) are often simpler; quickselect matters when n is large and you need one order statistic, or when the partitioned array itself is useful (the k smallest elements, unordered).

# file: quickselect.py
import random
from check import stress, rand_list

def quickselect(a, k, rng=random.Random(0)):       # k-th smallest, 0-based
    a = list(a)
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while True:
        p = a[rng.randint(lo, hi)]
        lt, i, gt = lo, lo, hi                      # three-way partition of a[lo..hi]
        while i <= gt:
            if a[i] < p:
                a[lt], a[i] = a[i], a[lt]; lt += 1; i += 1
            elif a[i] > p:
                a[i], a[gt] = a[gt], a[i]; gt -= 1
            else:
                i += 1
        if k < lt:
            hi = lt - 1
        elif k > gt:
            lo = gt + 1
        else:
            return p                                # k falls in the band equal to the pivot

print(stress(quickselect, lambda a, k: sorted(a)[k], lambda rng: ((a := rand_list(rng, -5, 5, 12, 1)), rng.randrange(len(a)))))
$ PYTHONPATH=../lib python3 quickselect.py
2000 stress tests ok

Why quickselect is O(n) on average

Quicksort recurses into both sides of the pivot; quickselect recurses into one. With a random pivot the side kept is, on average, at most three quarters of the array, so the work is n + ¾n + (¾)²n + … ≤ 4n — a geometric series, hence O(n). The worst case (always picking the largest element) is still O(n²); the median of medians pivot rule guarantees O(n) but has a large constant and is almost never used in practice. In Python, heapq.nsmallest(k, a) (O(n log k)) is usually faster than a hand-written quickselect, because it runs in C.

One more problem: the k closest points to the origin

Selecting the k smallest by distance is quickselect with a key; the result does not need to be sorted, which is what makes O(n) possible.

# file: k_closest.py
import random
from check import stress

def k_closest(points, k, rng=random.Random(1)):
    pts = list(points)
    d = lambda p: p[0] * p[0] + p[1] * p[1]
    lo, hi = 0, len(pts) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        pivot = d(pts[rng.randint(lo, hi)])
        i, j = lo, hi
        while i <= j:                                  # Hoare-style partition by distance
            while d(pts[i]) < pivot: i += 1
            while d(pts[j]) > pivot: j -= 1
            if i <= j:
                pts[i], pts[j] = pts[j], pts[i]
                i, j = i + 1, j - 1
        if k - 1 <= j:
            hi = j
        elif k - 1 >= i:
            lo = i
        else:
            break
    return pts[:k]

def same_set(fast, _brute, args):
    points, k = args
    d = lambda p: p[0] ** 2 + p[1] ** 2
    return len(fast) == k and sorted(map(d, fast)) == sorted(map(d, points))[:k]

def gen(rng):
    pts = [(rng.randint(-4, 4), rng.randint(-4, 4)) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 10))]
    return pts, rng.randint(1, len(pts))

print(sorted(k_closest([(1, 3), (-2, 2), (5, 8), (0, 1)], 2)))
print(stress(k_closest, lambda p, k: None, gen, same=same_set))

Unit 15.2 solves the same problem with a size-k heap in O(n log k); quickselect is O(n) on average. The checker compares the multiset of distances, because when several points tie at the cut-off distance any of them is a correct answer.

Topic 7C — Sorting as a step

Unit 7.5 — Sort first

One-line summary: Sorting costs O(n log n) and buys a great deal: equal elements become adjacent (duplicates, grouping), two pointers work (Chapter 4), binary search works (Chapter 6), greedy choices become safe (intervals by end time, Chapter 37), and neighbours in sorted order are the only candidates for “closest pair” questions in one dimension.

Recognise it when: the problem asks about values or relationships between values, not positions — “minimum difference between any two”, “merge overlapping”, “assign tasks to workers”, “can these be paired so that…”.

# file: sort_first.py
from itertools import combinations
from check import stress, rand_list

def min_abs_difference(a):                         # closest pair of values: only sorted neighbours matter
    b = sorted(a)
    return min(b[i + 1] - b[i] for i in range(len(b) - 1))

def can_pair_with_sum_at_least(a, k):
    """Can the 2m elements be split into m pairs, each with sum >= k? Greedy: smallest with largest."""
    b = sorted(a)
    return all(b[i] + b[-1 - i] >= k for i in range(len(b) // 2))

def can_pair_brute(a, k):
    if not a:
        return True
    first, rest = a[0], a[1:]
    return any(first + rest[i] >= k and can_pair_brute(rest[:i] + rest[i + 1:], k) for i in range(len(rest)))

def h_index(citations):                            # largest h: h papers with >= h citations each
    c = sorted(citations, reverse=True)
    h = 0
    while h < len(c) and c[h] >= h + 1:
        h += 1
    return h

print(stress(min_abs_difference, lambda a: min(abs(x - y) for x, y in combinations(a, 2)), lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, -20, 20, 9, 2),)))
print(stress(can_pair_with_sum_at_least, can_pair_brute, lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 9, 4, 0) * 2, rng.randint(0, 15))))
print(stress(h_index, lambda c: max(h for h in range(len(c) + 1) if sum(x >= h for x in c) >= h), lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 8, 9),)))

Pattern

P-8. When stuck, sort — and ask what sorted order makes easy. (Practice) Sorting is cheap relative to most targets (n log n), it never loses information if you keep original indices, and it unlocks two pointers, binary search, greedy exchange arguments, and adjacency arguments. The question to ask is “sorted by what?” — value, end time, ratio, a custom comparator. Trade-off: if the problem depends on original order (subarrays, “the first … from the left”), sorting destroys exactly what matters; use prefix structures or monotonic stacks instead.

Mastery check

  1. Predict. Is sorted(xs, key=abs) stable for [-2, 1, 2, -1]? What does it return?
  2. Predict. What is the worst-case number of comparisons any comparison sort needs for 5 elements? (Compute ⌈log₂ 120⌉.)

Chapter 7 Project — Measuring the sorts, and breaking quicksort

Goal: benchmark the sorts of this chapter on four input families — random, already sorted, reversed, and “few distinct values” — including a deliberately naive quicksort (last-element pivot, two-way partition), and observe the worst cases predicted by DT-13.

# file: bench/bench.py
import random
import sys
import time
sys.setrecursionlimit(100_000)
from sorts import merge_sort, quicksort, heap_sort

def naive_quicksort(a):                            # last element as pivot, Lomuto two-way partition
    a = list(a)
    def sort(lo, hi):
        if lo >= hi:
            return
        p, i = a[hi], lo
        for j in range(lo, hi):
            if a[j] < p:
                a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
                i += 1
        a[i], a[hi] = a[hi], a[i]
        sort(lo, i - 1)
        sort(i + 1, hi)
    sort(0, len(a) - 1)
    return a

def run(f, data, limit_ms=4000):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = f(data)
    ms = (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000
    assert out == sorted(data)
    return ms

rng = random.Random(5)
n = 5000
families = {
    "random": [rng.randint(0, 10**6) for _ in range(n)],
    "sorted": list(range(n)),
    "reversed": list(range(n, 0, -1)),
    "few distinct (0..3)": [rng.randint(0, 3) for _ in range(n)],
}
print(f"{'n=' + str(n):<22}" + "".join(f"{name:>22}" for name in families))
for f in (sorted, merge_sort, quicksort, heap_sort, naive_quicksort):
    print(f"{f.__name__:<22}" + "".join(f"{run(f, d):>19.1f} ms" for d in families.values()))

merge_sort                            6.2 ms                4.0 ms                4.2 ms                5.5 ms

The table reproduces the textbook in a few seconds. The naive quicksort is the fastest of the hand-written sorts on random data, but sorted and reversed inputs push it to Θ(n²) — over a hundred times slower at only 5,000 elements, with recursion depth n (hence the raised recursion limit). On few-distinct data it is about seventeen times slower: quadratic within each band of equal values, because a two-way partition puts all elements equal to the pivot on one side. The random-pivot, three-way quicksort is fast on every family, and on few-distinct data it is faster than on random data, because each pass removes a whole band of equal keys. sorted() (TimSort) is fastest everywhere and is nearly free on sorted and reversed input, because it detects existing runs — which is why, in Python, you sort with sorted and implement sorting algorithms only when the algorithm is the point (merge sort’s merge step for counting inversions, quickselect, partitioning).

Review checklist

  • Why is heap sort slower than merge sort here despite the same complexity? (Memory access pattern: heap indices jump around.)
  • How deep does the recursion of quicksort go in the worst case, given that it recurses on the smaller side only?
  • Construct an input that makes a median-of-three pivot quicksort quadratic (the “median-of-3 killer”).

Answers to the Chapter 7 prediction questions

7.5 Q1. Yes — sorted is always stable. Keys are 2, 1, 2, 1; elements with key 1 keep their order (1, −1) and those with key 2 keep theirs (−2, 2): [1, -1, -2, 2].

7.5 Q2. ⌈log₂ 5!⌉ = ⌈log₂ 120⌉ = 7 comparisons in the worst case — and 7 is achievable (merge insertion, Ford–Johnson).

Chapter 8 — Linked Lists

Goal: manipulate linked lists without losing nodes or getting lost — dummy heads, fast and slow pointers (middle, cycles, k-th from the end), in-place reversal (whole list, sublists, k-groups), merging — and use Floyd’s cycle detection on problems that do not look like linked lists at all.

Linked-list problems are rarely about efficiency; they test whether you can rewire pointers correctly. The patterns below reduce that to a few templates and a drawing habit: before changing a next pointer, know which node you will lose access to.

What you will be able to do after this chapter

  • Use a dummy (sentinel) head to remove special cases at the front of a list.
  • Find the middle, the k-th node from the end, and detect cycles (and their entry) with two pointers.
  • Reverse a whole list, a sublist, and every k nodes, in place.
  • Merge sorted lists, and combine patterns (reorder, palindrome check, sort).
  • Recognise implicit linked lists in arrays (functional graphs) and apply Floyd’s algorithm.

Topic 8A — Tools

Unit 8.1 — Nodes, helpers, and the dummy head

One-line summary: A dummy head — a node placed before the real head — makes inserting or deleting at the front identical to doing it anywhere else; return dummy.next at the end.

# file: ../lib/linked.py
"""Linked-list node and helpers used throughout the book."""
class ListNode:
    __slots__ = ("val", "next")
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next

def from_list(values):
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    for v in values:
        tail.next = ListNode(v)
        tail = tail.next
    return dummy.next

def to_list(head, limit=10_000):
    out = []
    while head and len(out) < limit:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out
# file: basics.py
from check import stress, rand_list
from linked import ListNode, from_list, to_list

def remove_value(head, val):                       # delete every node with this value
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    prev = dummy
    while prev.next:
        if prev.next.val == val:
            prev.next = prev.next.next             # unlink; prev stays, its next is new
        else:
            prev = prev.next
    return dummy.next

def remove_duplicates_sorted_all(head):            # sorted list: remove ALL values that appear more than once
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    prev = dummy
    while prev.next:
        cur = prev.next
        if cur.next and cur.next.val == cur.val:
            while cur.next and cur.next.val == cur.val:
                cur = cur.next
            prev.next = cur.next                   # skip the whole run
        else:
            prev = cur
    return dummy.next

print(stress(lambda a, v: to_list(remove_value(from_list(a), v)), lambda a, v: [x for x in a if x != v],
             lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 3), rng.randint(0, 3))))
print(stress(lambda a: to_list(remove_duplicates_sorted_all(from_list(a))), lambda a: [x for x in a if a.count(x) == 1],
             lambda rng: (sorted(rand_list(rng, 0, 4, 10)),)))

Why the dummy head removes special cases

Without a dummy, deleting the first node changes head, so every deletion routine needs an if for it — and that branch is where most linked-list bugs live. A dummy node placed before the head makes every real node have a predecessor; the answer is dummy.next. The cost is one extra allocation, which is nothing.

One more problem: add two numbers stored as lists

Digits are stored in reverse order (least significant first), one per node. Walk both lists together with a carry; the dummy head collects the result without special-casing the first digit, and the loop continues while either list or the carry is non-empty.

# file: add_lists.py
from check import stress

class Node:
    __slots__ = ("val", "next")
    def __init__(self, val, nxt=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, nxt

def from_digits(n):
    dummy = tail = Node(0)
    for ch in reversed(str(n)):
        tail.next = Node(int(ch))
        tail = tail.next
    return dummy.next

def to_int(head):
    digits = []
    while head:
        digits.append(str(head.val))
        head = head.next
    return int("".join(reversed(digits)))

def add(a, b):
    dummy = tail = Node(0)
    carry = 0
    while a or b or carry:
        s = carry + (a.val if a else 0) + (b.val if b else 0)
        carry, digit = divmod(s, 10)
        tail.next = Node(digit)
        tail = tail.next
        a = a.next if a else None
        b = b.next if b else None
    return dummy.next

print(to_int(add(from_digits(342), from_digits(465))), to_int(add(from_digits(9999), from_digits(1))))
print(stress(lambda x, y: to_int(add(from_digits(x), from_digits(y))), lambda x, y: x + y,
             lambda rng: (rng.randint(0, 10 ** rng.randint(1, 12)), rng.randint(0, 10 ** rng.randint(1, 12)))))

Topic 8B — Fast and slow pointers

Unit 8.2 — Middle, k-th from the end, and cycles

One-line summary: Move slow one step and fast two steps: when fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle; if they ever meet, there is a cycle (Floyd’s tortoise and hare). To find the cycle’s entry, restart one pointer at the head and move both one step at a time — they meet at the entry. For the k-th node from the end, give one pointer a head start of k.

Why the entry trick works: let the distance from head to entry be μ and the cycle length λ. When they meet, slow has walked μ + x and fast 2(μ + x), and the difference μ + x is a multiple of λ. So walking μ more steps from the meeting point lands on x + μ ≡ 0 (mod λ) past the entry — exactly the entry — at the same moment a pointer from the head arrives there.

# file: fast_slow.py
from check import stress, rand_list
from linked import ListNode, from_list, to_list

def middle(head):                                  # second middle for even lengths
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
    return slow

def kth_from_end(head, k):
    lead = trail = head
    for _ in range(k):
        lead = lead.next
    while lead:
        lead, trail = lead.next, trail.next
    return trail

def cycle_entry(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:                           # met inside the cycle
            p = head
            while p is not slow:
                p, slow = p.next, slow.next
            return p
    return None

def build_with_cycle(values, pos):                 # tail links to node at index pos (or no cycle if pos < 0)
    nodes = [ListNode(v) for v in values]
    for a, b in zip(nodes, nodes[1:]):
        a.next = b
    if pos >= 0:
        nodes[-1].next = nodes[pos]
    return nodes[0], nodes

def cycle_case(values, pos):
    head, nodes = build_with_cycle(values, pos)
    e = cycle_entry(head)
    return None if e is None else nodes.index(e)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(stress(lambda a: middle(from_list(a)).val, lambda a: a[len(a) // 2], lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 9, 9, 1),)))
    print(stress(lambda a, k: kth_from_end(from_list(a), k).val, lambda a, k: a[-k],
                 lambda rng: ((a := rand_list(rng, 0, 9, 9, 1)), rng.randint(1, len(a)))))
    print(stress(cycle_case, lambda v, pos: pos if pos >= 0 else None,
                 lambda rng: ((v := list(range(rng.randint(1, 9)))), rng.randint(-1, len(v) - 1))))

Deep & Tricky

DT-15. Floyd’s algorithm works on any function f from a finite set to itself: the sequence x, f(x), f(f(x)), … is a “rho”-shaped linked list. (Mathematics: functional graphs) “Find the duplicate number in an array of n+1 integers in [1, n] without modifying it and with O(1) memory” becomes cycle detection on i → a[i]: index 0 is never a value, so it is a tail outside the cycle, and the duplicate value is exactly where two arrows enter the same node — the cycle entry. The same idea underlies Pollard’s rho factorisation and detecting cycles in pseudo-random generators.

# file: find_duplicate.py
from check import stress

def find_duplicate(a):                              # n+1 values in [1, n]; exactly one value repeats (possibly many times)
    slow = fast = 0
    while True:
        slow, fast = a[slow], a[a[fast]]
        if slow == fast:
            break
    p = 0
    while p != slow:
        p, slow = a[p], a[slow]
    return p

def gen(rng):
    n = rng.randint(1, 8)
    dup = rng.randint(1, n)
    others = rng.sample([v for v in range(1, n + 1) if v != dup], rng.randint(0, n - 1))
    a = others + [dup] * (n + 1 - len(others))
    rng.shuffle(a)
    return (a,)

print(stress(find_duplicate, lambda a: next(x for x in a if a.count(x) > 1), gen))

Topic 8C — Reversal and merging

Unit 8.3 — Reversing in place

One-line summary: Walk the list with prev, cur; at each step save nxt = cur.next, point cur.next = prev, then advance. To reverse a sublist from position m to n, stop before it, reverse n − m + 1 nodes, and reconnect both ends. To reverse every k nodes, repeat the sublist reversal while at least k nodes remain.

# file: reverse.py
from check import stress, rand_list
from linked import ListNode, from_list, to_list

def reverse(head):
    prev, cur = None, head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next                             # save before overwriting
        cur.next = prev
        prev, cur = cur, nxt
    return prev

def reverse_between(head, m, n):                   # 1-based positions m..n inclusive
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    before = dummy
    for _ in range(m - 1):
        before = before.next
    first = before.next                            # will become the last of the reversed part
    prev, cur = None, first
    for _ in range(n - m + 1):
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev, cur = cur, nxt
    before.next = prev                             # reconnect: front -> new first
    first.next = cur                               # old first -> rest
    return dummy.next

def reverse_k_group(head, k):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    before = dummy
    while True:
        check = before
        for _ in range(k):                          # are there k nodes left?
            check = check.next
            if check is None:
                return dummy.next
        first, prev, cur = before.next, None, before.next
        for _ in range(k):
            nxt = cur.next
            cur.next = prev
            prev, cur = cur, nxt
        before.next, first.next = prev, cur
        before = first

def rev_k_brute(a, k):
    out = []
    for i in range(0, len(a), k):
        chunk = a[i:i + k]
        out += chunk[::-1] if len(chunk) == k else chunk
    return out

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(stress(lambda a: to_list(reverse(from_list(a))), lambda a: a[::-1], lambda rng: (rand_list(rng),)))
    print(stress(lambda a, m, n: to_list(reverse_between(from_list(a), m, n)), lambda a, m, n: a[:m - 1] + a[m - 1:n][::-1] + a[n:],
                 lambda rng: ((a := rand_list(rng, 0, 9, 9, 1)), (m := rng.randint(1, len(a))), rng.randint(m, len(a)))))
    print(stress(lambda a, k: to_list(reverse_k_group(from_list(a), k)), rev_k_brute, lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 9, 10), rng.randint(1, 4))))

Trace the three pointers once

Reversing 1 → 2 → 3 keeps prev (the reversed part), cur (the next node to move), and saves nxt before breaking the link:

step prev cur list state
start None 1 1→2→3
move 1 1 2 None←1 2→3
move 2 2 3 None←1←2 3
move 3 3 None None←1←2←3

The new head is prev. Saving cur.next before overwriting it is the whole trick; forgetting it loses the rest of the list.

One more problem: rotate a list right by k

Find the length and the tail in one pass, connect the tail to the head to make a ring, then cut it n − k % n steps from the old head.

# file: rotate_list.py
from check import stress, rand_list

class Node:
    __slots__ = ("val", "next")
    def __init__(self, val, nxt=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, nxt

def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = Node(v, head)
    return head

def to_list(h):
    out = []
    while h:
        out.append(h.val)
        h = h.next
    return out

def rotate_right(head, k):
    if not head:
        return None
    n, tail = 1, head
    while tail.next:
        tail, n = tail.next, n + 1
    k %= n
    if k == 0:
        return head
    tail.next = head                           # make a ring
    new_tail = head
    for _ in range(n - k - 1):
        new_tail = new_tail.next
    new_head = new_tail.next
    new_tail.next = None                       # cut the ring
    return new_head

def brute(vals, k):
    if not vals:
        return []
    k %= len(vals)
    return vals[-k:] + vals[:-k] if k else vals

print(to_list(rotate_right(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 2)), to_list(rotate_right(build([0, 1, 2]), 4)))
print(stress(lambda v, k: to_list(rotate_right(build(v), k)), brute, lambda rng: (rand_list(rng), rng.randint(0, 20))))

Unit 8.4 — Merging and combined list problems

One-line summary: Merge two sorted lists with a dummy head and a tail pointer, always attaching the smaller head. Many “hard” list problems are compositions of the basic moves: reorder L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln−1 … = find middle + reverse second half + interleave; palindrome list in O(1) space = find middle + reverse second half + compare (+ restore).

# file: combined.py
from check import stress, rand_list
from linked import ListNode, from_list, to_list
from fast_slow import middle
from reverse import reverse

def merge(a, b):
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    while a and b:
        if a.val <= b.val:
            tail.next, a = a, a.next
        else:
            tail.next, b = b, b.next
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = a or b
    return dummy.next

def reorder(head):
    if not head or not head.next:
        return head
    slow, fast = head, head.next                    # slow ends at the end of the first half
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
    second = reverse(slow.next)
    slow.next = None
    first = head
    while second:                                   # interleave
        n1, n2 = first.next, second.next
        first.next, second.next = second, n1
        first, second = n1, n2
    return head

def reorder_brute(a):
    out, i, j = [], 0, len(a) - 1
    while i <= j:
        out.append(a[i])
        if i != j:
            out.append(a[j])
        i, j = i + 1, j - 1
    return out

def is_palindrome(head):
    if not head:
        return True
    slow, fast = head, head.next
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
    second = reverse(slow.next)
    p, q, ok = head, second, True
    while q:
        if p.val != q.val:
            ok = False
            break
        p, q = p.next, q.next
    slow.next = reverse(second)                     # restore the input: good manners for a predicate
    return ok

print(stress(lambda a, b: to_list(merge(from_list(a), from_list(b))), lambda a, b: sorted(a + b),
             lambda rng: (sorted(rand_list(rng)), sorted(rand_list(rng)))))
print(stress(lambda a: to_list(reorder(from_list(a))), reorder_brute, lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 9, 9),)))
def pal_and_restored(a):
    h = from_list(a)
    r = is_palindrome(h)
    return r, to_list(h)
print(stress(pal_and_restored, lambda a: (a == a[::-1], a), lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 1, 7),)))

Pattern

P-9. Draw the pointers before and after every rewiring step, and save next before you overwrite it. (Practice) Nearly every linked-list bug is a lost reference (a next overwritten before it was saved) or a cycle created by forgetting to cut the old link (slow.next = None in reorder). Composition is the other half of the skill: middle, reverse, merge, and interleave are the building blocks of most list problems. Trade-off: converting the list to a Python list, solving, and rebuilding is O(n) extra memory — often acceptable in practice, rarely in an interview that asks for O(1) space.

Mastery check

  1. Predict. In reorder, why does fast start at head.next rather than head? What happens for the list [1, 2] if both start at head?
  2. Predict. Can Floyd’s algorithm return a wrong entry if the cycle includes the head?

Chapter 8 Project — Sorting a linked list in O(n log n) time and O(1) space

Goal: sort a singly linked list in O(n log n) time with O(1) extra memory. Top-down merge sort (split at the middle, recurse, merge) is O(n log n) but uses O(log n) recursion stack; the bottom-up version merges runs of length 1, 2, 4, … in place with only a few pointers — O(1) extra space, and stable.

# file: sortlist/sortlist.py
import random
import time
from check import stress, rand_list
from linked import ListNode, from_list, to_list

def split(head, size):
    """Cut `size` nodes off the front of `head`; return the rest."""
    for _ in range(size - 1):
        if not head:
            return None
        head = head.next
    if not head:
        return None
    rest, head.next = head.next, None
    return rest

def merge_into(tail, a, b):
    """Merge sorted lists a and b after `tail`; return the new tail."""
    while a and b:
        if a.val <= b.val:
            tail.next, a = a, a.next
        else:
            tail.next, b = b, b.next
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = a or b
    while tail.next:
        tail = tail.next
    return tail

def sort_list(head):
    n, p = 0, head
    while p:
        n, p = n + 1, p.next
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    size = 1
    while size < n:
        tail, cur = dummy, dummy.next
        while cur:
            left = cur
            right = split(left, size)
            cur = split(right, size)
            tail = merge_into(tail, left, right)
        size *= 2
    return dummy.next

def stable_check(a):                                  # sort (key, original index) pairs by key, check stability
    head = from_list([(x, i) for i, x in enumerate(a)])
    # compare only keys: wrap values so that <= looks at the key
    class K:
        __slots__ = ("k", "i")
        def __init__(self, p): self.k, self.i = p
        def __le__(self, o): return self.k <= o.k
    p = head
    while p:
        p.val = K(p.val)
        p = p.next
    out = to_list(sort_list(head))
    return [(v.k, v.i) for v in out]

print(stress(lambda a: to_list(sort_list(from_list(a))), sorted, lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, -5, 5, 16),)))
print(stress(stable_check, lambda a: sorted(((x, i) for i, x in enumerate(a)), key=lambda p: p[0]), lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 2, 12),)))
rng = random.Random(1)
vals = [rng.randint(0, 10**9) for _ in range(300_000)]
t = time.perf_counter()
out = to_list(sort_list(from_list(vals)), limit=10**7)
print(f"n=300,000: sorted in {(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000:.0f} ms, correct: {out == sorted(vals)}")

Review checklist

  • Why is the bottom-up version O(1) in extra space while the top-down one is O(log n)?
  • merge_into uses <= — which test would fail with <? (The stability check: equal keys would swap.)
  • Why must split cut the link (head.next = None) rather than just return the next node?

Answers to the Chapter 8 prediction questions

8.4 Q1. With fast = head.next, slow stops at the last node of the first half, so slow.next is the start of the second half and slow.next = None cuts correctly. If both start at head, for [1, 2] slow moves to node 2, the “second half” slow.next is empty, and the cut leaves [1, 2] unchanged — harmless here, but for [1, 2, 3, 4] it produces 1 → 4 → 2 → 3, wrong.

8.4 Q2. No. If the head is on the cycle, μ = 0, the meeting point x satisfies x ≡ 0 (mod λ) after the derivation — i.e. they meet at the head — and the second phase returns immediately with the head, which is the correct entry.

Chapter 9 — Stacks, Queues, and Monotonic Structures

Goal: use stacks for nesting and “most recent unmatched” questions, monotonic stacks for “next greater / previous smaller” and the many problems built on them (histograms, subarray minimums, removing digits), monotonic deques over prefix sums, and stacks for expression parsing.

What you will be able to do after this chapter

  • Match brackets and process nested structures with a stack.
  • Compute next/previous greater or smaller elements for every index in O(n).
  • Solve “largest rectangle in a histogram”, “sum of subarray minimums”, and “remove k digits”.
  • Find the shortest subarray with sum ≥ k even with negative numbers (prefix sums + monotonic deque).
  • Evaluate arithmetic expressions with precedence and parentheses.
  • Build a stack with O(1) minimum and a queue from two stacks.

Topic 9A — Stacks

Unit 9.1 — Matching and nesting

One-line summary: A stack answers “what is the most recent unmatched thing?” — the opening bracket a closing bracket must match, the enclosing context of a nested string, the directory before ...

Recognise it when: brackets, tags, nested encodings (3[a2[c]]), undo, path simplification, “the nearest earlier element that…”.

# file: matching.py
from check import stress, examples

def valid_brackets(s):
    pairs, stack = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}, []
    for ch in s:
        if ch in "([{":
            stack.append(ch)
        elif not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:
            return False
    return not stack

def valid_brackets_brute(s):                     # repeatedly delete adjacent matched pairs
    prev = None
    while prev != s:
        prev, s = s, s.replace("()", "").replace("[]", "").replace("{}", "")
    return s == ""

def decode(s):                                   # "3[a2[c]]" -> "accaccacc"
    stack, cur, num = [], "", 0
    for ch in s:
        if ch.isdigit():
            num = num * 10 + int(ch)
        elif ch == "[":
            stack.append((cur, num))             # save the context we are leaving
            cur, num = "", 0
        elif ch == "]":
            prev, k = stack.pop()
            cur = prev + cur * k
        else:
            cur += ch
    return cur

def simplify_path(path):
    stack = []
    for part in path.split("/"):
        if part == "..":
            if stack:
                stack.pop()
        elif part and part != ".":
            stack.append(part)
    return "/" + "/".join(stack)

print(stress(valid_brackets, valid_brackets_brute, lambda rng: ("".join(rng.choice("()[]{}") for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 8))),)))
print(examples(decode, [(("3[a]2[bc]",), "aaabcbc"), (("3[a2[c]]",), "accaccacc"), (("2[abc]3[cd]ef",), "abcabccdcdcdef"), (("10[a]",), "a" * 10)]))
print(examples(simplify_path, [(("/home//foo/",), "/home/foo"), (("/../",), "/"), (("/a/./b/../../c/",), "/c")]))

Why a stack fits nesting

Brackets close in the reverse order they open — the last opened must be the first closed — which is exactly last-in, first-out. Whenever a problem has “the most recent unmatched thing” (HTML tags, function calls, undo, directories in a path), a stack is the structure. The common bugs: forgetting to check the stack is non-empty before popping (input ")"), and forgetting to check it is empty at the end (input "((").

One more problem: minimum additions to make brackets valid, and longest valid substring

# file: brackets2.py
from check import stress

def min_add_to_make_valid(s):
    open_needed = balance = 0
    for ch in s:
        if ch == "(":
            balance += 1
        elif balance:
            balance -= 1
        else:
            open_needed += 1                 # a ')' with nothing to match
    return open_needed + balance             # plus every '(' left unmatched

def longest_valid(s):
    stack, best = [-1], 0                    # stack of indices; bottom = last unmatched position
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch == "(":
            stack.append(i)
        else:
            stack.pop()
            if not stack:
                stack.append(i)              # unmatched ')': new base
            else:
                best = max(best, i - stack[-1])
    return best

def is_valid(t):
    bal = 0
    for ch in t:
        bal += 1 if ch == "(" else -1
        if bal < 0:
            return False
    return bal == 0

def brute_longest(s):
    return max((j - i for i in range(len(s)) for j in range(i, len(s) + 1) if is_valid(s[i:j])), default=0)

def gen(rng):
    return ("".join(rng.choice("()") for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 12))),)

print(min_add_to_make_valid("())"), min_add_to_make_valid("((("), longest_valid(")()())"), longest_valid("(()"))
print(stress(longest_valid, brute_longest, gen))

The -1 at the bottom of the stack is a sentinel meaning “the valid run starts after this index” — the same idea as the dummy head in linked lists.

Unit 9.2 — Monotonic stacks: next greater element

One-line summary: Scan left to right keeping a stack of indices whose values are decreasing. When a new value x arrives, every index on the stack with a smaller value has just found its next greater element (x) — pop it and record. Each index is pushed and popped once: O(n).

Recognise it when: “next greater/smaller”, “previous greater/smaller”, “how many days until a warmer temperature”, “span”, “visible people in a queue”, or any formula involving “the nearest element to the left/right that is bigger/smaller”.

Four variants, one template:

Want Scan Keep stack Pop while
next greater left → right decreasing a[top] < x (record x for top)
next smaller left → right increasing a[top] > x
previous greater left → right decreasing a[top] <= x (then top is the answer for x)
previous smaller left → right increasing a[top] >= x 
# file: monotonic.py
from check import stress, rand_list

def next_greater(a):                              # value of the next strictly greater element, or -1
    out, stack = [-1] * len(a), []
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        while stack and a[stack[-1]] < x:
            out[stack.pop()] = x                  # x is the first greater element to the right
        stack.append(i)
    return out

def next_greater_brute(a):
    return [next((a[j] for j in range(i + 1, len(a)) if a[j] > a[i]), -1) for i in range(len(a))]

def next_greater_circular(a):                     # wrap around: scan the array twice
    n, out, stack = len(a), [-1] * len(a), []
    for i in range(2 * n):
        x = a[i % n]
        while stack and a[stack[-1]] < x:
            out[stack.pop()] = x
        if i < n:
            stack.append(i)
    return out

def daily_temperatures(t):                        # days to wait for a warmer day
    out, stack = [0] * len(t), []
    for i, x in enumerate(t):
        while stack and t[stack[-1]] < x:
            j = stack.pop()
            out[j] = i - j
        stack.append(i)
    return out

def previous_smaller(a):                          # index of the previous strictly smaller element, or -1
    out, stack = [-1] * len(a), []
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        while stack and a[stack[-1]] >= x:
            stack.pop()
        out[i] = stack[-1] if stack else -1
        stack.append(i)
    return out

print(stress(next_greater, next_greater_brute, lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 5, 10),)))
print(stress(next_greater_circular, lambda a: [next((a[(i + d) % len(a)] for d in range(1, len(a)) if a[(i + d) % len(a)] > a[i]), -1) for i in range(len(a))],
             lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 5, 10),)))
print(stress(daily_temperatures, lambda t: [next((j - i for j in range(i + 1, len(t)) if t[j] > t[i]), 0) for i in range(len(t))],
             lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 30, 35, 10),)))
print(stress(previous_smaller, lambda a: [next((j for j in range(i - 1, -1, -1) if a[j] < a[i]), -1) for i in range(len(a))],
             lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 5, 10),)))

Unit 9.3 — Applications: histogram, subarray minimums, removing digits

One-line summary: The largest rectangle in a histogram has, for each bar, width = (next smaller index) − (previous smaller index) − 1. The sum of the minimums of all subarrays counts, for each element, how many subarrays it is the minimum of: (i − prev_smaller) × (next_smaller − i) — with one side strict and the other non-strict so that equal values are not counted twice. Removing k digits to make the smallest number keeps an increasing stack, popping larger digits while removals remain.

# file: applications.py
from check import stress, rand_list

def largest_rectangle(h):
    stack, best = [], 0                            # increasing heights (indices)
    for i, x in enumerate(h + [0]):                # sentinel 0 flushes the stack at the end
        while stack and h[stack[-1]] >= x:
            height = h[stack.pop()]
            left = stack[-1] if stack else -1      # previous smaller
            best = max(best, height * (i - left - 1))
        stack.append(i)
    return best

def largest_rectangle_brute(h):
    return max([min(h[i:j]) * (j - i) for i in range(len(h)) for j in range(i + 1, len(h) + 1)], default=0)

def sum_subarray_mins(a):
    n = len(a)
    left, right, stack = [0] * n, [0] * n, []
    for i in range(n):                             # previous strictly smaller
        while stack and a[stack[-1]] >= a[i]:
            stack.pop()
        left[i] = stack[-1] if stack else -1
        stack.append(i)
    stack = []
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):                 # next smaller-or-equal: ties go to the leftmost minimum
        while stack and a[stack[-1]] > a[i]:
            stack.pop()
        right[i] = stack[-1] if stack else n
        stack.append(i)
    return sum(a[i] * (i - left[i]) * (right[i] - i) for i in range(n))

def remove_k_digits(num, k):
    stack = []
    for d in num:
        while k and stack and stack[-1] > d:       # a larger digit before a smaller one: remove it
            stack.pop()
            k -= 1
        stack.append(d)
    stack = stack[:len(stack) - k] if k else stack # remaining removals come off the end
    return "".join(stack).lstrip("0") or "0"

def remove_k_brute(num, k):
    from itertools import combinations
    best = None
    for keep in combinations(range(len(num)), len(num) - k):
        s = "".join(num[i] for i in keep).lstrip("0") or "0"
        if best is None or (len(s), s) < (len(best), best):
            best = s
    return best

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(stress(largest_rectangle, largest_rectangle_brute, lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 6, 10),)))
    print(stress(sum_subarray_mins, lambda a: sum(min(a[i:j]) for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(i + 1, len(a) + 1)),
                 lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 1, 4, 10),)))
    print(stress(remove_k_digits, remove_k_brute, lambda rng: ((s := "".join(rng.choice("01239") for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 7)))), rng.randint(0, len(s)))))

Deep & Tricky

DT-16. When counting “subarrays where a[i] is the minimum”, equal values must be broken asymmetrically — strict on one side, non-strict on the other — or subarrays with repeated minimums are counted twice or not at all. (Algorithm invariant) In [2, 2], the subarray [2, 2] has two candidate minimums. Using “previous strictly smaller” and “next smaller-or-equal” assigns it to exactly one of them (the leftmost). Making both comparisons strict counts it twice; both non-strict counts it zero times. The stress test with values in 1..4 — many ties — catches either mistake instantly.

Unit 9.4 — Monotonic deque over prefix sums

One-line summary: The shortest subarray with sum ≥ k, with negative numbers allowed, cannot use a plain window (DT-11). Instead, over prefix sums P, find the closest pair i < j with P[j] − P[i] ≥ k: keep a deque of indices with increasing P. For each j, pop from the front while P[j] − P[front] ≥ k (record; the front can never give a shorter answer later), and pop from the back while P[back] ≥ P[j] (j is a better start: smaller sum and later).

# file: shortest_k.py
from collections import deque
from check import stress, rand_list

def shortest_subarray_at_least(a, k):
    P = [0]
    for x in a:
        P.append(P[-1] + x)
    dq, best = deque(), float("inf")
    for j in range(len(P)):
        while dq and P[j] - P[dq[0]] >= k:
            best = min(best, j - dq.popleft())
        while dq and P[dq[-1]] >= P[j]:
            dq.pop()
        dq.append(j)
    return -1 if best == float("inf") else best

def brute(a, k):
    return min([j - i for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(i + 1, len(a) + 1) if sum(a[i:j]) >= k], default=-1)

print(stress(shortest_subarray_at_least, brute, lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, -5, 5, 10), rng.randint(1, 10))))
$ PYTHONPATH=../lib python3 shortest_k.py
2000 stress tests ok

Why the deque holds increasing prefix sums

For a right end j, we want the latest i < j with P[j] − P[i] ≥ k. Two facts prune candidates. If P[i] ≥ P[j] for an earlier i, then i is never better than j as a start (it is earlier and has a larger prefix), so it can be dropped from the back — the deque stays increasing. And once i has served as a start for some j, any later j would give a longer subarray, so i can be dropped from the front. Each index enters and leaves once: O(n).

One more problem: maximum of y_i + y_j + |x_i − x_j| with x_j − x_i ≤ k

With sorted x, the expression for i < j is (y_i − x_i) + (y_j + x_j): keep a decreasing deque of y_i − x_i over the window x_j − x_i ≤ k.

# file: max_equation.py
from collections import deque
from check import stress

def max_value(points, k):
    dq, best = deque(), float("-inf")           # (y - x, x), decreasing in y - x
    for x, y in points:
        while dq and x - dq[0][1] > k:
            dq.popleft()                        # too far to the left
        if dq:
            best = max(best, dq[0][0] + y + x)
        while dq and dq[-1][0] <= y - x:
            dq.pop()                            # dominated by the new point
        dq.append((y - x, x))
    return best

def brute(points, k):
    return max((yi + yj + xj - xi for i, (xi, yi) in enumerate(points) for xj, yj in points[i + 1:] if xj - xi <= k),
               default=float("-inf"))

def gen(rng):
    xs = sorted(rng.sample(range(0, 20), rng.randint(2, 8)))
    return [(x, rng.randint(-5, 5)) for x in xs], rng.randint(1, 6)

print(max_value([(1, 3), (2, 0), (5, 10), (6, -10)], 1))
print(stress(max_value, brute, gen))

Topic 9B — Expressions and design

Unit 9.5 — Evaluating expressions

One-line summary: With precedence, use two stacks (operands and operators): push numbers; before pushing an operator, apply every operator on the stack with greater or equal precedence (left-associative); on ( push, on ) apply until (. Alternatively, write a recursive-descent parser with one function per precedence level — the more extensible approach.

# file: calculator.py
import operator
import random
from check import stress

OPS = {"+": (1, operator.add), "-": (1, operator.sub), "*": (2, operator.mul), "/": (2, lambda a, b: int(a / b))}

def calculate(s):
    """Integers, + - * /, parentheses, unary minus. Division truncates toward zero."""
    nums, ops = [], []
    def apply():
        b, a = nums.pop(), nums.pop()
        nums.append(OPS[ops.pop()][1](a, b))
    i, expect_operand = 0, True
    while i < len(s):
        ch = s[i]
        if ch == " ":
            i += 1
            continue
        if ch.isdigit():
            j = i
            while j < len(s) and s[j].isdigit():
                j += 1
            nums.append(int(s[i:j]))
            i, expect_operand = j, False
            continue
        if ch == "(":
            ops.append(ch)
        elif ch == ")":
            while ops[-1] != "(":
                apply()
            ops.pop()
            expect_operand = False
            i += 1
            continue
        elif ch == "-" and expect_operand:           # unary minus: rewrite -x as 0 - x
            nums.append(0)
            ops.append("-")
            i += 1
            continue
        else:
            while ops and ops[-1] != "(" and OPS[ops[-1]][0] >= OPS[ch][0]:
                apply()
            ops.append(ch)
        expect_operand = True
        i += 1
    while ops:
        apply()
    return nums[-1]

def random_expr(rng, depth=0):
    if depth > 2 or rng.random() < 0.3:
        return str(rng.randint(0, 9))
    kind = rng.random()
    if kind < 0.15:
        return "(" + random_expr(rng, depth + 1) + ")"
    op = rng.choice("+-*")
    return random_expr(rng, depth + 1) + f" {op} " + random_expr(rng, depth + 1)

def reference(s):                                    # Python evaluates + - * with the same rules
    return eval(s)

print(stress(calculate, reference, lambda rng: (random_expr(rng),)))
print(calculate("2*(3+4) - -5"), calculate("14/3*2"), calculate("-(2+3)*2"))

Precedence with two stacks, in one sentence

Push numbers to one stack and operators to another; before pushing an operator, first apply every operator on the stack with higher or equal precedence (equal, because - and / are left-associative: 8 - 3 - 2 is (8 − 3) − 2). A ( blocks this popping; ) applies everything back to its (. This is Dijkstra’s shunting-yard algorithm, and it extends to any set of binary operators by giving each a precedence number.

One more problem: evaluate Reverse Polish Notation

RPN (postfix) has no precedence and no parentheses — which is why compilers and calculators convert to it. Evaluation is a single stack. Note the division rule most problems require: truncate toward zero, which Python’s // does not do for negative results.

# file: rpn.py
from check import stress

def eval_rpn(tokens):
    st = []
    for t in tokens:
        if t in "+-*/" and len(t) == 1:
            b, a = st.pop(), st.pop()                 # order matters for - and /
            if t == "+": st.append(a + b)
            elif t == "-": st.append(a - b)
            elif t == "*": st.append(a * b)
            else: st.append(int(a / b))              # truncate toward zero; not a // b
        else:
            st.append(int(t))
    return st[0]

def to_rpn(rng, depth=0):
    if depth > 2 or rng.random() < 0.3:
        return [str(rng.randint(-9, 9))], None
    left, _ = to_rpn(rng, depth + 1)
    right, _ = to_rpn(rng, depth + 1)
    return left + right + [rng.choice("+-*")], None

def brute(tokens):
    st = []
    for t in tokens:
        if t in "+-*":
            b, a = st.pop(), st.pop()
            st.append(eval(f"({a}){t}({b})"))
        else:
            st.append(int(t))
    return st[0]

print(eval_rpn(["2", "1", "+", "3", "*"]), eval_rpn(["4", "13", "5", "/", "+"]), eval_rpn(["-7", "2", "/"]), -7 // 2)
print(stress(eval_rpn, brute, lambda rng: (to_rpn(rng)[0],)))

-7 / 2 truncated toward zero is -3; Python’s floor division gives -4 — the bug that fails the hidden test case with a negative operand.

Unit 9.6 — Min stack and queue from two stacks

One-line summary: A min stack stores, with each element, the minimum of the stack at the time it was pushed — so getMin is O(1). A queue from two stacks pushes onto inbox and pops from outbox, refilling outbox (reversing inbox) only when it is empty: each element moves at most twice, so operations are amortised O(1).

# file: design.py
import random
from collections import deque

class MinStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.s = []                                  # (value, min so far)
    def push(self, x):
        self.s.append((x, min(x, self.s[-1][1]) if self.s else x))
    def pop(self):
        return self.s.pop()[0]
    def get_min(self):
        return self.s[-1][1]

class TwoStackQueue:
    def __init__(self):
        self.inbox, self.outbox = [], []
    def push(self, x):
        self.inbox.append(x)
    def pop(self):
        if not self.outbox:
            while self.inbox:
                self.outbox.append(self.inbox.pop())  # reverse once: oldest on top
        return self.outbox.pop()
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.inbox) + len(self.outbox)

rng = random.Random(3)
ms, ref = MinStack(), []
q, qref = TwoStackQueue(), deque()
for _ in range(20_000):
    if ref and rng.random() < 0.45:
        assert ms.pop() == ref.pop()
    else:
        x = rng.randint(-1000, 1000)
        ms.push(x); ref.append(x)
    if ref:
        assert ms.get_min() == min(ref)
    if qref and rng.random() < 0.5:
        assert q.pop() == qref.popleft()
    else:
        x = rng.random()
        q.push(x); qref.append(x)
print("20,000 random operations: MinStack and TwoStackQueue agree with reference implementations")

Pattern

P-10. “Nearest element to the left/right that is greater/smaller” means a monotonic stack; “best element within a sliding range” means a monotonic deque. (Practice) Both keep only the candidates that can still be an answer, discarding elements that are dominated (older and worse). Write the stack’s monotonic direction and the pop condition explicitly, and decide how ties are broken. Many hard-looking problems — histograms, subarray-minimum sums, “remove k digits”, “132 pattern”, “car fleet” — are a single monotonic stack once you see which “nearest” relation they depend on. Trade-off: monotonic stacks answer “nearest” queries for all indices offline in one pass; for arbitrary range queries online, use a sparse table or segment tree (Chapters 18–19).

Mastery check

  1. Predict. For largest_rectangle([2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]), which bar produces the answer, and what is it?
  2. Predict. In remove_k_digits("10200", 1), what does the stack contain before stripping zeros, and what is returned?

Chapter 9 Project — Maximal rectangle of 1s in a binary matrix

Goal: find the area of the largest rectangle containing only 1s in an R × C binary matrix. Combine: for each row, compute a histogram of consecutive 1s ending at that row in each column; the largest rectangle whose bottom edge is on that row is the largest rectangle in that histogram (Unit 9.3). Total O(R·C).

# file: maximal/maximal.py
import random
import time
from check import stress
from applications import largest_rectangle

def maximal_rectangle(grid):
    if not grid:
        return 0
    heights = [0] * len(grid[0])
    best = 0
    for row in grid:
        for j, cell in enumerate(row):
            heights[j] = heights[j] + 1 if cell else 0    # 1s stacked above, ending at this row
        best = max(best, largest_rectangle(heights))
    return best

def maximal_brute(grid):
    R, C = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    best = 0
    for r1 in range(R):
        for r2 in range(r1, R):
            for c1 in range(C):
                for c2 in range(c1, C):
                    if all(grid[i][j] for i in range(r1, r2 + 1) for j in range(c1, c2 + 1)):
                        best = max(best, (r2 - r1 + 1) * (c2 - c1 + 1))
    return best

def gen(rng):
    R, C = rng.randint(1, 5), rng.randint(1, 5)
    return ([[int(rng.random() < 0.7) for _ in range(C)] for _ in range(R)],)

print(stress(maximal_rectangle, maximal_brute, gen))
rng = random.Random(4)
g = [[int(rng.random() < 0.9) for _ in range(500)] for _ in range(500)]
t = time.perf_counter()
print(f"500x500 matrix (90% ones): largest rectangle {maximal_rectangle(g)} in {(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000:.0f} ms")

The reduction is the same move as Chapter 2’s project — fix one dimension (the bottom row), reduce to a 1-D problem — but the 1-D problem here is solved with a monotonic stack instead of Kadane’s algorithm, and the per-row histogram is updated incrementally in O(C) rather than recomputed.

Review checklist

  • Why does the histogram reset to 0 at a 0 cell instead of keeping the height above it?
  • What changes to find the largest square of 1s? (A simpler DP: Chapter 29.)
  • How would you count all all-ones submatrices? (Per row, a monotonic stack summing rectangle counts — a cousin of sum_subarray_mins.)

Answers to the Chapter 9 prediction questions

9.6 Q1. The bars of height 5 and 6 (indices 2–3) form a rectangle of height 5 and width 2: area 10. It is recorded when the bar of height 5 is popped by the 2 at index 4: its previous smaller is index 1, so width = 4 − 1 − 1 = 2.

9.6 Q2. Processing 1, then 0 pops 1 (k becomes 0), so the stack is 0 2 0 0 → "0200"; stripping leading zeros gives "200".

Chapter 10 — Recursion and Backtracking

Goal: think recursively with confidence (trust the contract, define the base case), enumerate subsets, permutations, and combinations with one template, prune search trees aggressively, and solve constraint problems (N-Queens, Sudoku, word search) by backtracking.

What you will be able to do after this chapter

  • Write a recursive function from its contract, not by tracing every call.
  • Generate subsets, combinations, and permutations — with and without duplicates — from one “choose / explore / un-choose” template.
  • Prune: sort first, stop when a bound fails, skip equivalent branches.
  • Solve constraint-satisfaction problems with incremental state (sets or bitmasks) instead of re-checking from scratch.
  • Estimate the size of a search tree before writing it.

Topic 10A — Recursion

Unit 10.1 — The recursive leap of faith

One-line summary: To write f(problem), assume f already works on smaller problems, express the answer in terms of those, and handle the smallest problems (the base cases) directly. Do not trace the recursion in your head; check that every call is smaller and that every path reaches a base case.

Three questions for every recursive function:

  1. What exactly does f return? (The contract, in one sentence.)
  2. Which inputs are so small that the answer is obvious? (Base cases.)
  3. How does the answer for x combine answers for smaller inputs? (The recurrence.)
# file: recursion.py
import sys
from check import stress, rand_list, examples

def power(x, n):                                   # x**n in O(log n) multiplications
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    half = power(x, n // 2)                        # trust: correct for n // 2
    return half * half * (x if n % 2 else 1)

def flatten(nested):                               # contract: list of all integers, in order
    out = []
    for item in nested:
        if isinstance(item, list):
            out.extend(flatten(item))              # trust it for the smaller list
        else:
            out.append(item)
    return out

def hanoi(n, src="A", dst="C", via="B", moves=None):
    """Move n disks from src to dst. Contract: returns the list of moves."""
    moves = [] if moves is None else moves
    if n:
        hanoi(n - 1, src, via, dst, moves)         # clear the top n-1 out of the way
        moves.append((src, dst))                   # move the largest disk
        hanoi(n - 1, via, dst, src, moves)         # put the n-1 back on top
    return moves

def check_hanoi(n):
    pegs = {"A": list(range(n, 0, -1)), "B": [], "C": []}
    for s, d in hanoi(n):
        disk = pegs[s].pop()
        assert not pegs[d] or pegs[d][-1] > disk   # never a larger disk on a smaller one
        pegs[d].append(disk)
    return pegs["C"] == list(range(n, 0, -1)), len(hanoi(n))

print(stress(power, lambda x, n: x ** n, lambda rng: (rng.randint(-3, 3), rng.randint(0, 20))))
print(examples(flatten, [(([1, [2, [3, [4]], 5], [], [[6]]],), [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])]))
print([check_hanoi(n) for n in range(1, 8)])
print("default recursion limit:", sys.getrecursionlimit())

The Tower of Hanoi needs exactly 2ⁿ − 1 moves: T(n) = 2T(n − 1) + 1. Recursion makes that obvious; an iterative solution hides it.

Deep & Tricky

DT-17. Python’s default recursion limit (1000) is a guard, not a stack size; raising it with sys.setrecursionlimit can turn a clean RecursionError into a hard crash of the interpreter. (CPython documentation, sys.setrecursionlimit) Each Python frame also uses C stack in CPython; set the limit far higher than the thread’s C stack can support and deep recursion segfaults. Safe options for depth beyond a few thousand: convert to an explicit stack (Chapters 13 and 21), or run the recursion in a threading.Thread after threading.stack_size(…) raises the C stack. In an interview, mention the limit whenever recursion depth equals n (e.g. DFS on a 10⁵-node path).

Topic 10B — Backtracking

Unit 10.2 — Subsets, combinations, permutations

One-line summary: Backtracking is DFS over a tree of partial solutions: choose an option, explore recursively, un-choose (restore state). Subsets: at index i, include or skip. Combinations: choose the next element from start onwards so each set is produced once. Permutations: choose any unused element.

Template:

def backtrack(state):
    if state is a complete solution: record a copy; return
    for option in options(state):        # in an order that allows pruning
        if not feasible(option): continue
        apply(option)                    # choose
        backtrack(state)                 # explore
        undo(option)                     # un-choose
# file: enumerate_.py
from itertools import combinations, permutations
from check import stress, rand_list

def subsets(a):
    out, path = [], []
    def go(i):
        if i == len(a):
            out.append(path[:])                  # copy! path keeps changing
            return
        go(i + 1)                                # skip a[i]
        path.append(a[i]); go(i + 1); path.pop() # take a[i]
    go(0)
    return out

def combine(n, k):                               # all k-subsets of 1..n
    out, path = [], []
    def go(start):
        if len(path) == k:
            out.append(path[:])
            return
        for x in range(start, n - (k - len(path)) + 2):   # prune: leave room for the rest
            path.append(x); go(x + 1); path.pop()
    go(1)
    return out

def permute(a):
    out, path, used = [], [], [False] * len(a)
    def go():
        if len(path) == len(a):
            out.append(path[:])
            return
        for i, x in enumerate(a):
            if not used[i]:
                used[i] = True; path.append(x)
                go()
                path.pop(); used[i] = False
    go()
    return out

print(stress(lambda a: sorted(subsets(a)), lambda a: sorted(list(c) for r in range(len(a) + 1) for c in combinations(a, r)),
             lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 9, 6),), trials=500))
print(stress(combine, lambda n, k: [list(c) for c in combinations(range(1, n + 1), k)],
             lambda rng: ((n := rng.randint(0, 7)), rng.randint(0, n)), trials=500))
print(stress(lambda a: sorted(permute(a)), lambda a: sorted(list(p) for p in permutations(a)), lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 9, 5),), trials=500))
print(len(subsets(list(range(10)))), len(combine(10, 3)), len(permute(list(range(6)))))

Counting the output tells you the complexity

Backtracking that lists every answer can never be faster than the size of the output: there are 2ⁿ subsets, C(n, k) combinations, and n! permutations, and each takes O(n) to copy. So “all subsets of 20 items” is about 20 million operations (fine) and “all permutations of 12 items” is 479 million list copies (too slow in Python). Check the count before writing the code; if the problem only asks how many, look for a formula or a DP instead.

One more problem: letter combinations of a phone number

Each digit offers three or four letters; the tree has one level per digit. The backtrack(state) template applies directly: choose a letter, recurse, undo.

# file: phone_letters.py
from itertools import product
from check import stress

KEYS = {"2": "abc", "3": "def", "4": "ghi", "5": "jkl", "6": "mno", "7": "pqrs", "8": "tuv", "9": "wxyz"}

def letter_combinations(digits):
    if not digits:
        return []
    out, path = [], []
    def backtrack(i):
        if i == len(digits):
            out.append("".join(path))
            return
        for ch in KEYS[digits[i]]:
            path.append(ch)          # choose
            backtrack(i + 1)         # explore
            path.pop()               # undo
    backtrack(0)
    return out

def brute(digits):
    return ["".join(p) for p in product(*(KEYS[d] for d in digits))] if digits else []

print(letter_combinations("23"))
print(stress(letter_combinations, brute, lambda rng: ("".join(rng.choice("23456789") for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 4))),)))

Unit 10.3 — Duplicates and target sums

One-line summary: With duplicate inputs, sort and, at the same depth, skip an element equal to the previous one (i > start and a[i] == a[i-1]) — that branch would produce the same results. For target-sum problems, sort and break as soon as the candidate exceeds the remaining target.

# file: dupes.py
from itertools import combinations, permutations
from check import stress, rand_list

def subsets_with_dup(a):
    a, out, path = sorted(a), [], []
    def go(start):
        out.append(path[:])                       # every node is a subset
        for i in range(start, len(a)):
            if i > start and a[i] == a[i - 1]:    # same value already tried at this depth
                continue
            path.append(a[i]); go(i + 1); path.pop()
    go(0)
    return out

def permute_unique(a):
    a, out, path, used = sorted(a), [], [], [False] * len(a)
    def go():
        if len(path) == len(a):
            out.append(path[:])
            return
        for i in range(len(a)):
            if used[i] or (i and a[i] == a[i - 1] and not used[i - 1]):
                continue                          # use equal values only in left-to-right order
            used[i] = True; path.append(a[i]); go(); path.pop(); used[i] = False
    go()
    return out

def combination_sum(cands, target):               # each candidate unlimited times
    cands, out, path = sorted(set(cands)), [], []
    def go(start, remain):
        if remain == 0:
            out.append(path[:])
            return
        for i in range(start, len(cands)):
            if cands[i] > remain:
                break                             # sorted: every later candidate is bigger too
            path.append(cands[i]); go(i, remain - cands[i]); path.pop()   # i, not i+1: reuse allowed
    go(0, target)
    return out

def combination_sum_brute(cands, target):
    cands = sorted(set(cands))
    out = []
    def go(i, remain, path):
        if remain == 0:
            out.append(path); return
        if i == len(cands) or remain < 0:
            return
        go(i, remain - cands[i], path + [cands[i]])
        go(i + 1, remain, path)
    go(0, target, [])
    return sorted(out)

print(stress(lambda a: sorted(subsets_with_dup(a)), lambda a: sorted(list(c) for c in set(c for r in range(len(a) + 1) for c in combinations(sorted(a), r))),
             lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 1, 3, 7),), trials=500))
print(stress(lambda a: sorted(permute_unique(a)), lambda a: sorted(list(p) for p in set(permutations(a))),
             lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 1, 3, 6),), trials=500))
print(stress(lambda c, t: sorted(combination_sum(c, t)), combination_sum_brute,
             lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 1, 8, 5, 1), rng.randint(1, 15)), trials=500))
