Deep & Tricky

DT-18. In permute_unique, the condition not used[i - 1] (not used[i - 1]) forces equal values to be placed in their original left-to-right order; either condition removes duplicates, but this one prunes at the top of the tree and is much faster. (Algorithm invariant) Among equal values, exactly one ordering of their indices is allowed, so each distinct permutation is generated once. With not used[i-1], a branch that would place the second copy before the first is cut immediately. The variant used[i-1] enforces the reverse order instead but only discovers dead ends deep in the tree. Both pass the stress test; only a profile shows the difference — another reason to reason about why a skip condition is correct rather than copying it.

Unit 10.4 — Constraint search: N-Queens, Sudoku, word search

One-line summary: Keep the constraints as incremental state — sets or bitmasks of used columns and diagonals, used digits per row/column/box, visited cells — so that checking an option is O(1) and undoing it is O(1). Choose the most constrained variable next (fewest options) to shrink the tree.

# file: constraints.py
import time
from check import examples

def n_queens(n):                                     # count solutions with bitmasks
    full = (1 << n) - 1
    def go(cols, d1, d2):
        if cols == full:
            return 1
        count, free = 0, full & ~(cols | d1 | d2)
        while free:
            bit = free & -free                       # lowest free column
            free ^= bit
            count += go(cols | bit, ((d1 | bit) << 1) & full, (d2 | bit) >> 1)
        return count
    return go(0, 0, 0)

def solve_sudoku(board):                             # board: list of 9 strings, '.' empty; returns solved list
    g = [list(r) for r in board]
    rows, cols, boxes = [set() for _ in range(9)], [set() for _ in range(9)], [set() for _ in range(9)]
    empty = []
    for r in range(9):
        for c in range(9):
            if g[r][c] == ".":
                empty.append((r, c))
            else:
                d = g[r][c]
                rows[r].add(d); cols[c].add(d); boxes[r // 3 * 3 + c // 3].add(d)
    def go():
        if not empty:
            return True
        # most constrained cell first
        best = min(range(len(empty)), key=lambda k: 9 - len(rows[empty[k][0]] | cols[empty[k][1]] | boxes[empty[k][0] // 3 * 3 + empty[k][1] // 3]))
        empty[best], empty[-1] = empty[-1], empty[best]
        r, c = empty.pop()
        b = r // 3 * 3 + c // 3
        for d in "123456789":
            if d not in rows[r] and d not in cols[c] and d not in boxes[b]:
                g[r][c] = d; rows[r].add(d); cols[c].add(d); boxes[b].add(d)
                if go():
                    return True
                g[r][c] = "."; rows[r].discard(d); cols[c].discard(d); boxes[b].discard(d)
        empty.append((r, c))
        return False
    return ["".join(r) for r in g] if go() else None

def valid_solution(sol, puzzle):
    ok_given = all(p == "." or p == s for pr, sr in zip(puzzle, sol) for p, s in zip(pr, sr))
    units = [sol[r] for r in range(9)] + ["".join(sol[r][c] for r in range(9)) for c in range(9)]
    units += ["".join(sol[r][c] for r in range(br, br + 3) for c in range(bc, bc + 3)) for br in (0, 3, 6) for bc in (0, 3, 6)]
    return ok_given and all(sorted(u) == list("123456789") for u in units)

def word_search(grid, word):
    R, C = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    def go(r, c, i):
        if i == len(word):
            return True
        if not (0 <= r < R and 0 <= c < C) or grid[r][c] != word[i]:
            return False
        saved, grid[r][c] = grid[r][c], "#"          # mark visited in place
        found = any(go(r + dr, c + dc, i + 1) for dr, dc in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)))
        grid[r][c] = saved                           # un-choose
        return found
    return any(go(r, c, 0) for r in range(R) for c in range(C))

print("N-Queens solutions n=1..10:", [n_queens(n) for n in range(1, 11)])
hard = ["8........", "..36.....", ".7..9.2..", ".5...7...", "....457..", "...1...3.", "..1....68", "..85...1.", ".9....4.."]
t = time.perf_counter()
sol = solve_sudoku(hard)
print(f"hard sudoku solved: {valid_solution(sol, hard)} in {(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000:.0f} ms")
grid = [list("ABCE"), list("SFCS"), list("ADEE")]
print(examples(lambda w: word_search(grid, w), [(("ABCCED",), True), (("SEE",), True), (("ABCB",), False)]))

Pruning order matters more than code speed

Constraint search is fast or slow depending on which choice is tried first. For Sudoku, filling the empty cell with the fewest candidates first (the “minimum remaining values” heuristic) cuts the tree by orders of magnitude compared with filling cells left to right; for N-Queens, bitmasks make each check O(1). When a backtracking solution times out, look first at the order of choices and at checks that could fail earlier, not at micro-optimising the inner loop.

One more problem: palindrome partitioning

List every way to cut a string into pieces that are all palindromes. Prune at once: only recurse after a prefix that is a palindrome. Precomputing is_pal[i][j] with DP makes each check O(1).

# file: pal_partition.py
from itertools import combinations
from check import stress

def partitions(s):
    n = len(s)
    is_pal = [[False] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        for j in range(i, n):
            is_pal[i][j] = s[i] == s[j] and (j - i < 2 or is_pal[i + 1][j - 1])
    out, path = [], []
    def go(i):
        if i == n:
            out.append(list(path))
            return
        for j in range(i, n):
            if is_pal[i][j]:                         # prune: only palindromic prefixes
                path.append(s[i:j + 1])
                go(j + 1)
                path.pop()
    go(0)
    return out

def brute(s):
    res = []
    for k in range(len(s)):
        for cuts in combinations(range(1, len(s)), k):
            bounds = (0,) + cuts + (len(s),)
            parts = [s[a:b] for a, b in zip(bounds, bounds[1:])]
            if all(p == p[::-1] for p in parts):
                res.append(parts)
    return res

print(partitions("aab"))
print(stress(lambda s: sorted(partitions(s)), lambda s: sorted(brute(s)),
             lambda rng: ("".join(rng.choice("ab") for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 8))),)))

Unit 10.5 — Estimating the search tree

One-line summary: Before coding, multiply the branching factor by depth: subsets are 2ⁿ, permutations n!, combinations C(n, k). With n ≤ 20 subsets are fine (10⁶); permutations only up to n ≈ 10 (3.6 × 10⁶). If the estimate is too large, you need pruning, memoisation (Chapter 28), meet-in-the-middle (Chapter 41), or a different algorithm.

Search Leaves Comfortable n in Python
subsets 2ⁿ ≤ 20
permutations n! ≤ 9–10
k-combinations C(n, k) depends: C(30, 5) = 142,506
bitmask DP instead of subsets×perm 2ⁿ·n ≤ 20
meet in the middle 2^(n/2) ≤ 40 
# file: count_nodes.py
import math

def count_nodes_subsets(n):                       # nodes visited by the include/skip recursion
    return 2 ** (n + 1) - 1

def count_nodes_perms(n):                         # sum over depth d of n!/(n-d)!
    return sum(math.perm(n, d) for d in range(n + 1))

for n in (10, 15, 20):
    print(f"subsets n={n}: {count_nodes_subsets(n):>12,} nodes")
for n in (8, 10, 12):
    print(f"perms   n={n}: {count_nodes_perms(n):>12,} nodes")
$ python3 count_nodes.py

subsets n=15:       65,535 nodes
subsets n=20:    2,097,151 nodes
perms   n=8:      109,601 nodes
perms   n=10:    9,864,101 nodes
perms   n=12: 1,302,061,345 nodes

At ~10⁷ simple operations per second in pure Python (Chapter 0), permutations of 12 elements (~1.3 × 10⁹ nodes) are far out of reach without pruning.

Pattern

P-11. Backtracking = choose / explore / un-choose, with state that is cheap to update and undo, and pruning as early (as high in the tree) as possible. (Practice) The main levers, in order: sort so that a break is valid; skip duplicate siblings; keep constraints in sets or bitmasks; choose the most constrained variable first; abandon a branch when a bound shows it cannot beat the best answer found (branch and bound). Always append a copy of the path. Trade-off: backtracking is exponential in the worst case. If subproblems repeat (the same (index, remaining) reached by different paths), you should memoise — that is dynamic programming (Chapter 28).

Mastery check

  1. Predict. What does subsets return if out.append(path) is written instead of out.append(path[:])?
  2. Predict. In combination_sum, what changes if the recursive call is go(i + 1, …)?

Chapter 10 Project — Partition into k equal-sum subsets

Goal: decide whether an array of positive integers can be split into k groups with equal sums (n ≤ 16). This is NP-complete, so the job is to make the search fast with every pruning lever: check total % k, sort descending (big items fail early), fill buckets one at a time, skip a bucket whose current sum equals one already tried (symmetry), and stop if an item does not fit an empty bucket.

# file: partition/partition.py
import random
import time
from check import stress

def can_partition(nums, k):
    total = sum(nums)
    if total % k:
        return False
    target = total // k
    nums = sorted(nums, reverse=True)
    if nums and nums[0] > target:
        return False
    buckets = [0] * k
    def go(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            return True                          # all placed; sums must all be target
        tried = set()
        for b in range(k):
            if buckets[b] in tried or buckets[b] + nums[i] > target:
                continue                         # symmetry: same sum means same subtree
            tried.add(buckets[b])
            buckets[b] += nums[i]
            if go(i + 1):
                return True
            buckets[b] -= nums[i]
        return False
    return go(0)

def brute(nums, k):                              # assign each item a label 0..k-1
    total = sum(nums)
    if total % k:
        return False
    target = total // k
    def go(i, sums):
        if i == len(nums):
            return all(s == target for s in sums)
        for b in range(k):
            sums[b] += nums[i]
            if go(i + 1, sums):
                sums[b] -= nums[i]
                return True
            sums[b] -= nums[i]
        return False
    return go(0, [0] * k)

print(stress(can_partition, brute, lambda rng: ([rng.randint(1, 6) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 7))], rng.randint(1, 4)), trials=800))
def yes_instance(rng, k, per, target):           # k groups of `per` items, each summing to target
    nums = []
    for _ in range(k):
        cuts = sorted(rng.sample(range(1, target), per - 1))
        nums += [b - a for a, b in zip([0] + cuts, cuts + [target])]
    rng.shuffle(nums)
    return nums

rng = random.Random(5)
for k in (2, 4, 8):
    for label, nums in (("planted  ", yes_instance(rng, k, 16 // k, 10_000)),
                        ("perturbed", (lambda v: v[:-1] + [v[-1] + k])(yes_instance(rng, k, 16 // k, 10_000)))):
        t = time.perf_counter()
        r = can_partition(nums, k)
        print(f"n=16, k={k}, {label}: {r} in {(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000:.1f} ms")
$ cd partition && PYTHONPATH=../../lib python3 partition.py
800 stress tests ok
n=16, k=2, planted  : True in 0.1 ms
n=16, k=2, perturbed: True in 0.2 ms
n=16, k=4, planted  : True in 0.4 ms
n=16, k=4, perturbed: False in 2.6 ms
n=16, k=8, planted  : True in 0.0 ms
n=16, k=8, perturbed: False in 0.0 ms

A planted instance is built from k groups with equal sums, so the answer is True. The perturbed one adds k to one item: the total stays divisible, but the planted split is broken, and the search must either find another split (as it does for k = 2) or prove that none exists. When the search must prove “impossible”, it explores the whole pruned tree; the symmetry rule (tried) is what keeps that manageable. The guaranteed-polynomial-in-2ⁿ alternative is a bitmask DP over subsets (Chapter 33), which runs in O(2ⁿ · n) regardless of input.

Review checklist

  • Why is sorting in descending order better than ascending here?
  • Explain why skipping a bucket whose sum is already in tried cannot lose a solution.
  • What is the worst-case size of the search without any pruning? (kⁿ assignments.)

Answers to the Chapter 10 prediction questions

10.5 Q1. Every entry is the same list object, which is empty when the recursion finishes — so the result is 2ⁿ references to [].

10.5 Q2. Each candidate can then be used at most once, so combination_sum([2, 3], 6) would no longer find [2, 2, 2] or [3, 3] and would return [].

Chapter 11 — Bit Manipulation

Goal: read and write the standard bit tricks fluently, use XOR’s algebra for “find the odd one out” problems, represent sets as bitmasks and enumerate subsets and submasks, and know where Python’s unbounded integers differ from fixed-width machine integers.

What you will be able to do after this chapter

  • Test, set, clear, and toggle bits; isolate and remove the lowest set bit; count bits.
  • Solve single-number problems with XOR, including “two numbers appear once” and “every number appears three times except one”.
  • Enumerate all subsets of an n-element set and all submasks of a mask (the 3ⁿ trick).
  • Build a maximum-XOR-pair solver with a greedy bit-by-bit method.
  • Emulate 32-bit signed arithmetic in Python when a problem demands it.

Topic 11A — Tricks

Unit 11.1 — The essential operations

One-line summary: x & (1 << i) tests bit i; | sets, & ~ clears, ^ toggles; x & -x isolates the lowest set bit; x & (x - 1) removes it; x & (x - 1) == 0 tests for a power of two (x > 0).

Expression Meaning Example (x = 0b101100)
x >> i & 1 bit i i = 2 → 1
x \| 1 << i set bit i i = 0 → 0b101101
x & ~(1 << i) clear bit i i = 3 → 0b100100
x ^ 1 << i toggle bit i i = 5 → 0b001100
x & -x lowest set bit 0b000100
x & (x - 1) drop lowest set bit 0b101000
x.bit_length() index of highest bit + 1 6
x.bit_count() (3.10+) number of set bits 3

Why x & -x works: in two’s complement, -x = ~x + 1. Inverting flips every bit; adding 1 carries through the trailing 1s (which were the trailing 0s of x) and stops at x’s lowest set bit. So x and -x agree only at that bit.

# file: tricks.py
from check import stress

def popcount_kernighan(x):                     # one iteration per set bit
    c = 0
    while x:
        x &= x - 1
        c += 1
    return c

def counting_bits(n):                          # popcount of 0..n in O(n): drop the lowest bit
    out = [0] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        out[i] = out[i & (i - 1)] + 1
    return out

def reverse_bits32(x):
    r = 0
    for _ in range(32):
        r = (r << 1) | (x & 1)
        x >>= 1
    return r

x = 0b101100
print(bin(x & -x), bin(x & (x - 1)), x.bit_length(), x.bit_count())
print(stress(popcount_kernighan, lambda x: bin(x).count("1"), lambda rng: (rng.randint(0, 2**40),)))
print(stress(counting_bits, lambda n: [bin(i).count("1") for i in range(n + 1)], lambda rng: (rng.randint(0, 50),)))
print(stress(reverse_bits32, lambda x: int(f"{x:032b}"[::-1], 2), lambda rng: (rng.randint(0, 2**32 - 1),)))
print("is power of two:", [n for n in range(1, 70) if n & (n - 1) == 0])

Deep & Tricky

DT-19. Python integers have unbounded width and behave as if they had infinitely many sign bits: -1 >> 5 == -1, ~5 == -6, and bin(-6) prints -0b110, not a two’s-complement bit pattern. (Python Language Reference, “Binary bitwise operations” and “Shifting operations”) Bitwise operations on negative numbers act on the infinite two’s-complement representation, so identities like x & -x still work, but a loop while x: x >>= 1 never ends for negative x, and problems that assume 32-bit overflow need explicit masking: keep values in x & 0xFFFFFFFF and convert back with x - (1 << 32) if x >> 31 else x. Unit 11.4 uses exactly this to add integers without +.

Unit 11.2 — XOR algebra: finding the odd ones out

One-line summary: XOR is associative and commutative, a ^ a = 0, and a ^ 0 = a. XOR-ing everything cancels pairs. For two unpaired values, XOR everything to get a ^ b, pick any set bit (where a and b differ), and split the numbers into two groups by that bit. For “every value appears three times except one”, count each bit modulo 3.

# file: xor.py
from collections import Counter
from functools import reduce
from operator import xor
from check import stress

def single(a):
    return reduce(xor, a, 0)

def two_singles(a):
    ab = reduce(xor, a, 0)
    bit = ab & -ab                               # a bit where the two singles differ
    x = reduce(xor, (v for v in a if v & bit), 0)
    return sorted((x, ab ^ x))

def single_among_triples(a):                     # 32-bit signed inputs
    result = 0
    for i in range(32):
        if sum(v >> i & 1 for v in a) % 3:
            result |= 1 << i
    return result - (1 << 32) if result >> 31 else result   # sign-correct (DT-19)

def missing_number(a):                           # 0..n with one missing
    return reduce(xor, a, 0) ^ reduce(xor, range(len(a) + 1), 0)

def gen_pairs(rng, singles, times):
    vals = rng.sample(range(-1000, 1000), rng.randint(0, 5) + singles)
    a = [v for v in vals[singles:] for _ in range(times)] + vals[:singles]
    rng.shuffle(a)
    return (a,)

def odd_out(a):
    return sorted(v for v, c in Counter(a).items() if c % 2 == 1 or c == 1)

print(stress(single, lambda a: odd_out(a)[0], lambda rng: gen_pairs(rng, 1, 2)))
print(stress(two_singles, odd_out, lambda rng: gen_pairs(rng, 2, 2)))
print(stress(single_among_triples, lambda a: [v for v, c in Counter(a).items() if c == 1][0], lambda rng: gen_pairs(rng, 1, 3)))
print(stress(missing_number, lambda a: (set(range(len(a) + 1)) - set(a)).pop(),
             lambda rng: ((lambda n, m: [v for v in range(n + 1) if v != m])(*(lambda n: (n, rng.randint(0, n)))(rng.randint(0, 10))),)))

The three facts behind every XOR trick

x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x, and XOR is commutative and associative. So XOR-ing a whole list cancels every value that appears an even number of times, in any order. For “two singles”, the XOR of everything is a ^ b ≠ 0; any set bit of it (the lowest, d & -d) is a bit where a and b differ, and splitting the list by that bit puts them in different halves.

One more problem: the XOR of all subarray XORs, and the prefix-XOR trick

Prefix XOR works like prefix sums: X[j] ^ X[i] is the XOR of a[i..j−1], because the common prefix cancels. “Count subarrays whose XOR is k” is then Unit 2.2’s hash-map pattern with ^ instead of −.

# file: xor_subarrays.py
from collections import Counter
from functools import reduce
from operator import xor
from check import stress, rand_list

def count_xor_k(a, k):
    seen, x, total = Counter({0: 1}), 0, 0
    for v in a:
        x ^= v
        total += seen[x ^ k]                    # earlier prefix p with p ^ x == k
        seen[x] += 1
    return total

def brute(a, k):
    return sum(reduce(xor, a[i:j], 0) == k for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(i + 1, len(a) + 1))

print(count_xor_k([4, 2, 2, 6, 4], 6), count_xor_k([5, 6, 7, 8, 9], 5))
print(stress(count_xor_k, brute, lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 7, max_len=10), rng.randint(0, 7))))

Topic 11B — Bitmasks as sets

Unit 11.3 — Subsets and submasks

One-line summary: An integer mask in [0, 2ⁿ) is a subset of {0, …, n−1}: | is union, & intersection, & ~ difference. Enumerate all submasks of mask with sub = (sub - 1) & mask down to 0. Over all masks, the total number of (mask, submask) pairs is 3ⁿ — each element is in neither, only the mask, or both.

# file: masks.py
from check import stress

def submasks(mask):
    out, sub = [], mask
    while True:
        out.append(sub)
        if sub == 0:
            break
        sub = (sub - 1) & mask                   # next smaller submask
    return out

def subsets_of(a):                               # bitmask enumeration instead of recursion
    n = len(a)
    return [[a[i] for i in range(n) if m >> i & 1] for m in range(1 << n)]

def gosper_next(x):                              # next larger integer with the same popcount
    c = x & -x
    r = x + c
    return (((r ^ x) >> 2) // c) | r

print(stress(lambda m: sorted(submasks(m)), lambda m: [s for s in range(m + 1) if s & m == s], lambda rng: (rng.randint(0, 255),)))
for n in range(1, 11):
    pairs = sum(len(submasks(m)) for m in range(1 << n))
    assert pairs == 3 ** n
print("sum over masks of #submasks == 3^n for n = 1..10")
print(len(subsets_of(list("abcd"))), subsets_of(list("abc")))
x, out = 0b0111, []
while x < 1 << 6:
    out.append(f"{x:06b}")
    x = gosper_next(x)
print(len(out), "6-bit masks with 3 ones, e.g.", out[:4])

Why submask enumeration is O(3ⁿ) in total

sub = (sub - 1) & mask steps through the submasks of mask in decreasing order. Enumerating the submasks of every mask of n bits visits each pair (mask, submask) once; each bit is either outside the mask, in the mask but not the submask, or in both — three choices per bit, so 3ⁿ pairs in total, not 4ⁿ. For n = 15 that is 14 million: feasible. Unit 33.3 uses exactly this for DP over subsets.

One more problem: maximum product of word lengths with no common letters

A 26-bit mask per word turns “do these two words share a letter?” into mask1 & mask2 == 0, one machine operation.

# file: word_masks.py
from check import stress

def max_product(words):
    masks = {}
    for w in words:
        m = 0
        for ch in w:
            m |= 1 << (ord(ch) - 97)
        masks[m] = max(masks.get(m, 0), len(w))          # keep the longest word per letter set
    items = list(masks.items())
    best = 0
    for i, (m1, l1) in enumerate(items):
        for m2, l2 in items[i + 1:]:
            if m1 & m2 == 0:
                best = max(best, l1 * l2)
    return best

def brute(words):
    return max((len(a) * len(b) for i, a in enumerate(words) for b in words[i + 1:] if not set(a) & set(b)), default=0)

def gen(rng):
    return (["".join(rng.choice("abcdef") for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 4))) for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 7))],)

print(max_product(["abcw", "baz", "foo", "bar", "xtfn", "abcdef"]), max_product(["a", "aa", "aaa"]))
print(stress(max_product, brute, gen))

Unit 11.4 — Greedy by bits: maximum XOR, and arithmetic without +

One-line summary: To maximise an XOR, decide bits from the highest down: a 1 in bit k beats any combination of lower bits. For the maximum XOR of two array values, keep a candidate answer and, for each bit, check (with a set of prefixes) whether some pair can achieve the candidate with that bit set. Addition without +: XOR gives the sum without carries, (a & b) << 1 gives the carries; repeat until no carries — with 32-bit masking in Python.

# file: greedy_bits.py
from check import stress, rand_list

def max_xor_pair(a):
    best = 0
    for k in range(max(a).bit_length() - 1, -1, -1):
        want = best | 1 << k
        prefixes = {v >> k for v in a}
        # is there p, q in prefixes with p ^ q == want >> k ?  (p ^ q = t  <=>  q = p ^ t)
        if any((p ^ (want >> k)) in prefixes for p in prefixes):
            best = want
    return best

MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF
def add32(a, b):
    a, b = a & MASK, b & MASK
    while b:
        a, b = (a ^ b) & MASK, ((a & b) << 1) & MASK
    return a - (1 << 32) if a >> 31 else a

print(stress(max_xor_pair, lambda a: max(x ^ y for x in a for y in a), lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 1000, 12, 1),)))
print(stress(add32, lambda a, b: (a + b + 2**31) % 2**32 - 2**31, lambda rng: (rng.randint(-2**31, 2**31 - 1), rng.randint(-2**31, 2**31 - 1))))
print(add32(2**31 - 1, 1), add32(-7, 3))

max_xor_pair is O(n · B) for B bits. Chapter 16 does the same greedy walk on a binary trie, which also answers “maximum XOR with a query value” online.

Pattern

P-12. When a problem says “XOR”, “subsets of n ≤ 20”, “appears twice/three times”, or “power of two”, think bits: cancellation for XOR, bitmask for sets, per-bit counting for modular counts, and high-to-low greedy for maximising XOR. (Practice) Bitmasks turn set operations into single machine instructions and sets of sets into arrays indexed by integers — the foundation of bitmask DP (Chapter 33). Trade-off: bit tricks are compact but opaque; name them (lowbit(x)), comment the identity, and stress-test them, because an off-by-one shift is silent.

Mastery check

  1. Predict. What is 6 & -6, and why?
  2. Predict. How many times does the loop body in submasks(0b1011) run?

Chapter 11 Project — Minimum XOR-sum assignment with a bitmask

Goal: given two arrays a and b of length n ≤ 14, permute b to minimise Σ (aᵢ XOR bₚ₍ᵢ₎). Trying all n! permutations is 8.7 × 10¹⁰ for n = 14. Instead, process a in order and remember only which elements of b are used — a bitmask: best[mask] = minimum cost of matching the first popcount(mask) elements of a to the set mask of b. That is 2ⁿ · n ≈ 230,000 steps — a first taste of bitmask DP.

# file: xorsum/xorsum.py
import random
import time
from itertools import permutations
from check import stress, rand_list

def min_xor_sum(a, b):
    n = len(a)
    INF = float("inf")
    best = [INF] * (1 << n)
    best[0] = 0
    for mask in range(1 << n):
        if best[mask] == INF:
            continue
        i = mask.bit_count()                       # next element of a to match
        if i == n:
            continue
        for j in range(n):
            if not mask >> j & 1:
                nm = mask | 1 << j
                cost = best[mask] + (a[i] ^ b[j])
                if cost < best[nm]:
                    best[nm] = cost
    return best[(1 << n) - 1]

def brute(a, b):
    return min(sum(x ^ y for x, y in zip(a, p)) for p in permutations(b))

def gen(rng):
    n = rng.randint(1, 6)
    return ([rng.randint(0, 31) for _ in range(n)], [rng.randint(0, 31) for _ in range(n)])

print(stress(min_xor_sum, brute, gen, trials=500))
rng = random.Random(6)
a = [rng.randint(0, 10**7) for _ in range(14)]
b = [rng.randint(0, 10**7) for _ in range(14)]
t = time.perf_counter()
r = min_xor_sum(a, b)
print(f"n=14: minimum XOR sum {r} in {(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000:.0f} ms (vs 14! = {__import__('math').factorial(14):,} permutations)")

The key insight is what the state does not need to remember: the order in which b’s elements were used is irrelevant to the future, only the set. Collapsing n! orders into 2ⁿ sets is the whole trick.

Review checklist

  • Why can i be derived from mask instead of being part of the state?
  • How large can n be before 2ⁿ · n is too slow in Python? (About 20.)
  • This is the assignment problem; which polynomial algorithm solves it for large n? (Hungarian algorithm, O(n³) — Chapter 26.)

Answers to the Chapter 11 prediction questions

11.4 Q1. 6 = 0b110, -6 = …11010 in two’s complement; they share only bit 1, so 6 & -6 = 2, the lowest set bit.

11.4 Q2. 0b1011 has 3 set bits, so it has 2³ = 8 submasks (including 0 and itself); the body runs 8 times.

Chapter 12 — Math and Number Theory

Goal: handle the mathematical toolkit that interview and contest problems lean on — gcd and lcm, primes and sieves, modular arithmetic with fast exponentiation and inverses, counting with binomial coefficients, and a few classic identities — with code that is exact (no floating point where integers will do).

What you will be able to do after this chapter

  • Compute gcd, lcm, and solve ax + by = g with the extended Euclidean algorithm.
  • Generate primes with a sieve, factorise with a smallest-prime-factor table, and count divisors.
  • Compute a^b mod m in O(log b), modular inverses, and nCr mod p for many queries.

Topic 12A — Divisibility

Unit 12.1 — gcd, lcm, extended Euclid

One-line summary: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b) and gcd(a, 0) = a — O(log min(a, b)) steps. lcm(a, b) = a // gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to keep numbers small). The extended algorithm also returns x, y with a·x + b·y = gcd(a, b) (Bézout), which gives modular inverses and solves linear Diophantine equations.

# file: gcd.py
import math
from check import stress

def gcd(a, b):
    while b:
        a, b = b, a % b
    return abs(a)

def ext_gcd(a, b):
    """Return (g, x, y) with a*x + b*y == g == gcd(a, b)."""
    if b == 0:
        return (a, 1, 0)
    g, x, y = ext_gcd(b, a % b)                 # b*x + (a % b)*y == g
    return (g, y, x - (a // b) * y)             # since a % b == a - (a//b)*b

def solve_diophantine(a, b, c):                 # one integer solution of a*x + b*y == c, or None
    g, x, y = ext_gcd(a, b)
    if c % g:
        return None
    return (x * (c // g), y * (c // g))

print(stress(gcd, math.gcd, lambda rng: (rng.randint(0, 10**9), rng.randint(0, 10**9))))
def check_ext(a, b):
    g, x, y = ext_gcd(a, b)
    return g == math.gcd(a, b) and a * x + b * y == g
print(stress(check_ext, lambda a, b: True, lambda rng: (rng.randint(0, 10**6), rng.randint(0, 10**6))))
def check_dio(a, b, c):
    s = solve_diophantine(a, b, c)
    return (s is not None and a * s[0] + b * s[1] == c) or (s is None and c % math.gcd(a, b) != 0)
print(stress(check_dio, lambda a, b, c: True, lambda rng: (rng.randint(1, 50), rng.randint(1, 50), rng.randint(0, 200))))
print("lcm(4, 6) =", 4 // gcd(4, 6) * 6, "  math.lcm(4, 6, 10) =", math.lcm(4, 6, 10))

Why Euclid’s algorithm is fast

gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b) because any common divisor of a and b also divides a − qb. After two steps the larger number at least halves (if b ≤ a/2, then a mod b < b ≤ a/2; otherwise a mod b = a − b < a/2), so the number of steps is O(log min(a, b)). The worst case is consecutive Fibonacci numbers, which is Lamé’s theorem from 1844 — the first ever complexity analysis of an algorithm.

One more problem: can you measure exactly z litres with jugs of x and y?

By Bézout’s identity, the amounts you can produce are exactly the multiples of gcd(x, y) up to x + y. A BFS over the states (litres in jug 1, litres in jug 2) confirms it.

# file: jugs.py
from collections import deque
from math import gcd
from check import stress

def can_measure(x, y, z):
    if z > x + y:
        return False
    if z == 0:
        return True
    return z % gcd(x, y) == 0

def bfs(x, y, z):
    seen, q = {(0, 0)}, deque([(0, 0)])
    while q:
        a, b = q.popleft()
        if a + b == z:
            return True
        pour_ab, pour_ba = min(a, y - b), min(b, x - a)
        for nxt in [(x, b), (a, y), (0, b), (a, 0), (a - pour_ab, b + pour_ab), (a + pour_ba, b - pour_ba)]:
            if nxt not in seen:
                seen.add(nxt)
                q.append(nxt)
    return False

print(can_measure(3, 5, 4), can_measure(2, 6, 5), can_measure(1, 2, 3))
print(stress(can_measure, bfs, lambda rng: (rng.randint(1, 12), rng.randint(1, 12), rng.randint(0, 25))))

Unit 12.2 — Primes, sieves, and factorisation

One-line summary: Trial division up to √n tests one number in O(√n). The sieve of Eratosthenes marks all primes up to N in O(N log log N): for each prime p, cross out p², p² + p, … A smallest-prime-factor (SPF) sieve lets you factorise any number ≤ N in O(log N).

# file: primes.py
import time
from check import stress

def is_prime(n):
    if n < 2:
        return False
    i = 2
    while i * i <= n:
        if n % i == 0:
            return False
        i += 1
    return True

def sieve(n):                                   # bytearray: compact and fast
    is_p = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1)
    is_p[0:2] = b"\x00\x00"[: min(2, n + 1)]
    for p in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1):
        if is_p[p]:
            is_p[p * p :: p] = bytes(len(range(p * p, n + 1, p)))   # slice assignment: C speed
    return [i for i in range(n + 1) if is_p[i]]

def spf_table(n):
    spf = list(range(n + 1))
    for p in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1):
        if spf[p] == p:
            for m in range(p * p, n + 1, p):
                if spf[m] == m:
                    spf[m] = p
    return spf

def factorise(x, spf):
    out = {}
    while x > 1:
        p = spf[x]
        out[p] = out.get(p, 0) + 1
        x //= p
    return out

def divisor_count(factors):
    c = 1
    for e in factors.values():
        c *= e + 1                              # each exponent 0..e
    return c

print(stress(sieve, lambda n: [i for i in range(n + 1) if is_prime(i)], lambda rng: (rng.randint(0, 300),), trials=300))
spf = spf_table(10**5)
def factor_ok(x):
    f = factorise(x, spf)
    prod = 1
    for p, e in f.items():
        prod *= p ** e
    return prod == x and all(is_prime(p) for p in f)
print(stress(factor_ok, lambda x: True, lambda rng: (rng.randint(2, 10**5),)))
print(stress(lambda x: divisor_count(factorise(x, spf)), lambda x: sum(x % d == 0 for d in range(1, x + 1)), lambda rng: (rng.randint(2, 3000),), trials=300))
t = time.perf_counter()
ps = sieve(10**7)
print(f"primes below 10^7: {len(ps):,} in {(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000:.0f} ms")

Why the sieve is O(n log log n)

Each prime p crosses out about n / p numbers, starting from p². The sum of 1/p over primes up to n grows like log log n — so slowly that for n = 10⁷ it is about 3. In practice the sieve is limited by memory: a bytearray of 10⁷ entries is 10 MB, and a bit-packed or segmented sieve handles larger ranges.

One more problem: count primes in a range [L, R] with a segmented sieve

When R is large (10¹²) but R − L is small (10⁶), sieve only the window: cross out multiples of each prime up to √R inside [L, R].

# file: segmented.py
import math
from check import stress

def primes_upto(n):
    s = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1)
    s[0:2] = b"\x00\x00"
    for p in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1):
        if s[p]:
            s[p * p::p] = bytes(len(range(p * p, n + 1, p)))
    return [i for i, v in enumerate(s) if v]

def count_primes_range(L, R):
    if R < 2:
        return 0
    L = max(L, 2)
    mark = bytearray([1]) * (R - L + 1)
    for p in primes_upto(math.isqrt(R)):
        start = max(p * p, (L + p - 1) // p * p)       # first multiple of p in [L, R], not p itself
        mark[start - L::p] = bytes(len(range(start, R + 1, p)))
    return sum(mark)

def brute(L, R):
    return sum(1 for n in range(max(L, 2), R + 1) if all(n % d for d in range(2, math.isqrt(n) + 1)))

print(count_primes_range(1, 100), count_primes_range(10 ** 12, 10 ** 12 + 1000))
print(stress(count_primes_range, brute, lambda rng: ((L := rng.randint(0, 300)), L + rng.randint(0, 200))))
$ PYTHONPATH=../lib python3 segmented.py

2000 stress tests ok

Starting at p * p (not L rounded up when that is p itself) is what keeps the prime p from being crossed out when it lies inside the window.

Topic 12B — Modular arithmetic

Unit 12.3 — Fast power, inverses, and nCr mod p

One-line summary: Results “modulo 10⁹ + 7” keep numbers small; add, subtract, and multiply freely mod m, but division needs a modular inverse: for prime p and a ≢ 0, a⁻¹ ≡ a^(p−2) (Fermat’s little theorem) — in Python simply pow(a, -1, p) (3.8+). Precompute factorials and inverse factorials once, then each nCr mod p is O(1).

# file: modular.py
import math
from check import stress

MOD = 10**9 + 7

def power(a, b, m):                             # binary exponentiation, O(log b)
    result, a = 1, a % m
    while b:
        if b & 1:
            result = result * a % m
        a = a * a % m
        b >>= 1
    return result

class Binomial:
    def __init__(self, n, p=MOD):
        self.p = p
        self.fact = [1] * (n + 1)
        for i in range(1, n + 1):
            self.fact[i] = self.fact[i - 1] * i % p
        self.inv = [1] * (n + 1)
        self.inv[n] = pow(self.fact[n], p - 2, p)       # one inverse via Fermat
        for i in range(n, 0, -1):
            self.inv[i - 1] = self.inv[i] * i % p        # then walk down: 1/(i-1)! = i/i!
    def C(self, n, r):
        if r < 0 or r > n:
            return 0
        return self.fact[n] * self.inv[r] % self.p * self.inv[n - r] % self.p

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(stress(power, lambda a, b, m: pow(a, b, m), lambda rng: (rng.randint(0, 10**12), rng.randint(0, 10**12), rng.randint(1, 10**9))))
    print(stress(lambda a: a * pow(a, -1, MOD) % MOD, lambda a: 1, lambda rng: (rng.randint(1, MOD - 1),)))
    B = Binomial(10**5)
    print(stress(B.C, lambda n, r: math.comb(n, r) % MOD if 0 <= r <= n else 0, lambda rng: ((n := rng.randint(0, 2000)), rng.randint(-2, n + 2))))
    print("C(100000, 50000) mod p =", B.C(10**5, 5 * 10**4))
    print("6/4 == 3/2 mod p:", (6 * pow(4, -1, MOD)) % MOD == (3 * pow(2, -1, MOD)) % MOD, "  int(6/4) =", int(6 / 4))

Deep & Tricky

DT-20. Under a modulus, “a / b” is not (a % p) // (b % p) — it is a · b⁻¹ mod p, and the inverse exists only when gcd(b, p) = 1. (Number theory: Fermat’s little theorem; pow with exponent −1 in the Python Library Reference) Once numbers are reduced mod p, integer division is meaningless: 6/4 and 3/2 must be the same residue, and they are with inverses, while int(6/4) is 1. If the modulus is not prime (e.g. 10⁹ — composite), Fermat does not apply and many inverses do not exist; use pow(b, -1, m), which raises ValueError when no inverse exists, or restructure the computation (e.g. Pascal’s triangle instead of factorials). Also: in Python -3 % 7 == 4, but in C, Java, and Go it is −3 — a classic bug when porting.

Unit 12.4 — Counting

One-line summary: Stars and bars: the number of ways to write n as an ordered sum of k non-negative integers is C(n + k − 1, k − 1). Inclusion–exclusion: |A ∪ B ∪ C| = Σ|A| − Σ|A ∩ B| + |A ∩ B ∩ C|. Catalan numbers Cₙ = C(2n, n)/(n + 1) count balanced parentheses, binary tree shapes, monotone lattice paths below the diagonal, and triangulations.

# file: counting.py
import math
from itertools import product
from check import stress

def stars_and_bars(n, k):
    return math.comb(n + k - 1, k - 1)

def count_divisible(n, divisors):               # how many of 1..n are divisible by at least one divisor
    total = 0
    for mask in range(1, 1 << len(divisors)):
        l, bits = 1, 0
        for i, d in enumerate(divisors):
            if mask >> i & 1:
                l, bits = math.lcm(l, d), bits + 1
        total += (n // l) if bits % 2 else -(n // l)     # + for odd-sized intersections
    return total

def catalan(n):
    return math.comb(2 * n, n) // (n + 1)

def balanced(n):                                # brute force: count balanced strings of n pairs
    return sum(1 for s in product("()", repeat=2 * n)
               if all(s[:i].count("(") >= s[:i].count(")") for i in range(2 * n + 1)) and s.count("(") == n)

print(stress(stars_and_bars, lambda n, k: sum(1 for t in product(range(n + 1), repeat=k) if sum(t) == n),
             lambda rng: (rng.randint(0, 6), rng.randint(1, 4)), trials=300))
print(stress(count_divisible, lambda n, ds: sum(any(x % d == 0 for d in ds) for x in range(1, n + 1)),
             lambda rng: (rng.randint(1, 500), rng.sample(range(2, 15), rng.randint(1, 4))), trials=500))
print([catalan(n) for n in range(10)], [balanced(n) for n in range(7)])

Pattern

P-13. Keep arithmetic exact: integers and modular arithmetic for counts, fractions.Fraction or cross-multiplication for ratios, and math.isqrt instead of int(x ** 0.5). (Practice) Floating point fails silently: int((10**16 + 1) ** 0.5) is wrong, comparing slopes dy1/dx1 == dy2/dx2 with floats misclassifies near-collinear points, and large factorials overflow floats. Python’s big integers make exactness cheap. Reduce mod p after every multiplication when a modulus is given (in Python for speed; in fixed-width languages for correctness). Trade-off: big-integer arithmetic gets slower as numbers grow; for huge counts, the modulus keeps them word-sized.

Mastery check

  1. Predict. What does ext_gcd(240, 46) return for g?
  2. Predict. How many ways can 10 identical candies be given to 3 children if each child must get at least one?

Chapter 12 Project — Counting lattice paths around obstacles

Goal: count monotone paths (right/down only) from (0, 0) to (H−1, W−1) on a grid with up to 2,000 blocked cells and H, W up to 10⁵, modulo 10⁹ + 7. A grid DP is 10¹⁰ cells — impossible. Instead: the number of paths between two points is a binomial coefficient, and f[i] = number of paths from the start to obstacle i avoiding all earlier obstacles = paths(start → i) − Σ_{j before i} f[j] · paths(j → i). Sort obstacles by (row, col) and treat the target as a final “obstacle”: O(K²) with O(1) binomials.

# file: lattice/lattice.py
import random
import time
from check import stress
from modular import Binomial, MOD

def count_paths(H, W, blocked, B):
    pts = sorted(set(blocked)) + [(H - 1, W - 1)]
    def ways(r1, c1, r2, c2):
        if r2 < r1 or c2 < c1:
            return 0
        return B.C((r2 - r1) + (c2 - c1), r2 - r1)
    f = []
    for i, (r, c) in enumerate(pts):
        total = ways(0, 0, r, c)
        for j in range(i):
            rj, cj = pts[j]
            total -= f[j] * ways(rj, cj, r, c)           # first blocked cell on the path is j
        f.append(total % MOD)
    return f[-1] if (H - 1, W - 1) not in set(blocked) and (0, 0) not in set(blocked) else 0

def grid_dp(H, W, blocked):
    bl = set(blocked)
    dp = [[0] * W for _ in range(H)]
    for r in range(H):
        for c in range(W):
            if (r, c) in bl:
                continue
            dp[r][c] = 1 if r == c == 0 else ((dp[r - 1][c] if r else 0) + (dp[r][c - 1] if c else 0)) % MOD
    return dp[H - 1][W - 1]

B = Binomial(2 * 10**5 + 10)
def gen(rng):
    H, W = rng.randint(1, 7), rng.randint(1, 7)
    cells = [(r, c) for r in range(H) for c in range(W)]
    return (H, W, rng.sample(cells, rng.randint(0, min(6, len(cells)))))
print(stress(lambda H, W, bl: count_paths(H, W, bl, B), grid_dp, gen))
rng = random.Random(7)
H = W = 10**5
blocked = [(rng.randint(1, H - 2), rng.randint(1, W - 2)) for _ in range(2000)]
t = time.perf_counter()
r = count_paths(H, W, blocked, B)
print(f"H=W=10^5 with 2,000 obstacles: {r} paths (mod p) in {(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000:.0f} ms")

The subtraction is inclusion–exclusion organised by “the first obstacle a path hits”, which makes each bad path counted exactly once. Note % MOD after the subtraction: Python’s % always returns a non-negative result (DT-20), so no extra + MOD is needed — in C or Java it would be.

Review checklist

  • Why must obstacles be sorted by (row, col) before the O(K²) loop?
  • Why is ways zero when the second point is above or to the left of the first?
  • What is the largest factorial needed, and why is the table sized 2 × 10⁵?

Answers to the Chapter 12 prediction questions

12.4 Q1. gcd(240, 46) = 2 (240 = 5·46 + 10, 46 = 4·10 + 6, 10 = 6 + 4, 6 = 4 + 2, 4 = 2·2). The x, y it returns satisfy 240x + 46y = 2.

12.4 Q2. Give each child one candy first, leaving 7 to distribute freely among 3: C(7 + 2, 2) = 36.

Chapter 13 — Binary Trees

Goal: traverse trees in every order, recursively and iteratively; solve tree problems by deciding what each subtree must return to its parent; handle path problems that bend through a node; and serialise, reconstruct, and compare trees.

Most tree problems are one recursive function. The skill is choosing its return value: what does a parent need to know about each child’s subtree? Once that is fixed, the code writes itself.

What you will be able to do after this chapter

  • Traverse in preorder, inorder, postorder, and level order — recursively and with explicit stacks and queues.
  • Solve “bottom-up” problems (height, balance, diameter, maximum path sum) by returning summaries from children.
  • Solve “top-down” problems (root-to-leaf paths, path sums) by passing state down.
  • Find the lowest common ancestor.
  • Serialise and deserialise a tree; rebuild it from preorder + inorder.

Topic 13A — Traversals

Unit 13.1 — Four orders, two styles

One-line summary: Preorder visits node, left, right; inorder left, node, right (sorted order for a BST); postorder left, right, node (children before parent — needed when a node’s answer depends on its children’s); level order visits by depth with a queue. Every recursive traversal has an iterative version with an explicit stack, which avoids the recursion limit (DT-17).

# file: ../lib/tree.py
"""Binary-tree node and helpers (level-order lists with None for gaps, LeetCode style)."""
from collections import deque

class TreeNode:
    __slots__ = ("val", "left", "right")
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def build(values):
    if not values or values[0] is None:
        return None
    it = iter(values)
    root = TreeNode(next(it))
    q = [root]
    for node in q:                                     # a list may grow while we iterate it
        for side in ("left", "right"):
            v = next(it, None)
            if v is not None:
                child = TreeNode(v)
                setattr(node, side, child)
                q.append(child)
    return root

def to_values(root):
    out, q = [], deque([root])
    while q:
        node = q.popleft()
        out.append(node.val if node else None)
        if node:
            q.extend((node.left, node.right))
    while out and out[-1] is None:
        out.pop()
    return out

def random_tree(rng, n, lo=0, hi=9):
    """Random shape with n nodes (insert each node at a random free slot)."""
    if n == 0:
        return None
    root = TreeNode(rng.randint(lo, hi))
    slots = [(root, "left"), (root, "right")]
    for _ in range(n - 1):
        parent, side = slots.pop(rng.randrange(len(slots)))
        child = TreeNode(rng.randint(lo, hi))
        setattr(parent, side, child)
        slots += [(child, "left"), (child, "right")]
    return root
# file: traversals.py
from collections import deque
from check import stress
from tree import TreeNode, build, random_tree

def preorder_rec(root):
    return [root.val] + preorder_rec(root.left) + preorder_rec(root.right) if root else []

def inorder_rec(root):
    return inorder_rec(root.left) + [root.val] + inorder_rec(root.right) if root else []

def postorder_rec(root):
    return postorder_rec(root.left) + postorder_rec(root.right) + [root.val] if root else []

def preorder_it(root):
    out, stack = [], [root] if root else []
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        out.append(node.val)
        if node.right: stack.append(node.right)        # right first so left is popped first
        if node.left: stack.append(node.left)
    return out

def inorder_it(root):
    out, stack, node = [], [], root
    while stack or node:
        while node:                                    # go as far left as possible
            stack.append(node)
            node = node.left
        node = stack.pop()
        out.append(node.val)
        node = node.right
    return out

def postorder_it(root):                                # reverse of (node, right, left) preorder
    out, stack = [], [root] if root else []
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        out.append(node.val)
        if node.left: stack.append(node.left)
        if node.right: stack.append(node.right)
    return out[::-1]

def level_order(root):
    out, q = [], deque([root] if root else [])
    while q:
        level = []
        for _ in range(len(q)):                        # exactly the nodes of this depth
            node = q.popleft()
            level.append(node.val)
            if node.left: q.append(node.left)
            if node.right: q.append(node.right)
        out.append(level)
    return out

if __name__ == "__main__":
    gen = lambda rng: (random_tree(rng, rng.randint(0, 12)),)
    print(stress(preorder_it, preorder_rec, gen))
    print(stress(inorder_it, inorder_rec, gen))
    print(stress(postorder_it, postorder_rec, gen))
    root = build([3, 9, 20, None, None, 15, 7])
    print(preorder_it(root), inorder_it(root), postorder_it(root), level_order(root))

Which traversal to reach for

Pre-order sees a node before its children — use it to copy or serialise a tree, or to pass information down. In-order on a BST gives sorted order. Post-order sees a node after its children — use it whenever a node’s answer depends on its subtrees (heights, sizes, deleting a tree). Level order (BFS) answers “by depth” questions: the right side view, the minimum depth, zigzag printing. Recursion depth equals tree height, so on a degenerate tree of 100,000 nodes Python’s default limit of 1000 is exceeded — the iterative versions exist for that reason.

One more problem: zigzag level order

# file: zigzag.py
from collections import deque
from tree import random_tree
from check import stress

def zigzag(root):
    out, q, left_to_right = [], deque([root] if root else []), True
    while q:
        level = [q.popleft() for _ in range(len(q))]          # exactly one level
        vals = [n.val for n in level]
        out.append(vals if left_to_right else vals[::-1])
        left_to_right = not left_to_right
        for n in level:
            q.extend(c for c in (n.left, n.right) if c)
    return out

def brute(root):
    levels = {}
    def dfs(n, d):
        if n:
            levels.setdefault(d, []).append(n.val)
            dfs(n.left, d + 1)
            dfs(n.right, d + 1)
    dfs(root, 0)
    return [levels[d] if d % 2 == 0 else levels[d][::-1] for d in sorted(levels)]

print(stress(zigzag, brute, lambda rng: (random_tree(rng, rng.randint(0, 12)),)))

range(len(q)) is evaluated once, before the loop body adds children — the standard way to process a queue one level at a time.

Topic 13B — Recursion on trees

Unit 13.2 — Bottom-up: what does a subtree return?

One-line summary: Define f(node) = a summary of the subtree (height, size, sum, “is it balanced and how tall”), computed from f(left) and f(right) in postorder. Many problems need two things from a child — return a tuple, or update a global answer while returning a different value to the parent.

Recognise it when: the answer for a node depends on its whole subtree: height, balance, diameter, maximum path sum, subtree counts, “is this a valid X”.

The bend trick: a path can go up through a node and down the other side. The best path through node = node + best downward from left + best downward from right; but what you return to the parent is only one branch (node + max(left, right)), because a path cannot fork.

# file: bottom_up.py
from check import stress
from tree import TreeNode, random_tree

def is_balanced(root):
    def h(node):                                       # height, or -1 if unbalanced below
        if not node:
            return 0
        l, r = h(node.left), h(node.right)
        if l < 0 or r < 0 or abs(l - r) > 1:
            return -1
        return 1 + max(l, r)
    return h(root) >= 0

def diameter(root):                                    # longest path in edges
    best = 0
    def depth(node):
        nonlocal best
        if not node:
            return 0
        l, r = depth(node.left), depth(node.right)
        best = max(best, l + r)                        # path bending at node
        return 1 + max(l, r)                           # path continuing to parent
    depth(root)
    return best

def max_path_sum(root):                                # any node-to-node path, values may be negative
    best = float("-inf")
    def down(node):                                    # best downward path starting at node
        nonlocal best
        if not node:
            return 0
        l, r = max(down(node.left), 0), max(down(node.right), 0)   # drop negative branches
        best = max(best, node.val + l + r)
        return node.val + max(l, r)
    down(root)
    return best

# --- brute forces: enumerate all paths between pairs of nodes ---
def all_nodes(root):
    return [] if not root else [root] + all_nodes(root.left) + all_nodes(root.right)

def parents(root):
    par, stack = {root: None}, [root]
    while stack:
        n = stack.pop()
        for c in (n.left, n.right):
            if c:
                par[c] = n; stack.append(c)
    return par

def path_between(a, b, par):
    anc, x = [], a
    while x:
        anc.append(x); x = par[x]
    pos = {n: i for i, n in enumerate(anc)}
    tail, y = [], b
    while y not in pos:
        tail.append(y); y = par[y]
    return anc[:pos[y] + 1] + tail[::-1]

def brute_paths(root):
    if not root:
        return []
    par, ns = parents(root), all_nodes(root)
    return [path_between(a, b, par) for a in ns for b in ns]

def height_brute(node):
    return 0 if not node else 1 + max(height_brute(node.left), height_brute(node.right))
def balanced_brute(node):
    return not node or (abs(height_brute(node.left) - height_brute(node.right)) <= 1 and balanced_brute(node.left) and balanced_brute(node.right))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    gen = lambda rng: (random_tree(rng, rng.randint(0, 10), -5, 5),)
    print(stress(is_balanced, balanced_brute, gen))
    print(stress(diameter, lambda r: max((len(p) - 1 for p in brute_paths(r)), default=0), gen))
    print(stress(max_path_sum, lambda r: max(sum(n.val for n in p) for p in brute_paths(r)),
                 lambda rng: (random_tree(rng, rng.randint(1, 10), -5, 5),)))

The question to ask: what must a subtree report to its parent?

Bottom-up problems are solved by deciding what each recursive call returns. For diameter, the parent needs the longest downward path from each child (a height), while the answer itself (a path that bends at a node) is recorded in an outer variable. When the parent needs two things — “is it balanced, and how tall is it” — return a pair, or use a sentinel such as -1 for “already failed”.

One more problem: count subtrees whose values are all equal

Each call returns “is my subtree uni-valued?”; a node is uni-valued when both children are (or missing) and their values match its own. Note that both children must be visited — a short-circuiting and that skips the right subtree would miss counts there.

# file: univalue.py
from tree import random_tree
from check import stress

def count_unival(root):
    count = 0
    def go(n):
        nonlocal count
        if not n:
            return True
        left, right = go(n.left), go(n.right)          # visit both, no short-circuit
        if left and right and all(c is None or c.val == n.val for c in (n.left, n.right)):
            count += 1
            return True
        return False
    go(root)
    return count

def brute(root):
    def vals(n):
        return [] if not n else vals(n.left) + [n.val] + vals(n.right)
    def nodes(n):
        return [] if not n else [n] + nodes(n.left) + nodes(n.right)
    return sum(len(set(vals(n))) == 1 for n in nodes(root))

print(stress(count_unival, brute, lambda rng: (random_tree(rng, rng.randint(0, 12), 0, 1),)))

Unit 13.3 — Top-down: passing state to children

One-line summary: When the answer depends on the path from the root (sum so far, maximum so far, the path itself), pass that state down as parameters. Combine with prefix sums (Unit 2.2) to count any downward path with a given sum in O(n): keep a counter of prefix sums along the current root path, and undo on the way back up.

# file: top_down.py
from collections import Counter
from check import stress
from tree import random_tree

def root_to_leaf_paths(root, target):                  # all root-to-leaf paths summing to target
    out, path = [], []
    def go(node, remain):
        if not node:
            return
        path.append(node.val)
        if not node.left and not node.right and remain == node.val:
            out.append(path[:])
        go(node.left, remain - node.val)
        go(node.right, remain - node.val)
        path.pop()                                     # backtrack
    go(root, target)
    return out

def count_good_nodes(root):                            # nodes not smaller than any ancestor
    def go(node, mx):
        if not node:
            return 0
        good = node.val >= mx
        return good + go(node.left, max(mx, node.val)) + go(node.right, max(mx, node.val))
    return go(root, float("-inf"))

def path_sum_count(root, k):                           # downward paths (any start, any end) with sum k
    seen = Counter({0: 1})
    def go(node, prefix):
        if not node:
            return 0
        prefix += node.val
        found = seen[prefix - k]
        seen[prefix] += 1
        found += go(node.left, prefix) + go(node.right, prefix)
        seen[prefix] -= 1                              # leave this root path: undo
        return found
    return go(root, 0)

def downward_paths(root):                              # brute: all root-paths' contiguous slices
    out = []
    def go(node, path):
        if not node:
            return
        path = path + [node.val]
        out.extend(path[i:] for i in range(len(path)))  # every downward path ending here
        go(node.left, path); go(node.right, path)
    go(root, [])
    return out

def leaf_paths(root):
    if not root:
        return []
    if not root.left and not root.right:
        return [[root.val]]
    return [[root.val] + p for p in leaf_paths(root.left) + leaf_paths(root.right)]

gen = lambda rng: (random_tree(rng, rng.randint(0, 10), -3, 3), rng.randint(-3, 3))
print(stress(lambda r, t: sorted(root_to_leaf_paths(r, t)), lambda r, t: sorted(p for p in leaf_paths(r) if sum(p) == t), gen))
print(stress(path_sum_count, lambda r, k: sum(sum(p) == k for p in downward_paths(r)), gen))
def good_brute(root):                                  # check each node against its whole root path
    def go(node, path):
        if not node:
            return 0
        path = path + [node.val]
        return (node.val >= max(path)) + go(node.left, path) + go(node.right, path)
    return go(root, [])
print(stress(count_good_nodes, good_brute, lambda rng: (random_tree(rng, rng.randint(0, 10)),)))

Top-down or bottom-up?

Pass information down (as parameters) when a node’s answer depends on its ancestors — the path so far, the maximum seen above, the depth. Return information up when it depends on descendants. Many problems need both: path sums with a running total going down and counts coming up. A useful rule: if you find yourself returning a list of every path from a recursive call, you probably wanted a parameter.

One more problem: sum of all root-to-leaf numbers

Each root-to-leaf path spells a number (1 → 2 → 3 is 123). The number so far goes down as a parameter; leaves report it up.

# file: root_leaf_numbers.py
from tree import random_tree
from check import stress

def sum_numbers(root):
    def go(n, acc):
        if not n:
            return 0
        acc = acc * 10 + n.val
        if not n.left and not n.right:
            return acc
        return go(n.left, acc) + go(n.right, acc)
    return go(root, 0)

def brute(root):
    paths = []
    def dfs(n, path):
        if n:
            path = path + str(n.val)
            if not n.left and not n.right:
                paths.append(int(path))
            dfs(n.left, path)
            dfs(n.right, path)
    dfs(root, "")
    return sum(paths)

print(stress(sum_numbers, brute, lambda rng: (random_tree(rng, rng.randint(0, 10)),)))

Unit 13.4 — Lowest common ancestor

One-line summary: The LCA of p and q is the deepest node with both in its subtree. Recursively: return the node if it is p or q; otherwise ask both children; if both return non-null, this node is the LCA; else pass up whichever is non-null. O(n), one pass. (For many LCA queries on a fixed tree, use binary lifting — Chapter 25.)

# file: lca.py
from check import stress
from tree import random_tree
from bottom_up import all_nodes, parents

def lca(root, p, q):
    if root is None or root is p or root is q:
        return root
    l, r = lca(root.left, p, q), lca(root.right, p, q)
    if l and r:
        return root                                    # p and q are on different sides
    return l or r

def lca_brute(root, p, q):
    par = parents(root)
    anc = set()
    while p:
        anc.add(p); p = par[p]
    while q not in anc:
        q = par[q]
    return q

def gen(rng):
    root = random_tree(rng, rng.randint(1, 12))
    ns = all_nodes(root)
    return (root, rng.choice(ns), rng.choice(ns))

print(stress(lca, lca_brute, gen))

Deep & Tricky

DT-21. The one-pass LCA function assumes both p and q are in the tree; if one is missing, it returns the other instead of “no LCA”. (Algorithm invariant) lca stops descending as soon as it finds p, so when q is absent it cannot tell “q is below p” from “q does not exist”. If presence is not guaranteed, count how many of p and q were actually found (a full traversal that does not stop early) and return the LCA only if the count is 2. Read the problem’s guarantees — “p and q exist in the tree” is often stated precisely because of this.

Topic 13C — Building and comparing trees

Unit 13.5 — Serialise, deserialise, and reconstruct

One-line summary: A preorder with null markers uniquely describes a tree and can be parsed back with one recursive function that consumes tokens. Preorder (or postorder) plus inorder of a tree with distinct values also determines it: the first preorder value is the root; its position in inorder splits left and right subtrees.

# file: serialize.py
from check import stress
from tree import random_tree, to_values
from traversals import preorder_rec, inorder_rec

def serialize(root):
    out = []
    def go(node):
        if not node:
            out.append("#"); return
        out.append(str(node.val)); go(node.left); go(node.right)
    go(root)
    return ",".join(out)

def deserialize(s):
    from tree import TreeNode
    tokens = iter(s.split(","))
    def go():
        t = next(tokens)
        if t == "#":
            return None
        node = TreeNode(int(t))
        node.left, node.right = go(), go()             # same order as serialize
        return node
    return go()

def build_pre_in(pre, ino):
    from tree import TreeNode
    pos = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(ino)}            # distinct values
    it = iter(pre)
    def go(lo, hi):                                    # subtree whose inorder is ino[lo:hi]
        if lo >= hi:
            return None
        v = next(it)
        node = TreeNode(v)
        node.left = go(lo, pos[v])
        node.right = go(pos[v] + 1, hi)
        return node
    return go(0, len(ino))

def distinct_tree(rng):
    root = random_tree(rng, rng.randint(0, 12))
    vals = iter(rng.sample(range(100), 12))
    def relabel(n):
        if n:
            n.val = next(vals); relabel(n.left); relabel(n.right)
    relabel(root)
    return root

print(stress(lambda r: to_values(deserialize(serialize(r))), to_values, lambda rng: (random_tree(rng, rng.randint(0, 12), -50, 50),)))
print(stress(lambda r: to_values(build_pre_in(preorder_rec(r), inorder_rec(r))), to_values, lambda rng: (distinct_tree(rng),)))
print(serialize(deserialize("1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,5,#,#")))

Pattern

P-14. For a tree problem, first decide: does the answer flow up (return a summary from children — postorder) or down (pass state from the root — preorder)? If a path can bend at a node, compute the bent answer into a global while returning the straight one. (Practice) Write the return contract as a comment before the code. If you need two values from each child, return a tuple. Restore any shared state (path lists, counters) when leaving a node. Trade-off: recursive tree code is short but depth equals tree height; a degenerate (linked-list-shaped) tree of 10⁵ nodes needs an iterative version or a raised stack (DT-17).

Mastery check

  1. Predict. For the tree [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], what is the diameter, and which path achieves it?
  2. Predict. In max_path_sum, why are negative branch values replaced by 0 but the node’s own value is always included?

Chapter 13 Project — Vertical order and the right-side view of a large tree

Goal: implement two classic “coordinates” problems — the right-side view (last node of each level) and vertical order (group nodes by column, then by row, ties by value) — iteratively, and run them on a degenerate tree of 200,000 nodes where recursive versions would overflow the recursion limit.

# file: views/views.py
import sys
import time
from collections import defaultdict, deque
from check import stress
from tree import TreeNode, random_tree

def right_view(root):
    out, q = [], deque([root] if root else [])
    while q:
        for i in range(len(q)):
            node = q.popleft()
            if node.left: q.append(node.left)
            if node.right: q.append(node.right)
        out.append(node.val)                            # last node popped on this level
    return out

def vertical_order(root):
    cols = defaultdict(list)
    stack = [(root, 0, 0)] if root else []
    while stack:
        node, row, col = stack.pop()
        cols[col].append((row, node.val))
        if node.left: stack.append((node.left, row + 1, col - 1))
        if node.right: stack.append((node.right, row + 1, col + 1))
    return [[v for _, v in sorted(cols[c])] for c in sorted(cols)]

def right_view_rec(root):
    out = []
    def go(n, d):
        if n:
            if d == len(out): out.append(None)
            out[d] = n.val                              # later (more right, same depth) overwrites
            go(n.left, d + 1); go(n.right, d + 1)
    go(root, 0)
    return out

def vertical_rec(root):
    cells = []
    def go(n, r, c):
        if n:
            cells.append((c, r, n.val)); go(n.left, r + 1, c - 1); go(n.right, r + 1, c + 1)
    go(root, 0, 0)
    out, last = [], None
    for c, r, v in sorted(cells):
        if c != last:
            out.append([]); last = c
        out[-1].append(v)
    return out

gen = lambda rng: (random_tree(rng, rng.randint(0, 15)),)
print(stress(right_view, right_view_rec, gen))
print(stress(vertical_order, vertical_rec, gen))

n = 200_000                                             # a zig-zag path: depth n
root = node = TreeNode(0)
for i in range(1, n):
    child = TreeNode(i)
    if i % 2: node.left = child
    else: node.right = child
    node = child
t = time.perf_counter()
rv, vo = right_view(root), vertical_order(root)
print(f"depth {n:,} (zig-zag, so only columns 0 and -1): right view has {len(rv):,} entries, {len(vo)} columns, in {(time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000:.0f} ms")
try:
    right_view_rec(root)
except RecursionError as e:
    print("recursive version:", type(e).__name__, "at limit", sys.getrecursionlimit())

Review checklist

  • In right_view, why is node after the inner loop the rightmost node of that level?
  • What tie-break rule does sorted(cols[c]) apply, and where does the problem statement require it?
  • Rewrite diameter iteratively with a postorder stack — what must be stored per node?

Answers to the Chapter 13 prediction questions

13.5 Q1. The tree is 1 with children 2 and 3; 2 has children 4 and 5. The diameter is 3 edges, e.g. 4 → 2 → 1 → 3 (or 5 → 2 → 1 → 3).

13.5 Q2. A path must contain the node it bends at, so its value is mandatory; but extending into a child’s branch is optional — if the best downward sum from a child is negative, the path is better off not entering that child at all.

Chapter 14 — Binary Search Trees, Balanced Trees, and Order Statistics

Goal: use the BST invariant to search, validate, and navigate (floor, ceiling, successor, k-th smallest); understand why balance matters and how a randomised balanced tree (a treap) achieves it; and know the practical options in Python — bisect on a list, sortedcontainers.SortedList, or your own order-statistic tree.

What you will be able to do after this chapter

  • Search, insert, and delete in a BST, and validate the BST property correctly.
  • Find floor, ceiling, in-order successor, and the k-th smallest element.
  • Explain why an unbalanced BST degrades to O(n) and how rotations restore balance.
  • Implement a treap with split/merge and subtree sizes: insert, erase, rank, and select in O(log n) expected.
  • Solve “count of smaller numbers after self” and sliding-window median with an ordered multiset.

Topic 14A — The BST invariant

Unit 14.1 — Search, insert, delete, validate

One-line summary: In a BST, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger — the whole subtree, not just the child. Search walks one root-to-leaf path: O(height). Validate by passing down the allowed (low, high) range; checking only parent–child pairs is wrong.

# file: bst.py
from check import stress
from tree import TreeNode, random_tree

def insert(root, key):
    if not root:
        return TreeNode(key)
    if key < root.val:
        root.left = insert(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.val:
        root.right = insert(root.right, key)
    return root                                         # duplicates ignored

def delete(root, key):
    if not root:
        return None
    if key < root.val:
        root.left = delete(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.val:
        root.right = delete(root.right, key)
    else:
        if not root.left:
            return root.right                           # 0 or 1 child: splice out
        if not root.right:
            return root.left
        succ = root.right                               # 2 children: copy the successor, delete it
        while succ.left:
            succ = succ.left
        root.val = succ.val
        root.right = delete(root.right, succ.val)
    return root

def is_valid_bst(root, lo=float("-inf"), hi=float("inf")):
    if not root:
        return True
    return lo < root.val < hi and is_valid_bst(root.left, lo, root.val) and is_valid_bst(root.right, root.val, hi)

def is_valid_wrong(root):                               # checks only children: misses grandchildren
    if not root:
        return True
    if root.left and root.left.val >= root.val: return False
    if root.right and root.right.val <= root.val: return False
    return is_valid_wrong(root.left) and is_valid_wrong(root.right)

def inorder(root):
    return inorder(root.left) + [root.val] + inorder(root.right) if root else []

def bst_ops(ops):
    root = None
    for op, k in ops:
        root = insert(root, k) if op == "+" else delete(root, k)
    return inorder(root), is_valid_bst(root)

def set_ops(ops):
    s = set()
    for op, k in ops:
        (s.add if op == "+" else s.discard)(k)
    return sorted(s), True

if __name__ == "__main__":
  print(stress(bst_ops, set_ops, lambda rng: ([(rng.choice("++-"), rng.randint(0, 9)) for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 20))],)))
  print(stress(is_valid_bst, lambda r: (v := inorder(r)) == sorted(set(v)) and len(v) == len(set(v)), lambda rng: (random_tree(rng, rng.randint(0, 6), 0, 6),)))
  try:
      print(stress(is_valid_wrong, lambda r: (v := inorder(r)) == sorted(set(v)) and len(v) == len(set(v)), lambda rng: (random_tree(rng, rng.randint(0, 6), 0, 6),)))
  except AssertionError:
      from tree import build, to_values
      bad = build([5, 3, 8, None, 6])                 # 6 sits in 5's left subtree
      print("parent-child check is wrong on", to_values(bad), "->", is_valid_wrong(bad), "; range check ->", is_valid_bst(bad))

The counterexample is a tree where a grandchild violates the ancestor’s range — exactly the bug the (low, high) parameters prevent. An equivalent check: an in-order traversal must be strictly increasing.

The bug the stress test caught: validating only parent–child pairs

is_valid_wrong checks each node against its children only, and accepts [5, 1, 6, None, None, 3, 7] — where 3 sits in 5’s right subtree, which must hold values greater than 5. Validity is a property of all ancestors: each node must lie in an interval narrowed on the way down (lo < val < hi), or equivalently the in-order traversal must be strictly increasing. Interviewers ask this question to see whether you notice.

One more problem: convert a sorted array to a height-balanced BST

Pick the middle element as the root; the left half becomes the left subtree, the right half the right subtree. Heights of subtrees then differ by at most one at every node.

# file: sorted_to_bst.py
from tree import TreeNode
from check import stress

def to_bst(a, lo=0, hi=None):
    if hi is None:
        hi = len(a)
    if lo >= hi:
        return None
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    return TreeNode(a[mid], to_bst(a, lo, mid), to_bst(a, mid + 1, hi))

def check(a):
    root = to_bst(a)
    out = []
    def go(n):                                   # returns height; -1 marks "unbalanced"
        if not n:
            return 0
        l = go(n.left)
        out.append(n.val)
        r = go(n.right)
        return -1 if min(l, r) < 0 or abs(l - r) > 1 else 1 + max(l, r)
    balanced = go(root) >= 0
    return balanced and out == a

print(stress(check, lambda a: True, lambda rng: (sorted(rng.sample(range(100), rng.randint(0, 20))),)))

Unit 14.2 — Navigation: floor, ceiling, successor, k-th smallest

One-line summary: Floor (largest key ≤ x): walk down; whenever the node’s key ≤ x, record it and go right, otherwise go left. Ceiling is symmetric. Successor of a node = ceiling of (key + ε) = leftmost node of its right subtree, or else the nearest ancestor for which it is in the left subtree. k-th smallest: in-order traversal stopping at k — O(h + k); with subtree sizes, O(h).

# file: navigate.py
import bisect
from check import stress, rand_list
from bst import insert

def floor_key(root, x):
    best = None
    while root:
        if root.val <= x:
            best, root = root.val, root.right            # candidate; a larger one may be on the right
        else:
            root = root.left
    return best

def ceil_key(root, x):
    best = None
    while root:
        if root.val >= x:
            best, root = root.val, root.left
        else:
            root = root.right
    return best

def kth_smallest(root, k):                              # iterative in-order, stops early
    stack = []
    while True:
        while root:
            stack.append(root); root = root.left
        root = stack.pop()
        k -= 1
        if k == 0:
            return root.val
        root = root.right

def build_bst(keys):
    root = None
    for k in keys:
        root = insert(root, k)
    return root

def floor_brute(keys, x):
    s = sorted(set(keys)); i = bisect.bisect_right(s, x)
    return s[i - 1] if i else None
def ceil_brute(keys, x):
    s = sorted(set(keys)); i = bisect.bisect_left(s, x)
    return s[i] if i < len(s) else None

gen = lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 30, 12), rng.randint(-2, 32))
print(stress(lambda ks, x: floor_key(build_bst(ks), x), floor_brute, gen))
print(stress(lambda ks, x: ceil_key(build_bst(ks), x), ceil_brute, gen))
print(stress(lambda ks, k: kth_smallest(build_bst(ks), k), lambda ks, k: sorted(set(ks))[k - 1],
             lambda rng: ((ks := rand_list(rng, 0, 30, 12, 1)), rng.randint(1, len(set(ks))))))

One more problem: two-sum in a BST with two iterators

An in-order iterator from the left yields keys ascending; a reverse in-order iterator from the right yields them descending. Running Unit 4.1’s two-pointer pattern on the two iterators finds a pair with a given sum in O(n) time and O(h) memory — without copying the tree into a list.

# file: bst_two_sum.py
from tree import TreeNode
from check import stress

def insert(root, k):
    if not root:
        return TreeNode(k)
    if k < root.val:
        root.left = insert(root.left, k)
    else:
        root.right = insert(root.right, k)
    return root

def iterate(root, forward):
    stack, n = [], root
    while stack or n:
        while n:
            stack.append(n)
            n = n.left if forward else n.right
        n = stack.pop()
        yield n.val
        n = n.right if forward else n.left

def has_pair(root, target):
    lo, hi = iterate(root, True), iterate(root, False)
    a, b = next(lo, None), next(hi, None)
    while a is not None and b is not None and a < b:
        s = a + b
        if s == target:
            return True
        if s < target:
            a = next(lo, None)
        else:
            b = next(hi, None)
    return False

def gen(rng):
    keys = rng.sample(range(-20, 20), rng.randint(0, 10))
    root = None
    for k in keys:
        root = insert(root, k)
    return root, rng.randint(-20, 20), keys

def run(root, t, keys):
    return has_pair(root, t)

def brute(root, t, keys):
    return any(keys[i] + keys[j] == t for i in range(len(keys)) for j in range(i + 1, len(keys)))

print(stress(run, brute, gen))
