expected rolls to reach 10: 33495175/10077696 = 3.323693729201595
coupon collector n=50: exact 224.96, simulated over 2,000 runs 225.94

The expected number of fixed points of a random permutation is exactly 1 for every n ≥ 1 — the indicators “position i is fixed” are dependent, yet linearity still applies. A brute-force average over all n! permutations confirms it.

Deep & Tricky

DT-43. Backward expectation DP needs an acyclic state graph; if transitions can return to earlier states (snakes, retries, random walks), “E[s] depends on E[s]” and the DP has no valid order — the expectations satisfy a linear system instead, which must be solved. (Markov chain absorption: E = 1 + Q·E, so E = (I − Q)⁻¹·1 — Kemeny & Snell, “Finite Markov Chains”, 1960) Iterating the DP until it stops changing (“value iteration”) converges, but slowly when the chain mixes slowly and never exactly; Gaussian elimination with Fraction gives the exact answer for a few hundred states. A state with a self-loop is the smallest case: E = 1 + p·E gives E = 1/(1 − p), which no forward DP order produces. This chapter’s project solves a board game exactly this way.

Topic 35B — Games

Unit 35.3 — Winning and losing positions; minimax

One-line summary: In a two-player game with perfect information and no draws, a position is winning if some move leads to a losing position for the opponent, and losing if every move leads to a winning one (a position with no moves is losing under normal play). Memoise on the position. For score-based games, minimax: the player to move maximises (own score − opponent’s score) over moves.

# file: games.py
from functools import cache
from check import stress

def can_win_take_away(n, k):                        # take 1..k stones; who takes the last stone wins
    win = [False] * (n + 1)
    for s in range(1, n + 1):
        win[s] = any(not win[s - t] for t in range(1, min(k, s) + 1))
    return win[n]

def predict_divisor_game(n):                         # choose x with 0 < x < n and n % x == 0, replace n by n - x
    @cache
    def win(m):
        return any(not win(m - x) for x in range(1, m) if m % x == 0)
    return win(n)

print(stress(can_win_take_away, lambda n, k: n % (k + 1) != 0, lambda rng: (rng.randint(0, 60), rng.randint(1, 6))))
print(stress(predict_divisor_game, lambda n: n % 2 == 0, lambda rng: (rng.randint(1, 200),)))
$ PYTHONPATH=../lib python3 games.py
2000 stress tests ok
2000 stress tests ok

Both stress tests compare a game search with a closed-form rule (n mod (k + 1) ≠ 0; n even) — the usual way such rules are discovered: compute the win/lose table for small n, look for the pattern, then prove it.

Win/lose labelling, stated as a rule

A position is losing if every move leads to a winning position (including “no moves at all”), and winning if at least one move leads to a losing position. Labelling positions in order of distance from the end — a DP over a DAG of game states — solves any finite two-player game with perfect information and no chance. When the labels show a pattern (multiples of k + 1 lose in the take-away game), prove it by induction and replace the DP with a formula — but write the DP first: it is the checker for the formula.

Unit 35.4 — Sprague–Grundy: sums of impartial games

One-line summary: In an impartial game (both players have the same moves), every position has a Grundy number g = mex{g(next positions)}, where mex is the smallest non-negative integer not in the set; g = 0 exactly for losing positions. A position made of independent games played side by side (each move changes one component) has Grundy number equal to the XOR of the components’ numbers. Nim is the special case g(pile of n) = n.

# file: grundy.py
from functools import cache, reduce
from operator import xor
from check import stress

def mex(s):
    m = 0
    while m in s:
        m += 1
    return m

@cache
def g_subtraction(n, moves):                        # remove any amount in `moves` from a pile
    return mex({g_subtraction(n - m, moves) for m in moves if m <= n})

def first_player_wins(piles, moves):                # several independent piles
    return reduce(xor, (g_subtraction(p, moves) for p in piles), 0) != 0

def brute(piles, moves):                            # direct search over tuples of piles
    @cache
    def win(state):
        return any(not win(tuple(sorted(state[:i] + (state[i] - m,) + state[i + 1:])))
                   for i in range(len(state)) for m in moves if m <= state[i])
    return win(tuple(sorted(piles)))

gen = lambda rng: ([rng.randint(0, 8) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 3))], tuple(sorted(rng.sample(range(1, 5), rng.randint(1, 3)))))
print(stress(first_player_wins, brute, gen, trials=500))
print("Nim [3, 4, 5]:", "first player wins" if 3 ^ 4 ^ 5 else "second player wins", "| Grundy of pile 10 with moves {1,3,4}:", g_subtraction(10, (1, 3, 4)))
$ PYTHONPATH=../lib python3 grundy.py
500 stress tests ok
Nim [3, 4, 5]: first player wins | Grundy of pile 10 with moves {1,3,4}: 1

The brute force searches the combined game directly; the Sprague–Grundy version never looks at combinations, only at single piles — that is the theorem’s power: k piles of size n cost O(k·n) instead of O(nᵏ).

Pattern

P-36. Random processes on a DAG of states → forward probability DP or backward expectation DP; with cycles → linear system. “Expected number of …” → first try linearity over indicators. Two-player perfect-information games → win/lose DP or minimax; impartial games made of independent parts → Grundy numbers and XOR. (Practice) Use Fraction to get exact answers and compare them with simulation; compute small game tables and look for patterns before proving them. Trade-off: exact rational arithmetic grows denominators quickly; for large state spaces switch to floats (and say so), or to modular arithmetic when the problem asks for p·q⁻¹ mod a prime.

Mastery check

  1. Predict. In the take-away game with k = 3, is 8 stones a winning or losing position for the player to move?
  2. Predict. What is the Grundy number of a Nim position consisting of piles 1, 2, 3, and who wins?

Chapter 35 Project — Snakes and ladders, solved exactly

Goal: compute the exact expected number of turns to finish a 100-square snakes-and-ladders board (roll one die; overshooting 100 means you stay put; ladders move you up, snakes down). Because snakes create cycles, there is no DP order (DT-43): set up E[s] = 1 + (1/6)·Σ E[next(s, f)] for every square, solve the 100 × 100 linear system by Gaussian elimination over Fraction, and check against a Monte Carlo simulation.

# file: snakes/snakes.py
import random
import time
from fractions import Fraction
from check import stress

LADDERS = {1: 38, 4: 14, 9: 31, 21: 42, 28: 84, 36: 44, 51: 67, 71: 91, 80: 100}
SNAKES = {16: 6, 47: 26, 49: 11, 56: 53, 62: 19, 64: 60, 87: 24, 93: 73, 95: 75, 98: 78}

def next_square(s, roll, N, jumps):
    t = s + roll
    if t > N:
        return s                                     # overshoot: stay
    return jumps.get(t, t)

def solve(A, b):
    """Gaussian elimination over Fractions (exact)."""
    n = len(A)
    M = [row[:] + [b[i]] for i, row in enumerate(A)]
    for col in range(n):
        piv = next(r for r in range(col, n) if M[r][col] != 0)
        M[col], M[piv] = M[piv], M[col]
        inv = 1 / M[col][col]
        M[col] = [x * inv for x in M[col]]
        for r in range(n):
            if r != col and M[r][col] != 0:
                f = M[r][col]
                M[r] = [x - f * y for x, y in zip(M[r], M[col])]
    return [M[i][n] for i in range(n)]

def expected_turns(N, jumps):
    states = list(range(N))                          # squares 0..N-1; N is the goal (E = 0)
    idx = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(states)}
    A = [[Fraction(0)] * N for _ in range(N)]
    b = [Fraction(1)] * N
    for s in states:                                 # E[s] - (1/6) * sum E[next] = 1
        A[idx[s]][idx[s]] += 1
        for f in range(1, 7):
            t = next_square(s, f, N, jumps)
            if t != N:
                A[idx[s]][idx[t]] -= Fraction(1, 6)
    return solve(A, b)[0]

def simulate(N, jumps, games, rng):
    total = 0
    for _ in range(games):
        s, turns = 0, 0
        while s != N:
            s = next_square(s, rng.randint(1, 6), N, jumps); turns += 1
        total += turns
    return total / games

def value_iteration(N, jumps, sweeps):               # the "just iterate" approach, for comparison
    E = [0.0] * (N + 1)
    for _ in range(sweeps):
        E = [0.0 if s == N else 1 + sum(E[next_square(s, f, N, jumps)] for f in range(1, 7)) / 6 for s in range(N + 1)]
    return E[0]

def gen(rng):                                        # small random boards, checked against long simulation
    N = rng.randint(6, 15)
    jumps = {}
    for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 3)):
        a, b = rng.sample(range(1, N), 2)
        if a not in jumps and b not in jumps:
            jumps[a] = b
    return (N, jumps)

def close(N, jumps):
    exact = float(expected_turns(N, jumps))
    return abs(exact - value_iteration(N, jumps, 3000)) < 1e-6

print(stress(close, lambda N, j: True, gen, trials=100))
t = time.perf_counter()
E = expected_turns(100, {**LADDERS, **SNAKES})
el = time.perf_counter() - t
print(f"exact expected turns: {float(E):.6f}  (a fraction with a {len(str(E.denominator))}-digit denominator)  [{el:.1f} s]")
print(f"Monte Carlo, 100,000 games: {simulate(100, {**LADDERS, **SNAKES}, 100_000, random.Random(29)):.3f}")
for sweeps in (10, 50, 200, 1000):
    print(f"value iteration, {sweeps:>4} sweeps: {value_iteration(100, {**LADDERS, **SNAKES}, sweeps):.6f}")
$ cd snakes && PYTHONPATH=../../lib python3 snakes.py

Monte Carlo, 100,000 games: 39.165
value iteration,   10 sweeps: 9.979865
value iteration,   50 sweeps: 33.225689
value iteration,  200 sweeps: 39.212483
value iteration, 1000 sweeps: 39.225122

Value iteration approaches the exact answer only gradually — it is computing the expected number of turns truncated at the number of sweeps. The linear system gives the exact rational answer in one go; the simulation gives an independent check with the expected statistical error.

Review checklist

  • Why does “overshoot: stay” create self-loops, and how does the linear system handle them?
  • What changes if the rule is “overshoot: bounce back”?
  • Gaussian elimination is O(n³); for 10⁴ states, which property of this matrix (sparsity, structure) would you exploit?

Answers to the Chapter 35 prediction questions

35.4 Q1. Losing: 8 is a multiple of k + 1 = 4. Whatever the mover takes (1–3), the opponent takes the complement to 4 and keeps the total a multiple of 4.

35.4 Q2. 1 ⊕ 2 ⊕ 3 = 0, so the position is losing for the player to move: the second player wins.

Chapter 36 — DP Optimisations

Goal: speed up DPs whose transitions scan many previous states — with a monotonic deque (sliding-window maximum over dp), the convex hull trick and Li Chao trees (transitions that are linear functions), divide-and-conquer optimisation and Knuth’s optimisation (monotone optimal split points), and matrix exponentiation (linear recurrences with huge n).

These are the techniques that turn an O(n²) DP into O(n log n) or O(n), or an O(n) recurrence into O(log n). Each one applies only when a specific structure holds; the skill is recognising that structure in the transition formula.

Transition shape Condition Technique Speed-up
dp[i] = max(dp[j]) + c, i − k ≤ j < i window of previous states monotonic deque O(nk) → O(n)
dp[i] = min(dp[j] + b[j]·a[i]) linear in a[i] convex hull trick / Li Chao O(n²) → O(n log n)
dp[k][i] = min(dp[k−1][j] + C(j, i)) opt(i) monotone in i divide & conquer O(kn²) → O(kn log n)
dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][k] + dp[k][j]) + w(i, j) quadrangle inequality Knuth O(n³) → O(n²)
x[n] = M · x[n−1] fixed linear recurrence matrix power O(n) → O(log n)

Topic 36A — Windowed and linear transitions

Unit 36.1 — Monotonic deque over DP values

One-line summary: When dp[i] takes the best dp[j] over a sliding window of previous indices, maintain the window maximum with a monotonic deque (Unit 5.5) instead of scanning: amortised O(1) per step.

# file: window_dp.py
from collections import deque
from check import stress, rand_list

def max_jump_score(a, k):                            # start at 0, jump 1..k forward, end at n-1, maximise sum of visited
    n = len(a)
    dp = [0] * n
    dp[0] = a[0]
    dq = deque([0])                                  # indices with decreasing dp
    for i in range(1, n):
        while dq[0] < i - k:
            dq.popleft()                             # out of the window
        dp[i] = dp[dq[0]] + a[i]
        while dq and dp[dq[-1]] <= dp[i]:
            dq.pop()
        dq.append(i)
    return dp[-1]

def brute(a, k):
    dp = [a[0]] + [float("-inf")] * (len(a) - 1)
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        dp[i] = max(dp[j] for j in range(max(0, i - k), i)) + a[i]
    return dp[-1]

print(stress(max_jump_score, brute, lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, -9, 9, 15, 1), rng.randint(1, 4))))
$ PYTHONPATH=../lib python3 window_dp.py
2000 stress tests ok

When the DP transition is a sliding-window maximum

A recurrence of the form dp[i] = a[i] + max(dp[j] for j in [i − k, i − 1]) costs O(nk) when written directly. The window of candidate js slides by one each step, so the maximum over it is exactly Unit 5.5’s monotonic deque: drop indices that left the window from the front, drop dominated values from the back. O(n) total. Recognise it by “the best previous state within a fixed distance”.

Unit 36.2 — Convex hull trick and the Li Chao tree

One-line summary: If dp[i] = min over j of (m_j · x_i + c_j) — each earlier state contributes a line with slope m_j and intercept c_j evaluated at x_i — then the answer is the lower envelope of the lines at x_i. A Li Chao tree over the x-range stores lines in a segment tree, each node keeping the line that is better at its midpoint; insert and query are O(log X), with no ordering requirements on slopes or queries.

# file: ../lib/lichao.py
"""Li Chao tree for minimum of lines over integer x in [lo, hi)."""

class LiChao:
    def __init__(self, lo, hi):
        self.lo, self.hi = lo, hi
        self.line = {}                                  # node id -> (m, c); implicit tree, created lazily

    @staticmethod
    def _f(l, x):
        return l[0] * x + l[1]

    def add(self, m, c):
        new, node, lo, hi = (m, c), 1, self.lo, self.hi
        while True:
            cur = self.line.get(node)
            if cur is None:
                self.line[node] = new
                return
            mid = (lo + hi) // 2
            if self._f(new, mid) < self._f(cur, mid):
                self.line[node], new = new, cur          # keep the better line at mid here
            if hi - lo == 1:
                return
            if self._f(new, lo) < self._f(self.line[node], lo):
                node, hi = 2 * node, mid                 # the loser can still win on the left
            elif self._f(new, hi - 1) < self._f(self.line[node], hi - 1):
                node, lo = 2 * node + 1, mid             # ... or on the right
            else:
                return                                   # dominated everywhere in this range

    def query(self, x):
        node, lo, hi, best = 1, self.lo, self.hi, float("inf")
        while node in self.line:
            best = min(best, self._f(self.line[node], x))
            mid = (lo + hi) // 2
            if x < mid:
                node, hi = 2 * node, mid
            else:
                node, lo = 2 * node + 1, mid
        return best
# file: cht.py
from check import stress, rand_list
from lichao import LiChao

def lines_min(lines, xs):
    t = LiChao(-50, 51)
    for m, c in lines:
        t.add(m, c)
    return [t.query(x) for x in xs]

def frog(h, C):                                       # dp[i] = min_j dp[j] + (h[i]-h[j])^2 + C
    # (h_i - h_j)^2 = h_i^2 - 2 h_j h_i + h_j^2 : a line in x = h_i with slope -2h_j and intercept dp[j] + h_j^2
    t = LiChao(0, max(h) + 1)
    dp = [0] * len(h)
    t.add(-2 * h[0], dp[0] + h[0] ** 2)
    for i in range(1, len(h)):
        dp[i] = t.query(h[i]) + h[i] ** 2 + C
        t.add(-2 * h[i], dp[i] + h[i] ** 2)
    return dp[-1]

def frog_brute(h, C):
    dp = [0] * len(h)
    for i in range(1, len(h)):
        dp[i] = min(dp[j] + (h[i] - h[j]) ** 2 + C for j in range(i))
    return dp[-1]

print(stress(lines_min, lambda L, xs: [min(m * x + c for m, c in L) for x in xs],
             lambda rng: ([(rng.randint(-9, 9), rng.randint(-50, 50)) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 8))], [rng.randint(-50, 50) for _ in range(6)])))
print(stress(frog, frog_brute, lambda rng: (sorted(rand_list(rng, 1, 40, 10, 1)), rng.randint(0, 30))))

2000 stress tests ok
2000 stress tests ok

The algebra step is the whole technique: expand the cost, separate the terms that depend only on i (added after the query), only on j (the line’s intercept), and the product of the two (slope × x). If no such separation exists, the convex hull trick does not apply.

The geometry behind the convex hull trick

If dp[i] = min over j of (m_j · x_i + b_j), each earlier j contributes a line with slope m_j and intercept b_j, and the query asks for the lowest line at x = x_i. The lowest of a set of lines, as a function of x, is the lower envelope — a convex piecewise-linear curve. When slopes arrive in sorted order and queries are sorted too, a deque of envelope lines gives amortised O(1) per step; otherwise a Li Chao tree (this unit) handles arbitrary order in O(log C). Recognise it by a product of a term depending on i and a term depending on j inside a min or max.

Topic 36B — Monotone split points

Unit 36.3 — Divide-and-conquer optimisation

One-line summary: For layered DPs dp[k][i] = min over j < i of dp[k−1][j] + C(j, i) where the optimal j, opt(i), is non-decreasing in i (true when C satisfies the quadrangle inequality), compute dp[k][mid] for the middle i by scanning only [opt_lo, opt_hi], then recurse on the left half with [opt_lo, opt(mid)] and the right half with [opt(mid), opt_hi]. Each layer costs O(n log n).

# file: dnc_opt.py
from check import stress, rand_list

def partition_min_cost(a, K):                         # split a into K contiguous groups; cost of a group = (sum)^2
    n = len(a)
    P = [0]
    for x in a:
        P.append(P[-1] + x)
    C = lambda j, i: (P[i] - P[j]) ** 2               # cost of group a[j:i]
    INF = float("inf")
    prev = [0] + [INF] * n                            # 0 groups: only the empty prefix is free
    for _ in range(K):
        cur = [INF] * (n + 1)
        stack = [(1, n, 0, n - 1)]                     # (i_lo, i_hi, opt_lo, opt_hi), iterative recursion
        while stack:
            lo, hi, olo, ohi = stack.pop()
            if lo > hi:
                continue
            mid = (lo + hi) // 2
            best, arg = INF, olo
            for j in range(olo, min(mid - 1, ohi) + 1):
                v = prev[j] + C(j, mid)
                if v < best:
                    best, arg = v, j
            cur[mid] = best
            stack.append((lo, mid - 1, olo, arg))
            stack.append((mid + 1, hi, arg, ohi))
        prev = cur
    return prev[n]

def brute(a, K):
    n = len(a)
    P = [0]
    for x in a:
        P.append(P[-1] + x)
    INF = float("inf")
    prev = [0] + [INF] * n
    for _ in range(K):
        prev = [INF] + [min(prev[j] + (P[i] - P[j]) ** 2 for j in range(i)) for i in range(1, n + 1)]
    return prev[n]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(stress(partition_min_cost, brute, lambda rng: ((a := rand_list(rng, 0, 9, 12, 1)), rng.randint(1, len(a)))))

2000 stress tests ok

Deep & Tricky

DT-44. Divide-and-conquer and Knuth optimisations are valid only when the cost function satisfies the quadrangle inequality (C(a, c) + C(b, d) ≤ C(a, d) + C(b, c) for a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ d) or an equivalent monotonicity of optimal split points; applied to a cost that violates it, they return wrong answers with no error. (Yao, “Efficient dynamic programming using quadrangle inequalities”, STOC 1980; Knuth, “Optimum binary search trees”, Acta Informatica 1971) (sum)² over contiguous groups of non-negative numbers satisfies it; so does the optimal-BST weight function. With negative numbers allowed, (sum)² does not, and the optimisation can skip the true optimum. When the property is not obvious, check it numerically on random inputs — or stress-test against the unoptimised DP, which is what decides.

# file: dnc_negative.py
from check import stress, rand_list
from dnc_opt import partition_min_cost, brute

try:
    stress(partition_min_cost, brute, lambda rng: ((a := rand_list(rng, -9, 9, 10, 1)), rng.randint(1, len(a))))
    print("no counterexample found")
except AssertionError as e:
    print("with negative values the optimisation fails:", str(e).split(": ", 1)[1])

Unit 36.4 — Knuth’s optimisation

One-line summary: For interval DPs dp[i][j] = min over i ≤ k < j of dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + w(i, j) with w satisfying the quadrangle inequality and monotonicity, the optimal split satisfies opt[i][j−1] ≤ opt[i][j] ≤ opt[i+1][j]. Scanning only that range makes the total work telescope to O(n²). It applies to the optimal BST of Chapter 31 and to merging adjacent piles with cost = merged size.

# file: knuth.py
from check import stress, rand_list

def merge_piles(a):                                   # merge adjacent piles; cost of a merge = combined size
    n = len(a)
    P = [0]
    for x in a:
        P.append(P[-1] + x)
    dp = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    opt = [[i] * n for i in range(n)]
    for length in range(2, n + 1):
        for i in range(n - length + 1):
            j = i + length - 1
            best, arg = float("inf"), -1
            for k in range(opt[i][j - 1], min(opt[i + 1][j], j - 1) + 1):   # Knuth's range
                v = dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j]
                if v < best:
                    best, arg = v, k
            dp[i][j], opt[i][j] = best + P[j + 1] - P[i], arg
    return dp[0][n - 1] if n else 0

def brute(a):
    n = len(a)
    P = [0]
    for x in a:
        P.append(P[-1] + x)
    dp = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for length in range(2, n + 1):
        for i in range(n - length + 1):
            j = i + length - 1
            dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j] for k in range(i, j)) + P[j + 1] - P[i]
    return dp[0][n - 1] if n else 0

print(stress(merge_piles, brute, lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 20, 12),)))
$ PYTHONPATH=../lib python3 knuth.py
2000 stress tests ok

Knuth’s condition, and why it cuts O(n³) to O(n²)

For interval DPs dp[i][j] = min over k (dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j]) + cost(i, j), let opt[i][j] be the best split point. When the cost satisfies the quadrangle inequality and is monotone on nested intervals, opt[i][j − 1] ≤ opt[i][j] ≤ opt[i + 1][j]. Restricting the search for k to that range makes the work for each diagonal of the table telescope to O(n), so the whole table is O(n²). Verify the condition with a brute force on random inputs before relying on it — applying Knuth’s optimisation to a cost that does not satisfy it gives wrong answers silently.

Topic 36C — Huge n

Unit 36.5 — Matrix exponentiation

One-line summary: A linear recurrence of fixed order d — x[n] = c₁x[n−1] + … + c_d x[n−d] — is a matrix–vector product v[n] = M·v[n−1] with a d × d companion matrix. Then v[n] = Mⁿ·v[0], and Mⁿ is computed by repeated squaring in O(d³ log n). The same applies to counting walks of length n in a graph (powers of the adjacency matrix) and to any DP whose transition is the same linear map at every step.

# file: matpow.py
from check import stress

MOD = 10**9 + 7

def mat_mul(A, B):
    return [[sum(A[i][k] * B[k][j] for k in range(len(B))) % MOD for j in range(len(B[0]))] for i in range(len(A))]

def mat_pow(M, n):
    R = [[int(i == j) for j in range(len(M))] for i in range(len(M))]
    while n:
        if n & 1:
            R = mat_mul(R, M)
        M = mat_mul(M, M)
        n >>= 1
    return R

def linear_recurrence(coeffs, init, n):              # x[k] = sum coeffs[t] * x[k-1-t]; init = x[0..d-1]
    d = len(coeffs)
    if n < d:
        return init[n] % MOD
    M = [coeffs] + [[int(j == i) for j in range(d)] for i in range(d - 1)]   # companion matrix
    P = mat_pow(M, n - d + 1)
    state = init[::-1]                               # [x[d-1], ..., x[0]]
    return sum(P[0][j] * state[j] for j in range(d)) % MOD

def brute(coeffs, init, n):
    x = list(init)
    while len(x) <= n:
        x.append(sum(c * x[-1 - t] for t, c in enumerate(coeffs)) % MOD)
    return x[n] % MOD

def walks(adj, length):                               # number of walks of a given length between all pairs
    return mat_pow(adj, length)

print(stress(linear_recurrence, brute, lambda rng: ((c := [rng.randint(0, 5) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 4))]), [rng.randint(0, 5) for _ in c], rng.randint(0, 60))))
print("Fibonacci(10^18) mod p =", linear_recurrence([1, 1], [0, 1], 10**18))
print("walks of length 10 from 0 to 0 in a triangle:", walks([[0, 1, 1], [1, 0, 1], [1, 1, 0]], 10)[0][0])

Walks of length n from a vertex back to itself in a triangle number (2ⁿ + 2·(−1)ⁿ)/3 — for n = 10, (1024 + 2)/3 = 342 — a quick check of the matrix power.

Pattern

P-37. When a DP is correct but too slow, look at the transition’s shape: a sliding window of states → monotonic deque; a minimum of linear functions of the current index → convex hull trick / Li Chao; layered partition DPs with monotone optimal splits → divide and conquer; interval DPs with quadrangle-inequality costs → Knuth; the same linear step repeated n times with huge n → matrix power. (Practice) Always keep the slow DP as the stress-test oracle: these optimisations have preconditions that are easy to violate without noticing (DT-44). Trade-off: each technique adds complexity and constraints; if n is small enough for the plain DP, ship the plain DP.

Chapter 36 Project — Optimal BST in O(n²) with Knuth’s optimisation

Goal: apply Knuth’s optimisation to Chapter 31’s optimal binary search tree DP, verify that it returns exactly the same cost on random inputs, and measure the speed-up as n grows — O(n³) versus O(n²) made visible.

# file: obst_knuth/obst_knuth.py
import random
import time
from check import stress
from obst import optimal_bst

def optimal_bst_knuth(freq):
    n = len(freq)
    pre = [0]
    for f in freq:
        pre.append(pre[-1] + f)
    cost = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(n + 2)]       # half-open [i, j), as in Chapter 31
    root = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for i in range(n):
        cost[i][i + 1], root[i][i + 1] = freq[i], i
    for length in range(2, n + 1):
        for i in range(n - length + 1):
            j = i + length
            best, arg = float("inf"), -1
            for r in range(root[i][j - 1], root[i + 1][j] + 1):   # Knuth: opt[i][j-1] <= opt[i][j] <= opt[i+1][j]
                c = cost[i][r] + cost[r + 1][j]
                if c < best:
                    best, arg = c, r
            cost[i][j], root[i][j] = best + pre[j] - pre[i], arg
    return cost[0][n]

print(stress(optimal_bst_knuth, lambda f: optimal_bst(f)[0], lambda rng: ([rng.randint(0, 20) for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 25))],), trials=500))
rng = random.Random(30)
for n in (100, 200, 400, 800):
    freq = [rng.randint(1, 1000) for _ in range(n)]
    t = time.perf_counter()
    a = optimal_bst_knuth(freq)
    tk = time.perf_counter() - t
    if n <= 400:
        t = time.perf_counter()
        b = optimal_bst(freq)[0]
        tc = time.perf_counter() - t
        print(f"n={n:>3}: Knuth {tk * 1000:6.0f} ms, cubic {tc * 1000:7.0f} ms, same cost: {a == b}")
    else:
        print(f"n={n:>3}: Knuth {tk * 1000:6.0f} ms  (cubic skipped: expected ~8x the n=400 time)")

Per doubling of n, the Knuth version’s time grows about 4–5× (O(n²), plus growing memory traffic) and the cubic version’s 8–13×; at n = 400 the gap is already a factor of about 30. Review checklist

  • Why does the total work of Knuth’s loops telescope to O(n²)?
  • Which property of the optimal-BST weight function w(i, j) = Σ freq makes Knuth’s inequality hold?
  • Would Knuth’s optimisation be valid for the matrix-chain DP of Unit 31.1? (Not in general — its cost term d[i]·d[k+1]·d[j+1] depends on k; Hu–Shing’s O(n log n) algorithm is the specialised solution.)

Answers to the Chapter 36 prediction questions

36.5 Q1. Expanding (h_i − h_j)² gives h_i² − 2h_j·h_i + h_j². For a fixed earlier j, the part that varies with the current i is −2h_j · h_i: a line in the variable x = h_i with slope −2h_j; dp[j] + h_j² is the intercept; h_i² + C is added after the minimum.

36.5 Q2. 10¹⁸ < 2⁶⁰, so about 60 squarings plus one multiplication per set bit of n (24 for 10¹⁸) — under 90 multiplications of 2 × 2 matrices.

Chapter 37 — Greedy Algorithms

Goal: recognise when a locally best choice is globally optimal, prove it with an exchange argument (or refute it with a counterexample found by brute force), and apply the classic greedy patterns: earliest finish time, sorting by a ratio or a deadline, heaps of candidates, two-pass constraints, reachability frontiers, and Huffman coding.

Greedy algorithms are the easiest to write and the easiest to get wrong. The discipline in this chapter is: never trust a greedy rule until a brute force agrees with it on thousands of random cases — and when you can, understand why with an exchange argument.

What you will be able to do after this chapter

  • Prove greedy rules with exchange arguments; find counterexamples to wrong ones.
  • Schedule intervals (activity selection), jobs with deadlines and profits, and minimise lateness.
  • Solve frontier problems: jump game, gas station.
  • Satisfy neighbour constraints with two passes (candy distribution).
  • Build Huffman codes and see why they are optimal.

Topic 37A — Proving greedy

Unit 37.1 — Exchange arguments: activity selection

One-line summary: To show a greedy choice is safe, take any optimal solution that differs from the greedy one at the first choice and exchange its choice for the greedy one without making it worse. Activity selection (maximum number of non-overlapping intervals): always pick the interval that finishes first — any optimal schedule’s first interval can be swapped for it, since it ends no later and so conflicts with nothing more.

# file: activity.py
from itertools import combinations
from check import stress

def max_non_overlapping(intervals):                  # half-open [s, e)
    count, end = 0, float("-inf")
    for s, e in sorted(intervals, key=lambda iv: iv[1]):
        if s >= end:
            count, end = count + 1, e
    return count

def by_start(intervals):                             # tempting but wrong: earliest start first
    count, end = 0, float("-inf")
    for s, e in sorted(intervals):
        if s >= end:
            count, end = count + 1, e
    return count

def by_length(intervals):                            # tempting but wrong: shortest first
    chosen = []
    for s, e in sorted(intervals, key=lambda iv: iv[1] - iv[0]):
        if all(e <= a or s >= b for a, b in chosen):
            chosen.append((s, e))
    return len(chosen)

def brute(intervals):
    for k in range(len(intervals), 0, -1):
        for sub in combinations(sorted(intervals), k):
            if all(a[1] <= b[0] for a, b in zip(sub, sub[1:])):
                return k
    return 0

gen = lambda rng: ([(s := rng.randint(0, 10), s + rng.randint(1, 6)) for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 7))],)
print("earliest finish:", stress(max_non_overlapping, brute, gen))
for wrong in (by_start, by_length):
    try:
        stress(wrong, brute, gen)
    except AssertionError as e:
        print(f"{wrong.__name__:>9} fails:", str(e).split(": ", 1)[1])

Each wrong rule is refuted by a small counterexample within seconds — the cheapest possible way to kill a bad idea.

Deep & Tricky

DT-45. A greedy algorithm is optimal exactly when the problem has the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure; matroids characterise a large family of such problems (maximum-weight independent sets in a matroid are found by sorting and adding greedily), but many greedy-looking problems — coin change with arbitrary denominations, 0/1 knapsack — are not matroids and greedy fails. (Edmonds, “Matroids and the greedy algorithm”, Math. Programming 1971; CLRS §16.4) Coins {1, 3, 4} and amount 6: greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins), but 3 + 3 uses two. Kruskal’s MST (Chapter 23) is the matroid greedy algorithm on the graphic matroid — which is why it is correct.

Topic 37B — Scheduling

Unit 37.2 — Deadlines, profits, and lateness

One-line summary: Minimise maximum lateness (one machine, jobs with durations and deadlines): sort by deadline (earliest deadline first); an exchange of adjacent out-of-order jobs never increases the maximum lateness. Maximise profit with unit jobs and deadlines (or “maximum number of courses finishable”): process in deadline order and keep the chosen jobs in a heap; when the schedule overflows, drop the worst chosen job.

# file: scheduling.py
import heapq
from itertools import permutations, combinations
from check import stress

def min_max_lateness(jobs):                          # (duration, deadline)
    t, worst = 0, 0
    for d, dl in sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: j[1]):
        t += d
        worst = max(worst, t - dl)
    return worst

def lateness_brute(jobs):
    best = float("inf")
    for order in permutations(jobs):
        t, worst = 0, 0
        for d, dl in order:
            t += d; worst = max(worst, t - dl)
        best = min(best, worst)
    return best if jobs else 0

def max_courses(courses):                            # (duration, last day); take as many as possible
    t, chosen = 0, []                                # max-heap of durations (negated)
    for d, last in sorted(courses, key=lambda c: c[1]):
        heapq.heappush(chosen, -d); t += d
        if t > last:
            t += heapq.heappop(chosen)               # drop the longest so far (pop returns -longest)
    return len(chosen)

def courses_brute(courses):
    for k in range(len(courses), 0, -1):
        for sub in combinations(courses, k):
            t, ok = 0, True
            for d, last in sorted(sub, key=lambda c: c[1]):   # EDF is optimal for a fixed set
                t += d; ok = ok and t <= last
            if ok:
                return k
    return 0

gen = lambda rng: ([(rng.randint(1, 5), rng.randint(1, 12)) for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 6))],)
print(stress(min_max_lateness, lateness_brute, gen))
print(stress(max_courses, courses_brute, gen))

The exchange argument for “earliest deadline first”

Take any schedule with two adjacent jobs where the later one has the earlier deadline. Swapping them does not change when the pair finishes as a whole; the job with the earlier deadline now finishes earlier, and the other finishes when the pair used to finish — which is no later than its own deadline relative to before, because its deadline is later. So the maximum lateness never increases, and repeated swaps reach the deadline-sorted order without ever getting worse. That is the structure of every exchange argument: show that fixing one “inversion” never hurts.

Unit 37.3 — Frontiers and two passes

One-line summary: Jump game (can you reach the end? fewest jumps?): keep the farthest reachable index; for fewest jumps, process the array in BFS-like layers of reach. Gas station: if total gas ≥ total cost, the answer is the station after the last point where the running tank went negative. Candy (each child gets ≥ 1; a higher rating than a neighbour means more candy): one pass left-to-right enforces the left neighbour, one pass right-to-left the right neighbour, taking the max.

# file: frontier.py
from collections import deque
from check import stress, rand_list

def min_jumps(a):                                    # a[i] = max jump length from i; -1 if unreachable
    jumps, cur_end, farthest = 0, 0, 0
    for i in range(len(a) - 1):
        if i > farthest:
            return -1
        farthest = max(farthest, i + a[i])
        if i == cur_end:                             # end of this layer: must jump
            jumps, cur_end = jumps + 1, farthest
    return jumps if farthest >= len(a) - 1 or len(a) == 1 else -1

def jumps_bfs(a):
    dist, q = {0: 0}, deque([0])
    while q:
        i = q.popleft()
        for j in range(i + 1, min(len(a), i + a[i] + 1)):
            if j not in dist:
                dist[j] = dist[i] + 1; q.append(j)
    return dist.get(len(a) - 1, -1)

def gas_station(gas, cost):
    if sum(gas) < sum(cost):
        return -1
    start, tank = 0, 0
    for i in range(len(gas)):
        tank += gas[i] - cost[i]
        if tank < 0:
            start, tank = i + 1, 0                   # no station in [start, i] can work
    return start

def gas_brute(gas, cost):
    n = len(gas)
    for s in range(n):
        tank = 0
        for k in range(n):
            i = (s + k) % n
            tank += gas[i] - cost[i]
            if tank < 0:
                break
        else:
            return s
    return -1

def candy(r):
    n = len(r)
    c = [1] * n
    for i in range(1, n):
        if r[i] > r[i - 1]: c[i] = c[i - 1] + 1
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
        if r[i] > r[i + 1]: c[i] = max(c[i], c[i + 1] + 1)
    return sum(c)

def candy_brute(r):                                   # relax constraints until stable
    c = [1] * len(r)
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for i in range(len(r)):
            for j in (i - 1, i + 1):
                if 0 <= j < len(r) and r[i] > r[j] and c[i] <= c[j]:
                    c[i] = c[j] + 1; changed = True
    return sum(c)

print(stress(min_jumps, jumps_bfs, lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 3, 10, 1),)))
print(stress(gas_station, gas_brute, lambda rng: ((g := rand_list(rng, 0, 5, 7, 1)), [rng.randint(0, 5) for _ in g])))
print(stress(candy, candy_brute, lambda rng: (rand_list(rng, 0, 4, 10, 1),)))

gas_station returns the first valid start; when several exist, so does the brute force — both scan starts in increasing order — which is why the stress test can compare them exactly.

Pattern

P-38. Suspect greedy when a problem asks for a maximum count or minimum cost and some ordering (by end time, deadline, ratio, size) seems natural. Then: (1) write the brute force, (2) stress-test the candidate rule, (3) if it survives, find the exchange argument. (Practice) Common safe rules: earliest finish (interval scheduling), earliest deadline (lateness), largest ratio (fractional knapsack), smallest two first (Huffman), farthest reach (jumps). When a greedy needs to “undo” a choice, keep the chosen items in a heap. Trade-off: when no greedy rule survives the stress test, the problem usually needs DP — the brute force you wrote is the start of it.

Chapter 37 Project — Huffman coding

Goal: compress a text with an optimal prefix code. Huffman’s algorithm: put every symbol in a min-heap by frequency; repeatedly merge the two least frequent trees into one whose frequency is their sum. Read the codes off the tree. Verify: decoding restores the text, the code is prefix-free, the total encoded length equals Σ freq × code length, it matches a brute-force optimum on small alphabets, and it lies within 1 bit per symbol of the entropy lower bound.

# file: huffman/huffman.py
import heapq
import math
from collections import Counter
from functools import cache
from check import stress

def huffman_codes(freq):
    if len(freq) == 1:
        return {next(iter(freq)): "0"}
    h = [(f, i, sym) for i, (sym, f) in enumerate(sorted(freq.items()))]
    heapq.heapify(h)
    counter = len(h)
    while len(h) > 1:
        f1, _, a = heapq.heappop(h)
        f2, _, b = heapq.heappop(h)
        heapq.heappush(h, (f1 + f2, counter, (a, b)))   # internal node: a pair of subtrees
        counter += 1
    codes = {}
    stack = [(h[0][2], "")]
    while stack:
        node, code = stack.pop()
        if isinstance(node, tuple):
            stack.append((node[0], code + "0")); stack.append((node[1], code + "1"))
        else:
            codes[node] = code
    return codes

def encoded_bits(freq, codes):
    return sum(freq[s] * len(codes[s]) for s in freq)

def optimal_brute(freq):
    """Minimum total cost of a full binary tree with leaves of these weights (merge any two, recursively)."""
    @cache
    def go(ws):
        if len(ws) == 1:
            return 0
        best = float("inf")
        for i in range(len(ws)):
            for j in range(i + 1, len(ws)):
                rest = ws[:i] + ws[i + 1:j] + ws[j + 1:]
                best = min(best, ws[i] + ws[j] + go(tuple(sorted(rest + (ws[i] + ws[j],)))))
        return best
    return go(tuple(sorted(freq.values()))) if len(freq) > 1 else sum(freq.values())

def check(freq):
    codes = huffman_codes(freq)
    words = list(codes.values())
    prefix_free = not any(a != b and b.startswith(a) for a in words for b in words)
    return encoded_bits(freq, codes), prefix_free

gen = lambda rng: ({chr(97 + i): rng.randint(1, 20) for i in range(rng.randint(1, 6))},)
print(stress(check, lambda f: (optimal_brute(f), True), gen, trials=500))

text = open(__file__).read() * 3                      # this program's own source as the test text
freq = Counter(text)
codes = huffman_codes(freq)
bits = "".join(codes[ch] for ch in text)
decode = {v: k for k, v in codes.items()}
out, cur = [], ""
for b in bits:
    cur += b
    if cur in decode:
        out.append(decode[cur]); cur = ""
n = len(text)
entropy = -sum(f / n * math.log2(f / n) for f in freq.values())
print(f"{n:,} characters, {len(freq)} distinct: {len(bits):,} bits = {len(bits) / n:.3f} bits/char "
      f"(entropy {entropy:.3f}, fixed-length {math.ceil(math.log2(len(freq)))}); decodes correctly: {''.join(out) == text}")
$ cd huffman && PYTHONPATH=../../lib python3 huffman.py
500 stress tests ok
7,515 characters, 60 distinct: 35,277 bits = 4.694 bits/char (entropy 4.671, fixed-length 6); decodes correctly: True

Huffman’s average code length L satisfies H ≤ L < H + 1 (Shannon’s source-coding bound), and the measured numbers sit just above the entropy. Its optimality proof is an exchange argument: in some optimal tree, the two least frequent symbols are siblings at the deepest level — so merging them first is safe.

Review checklist

  • Why does the heap store a counter as a tie-breaker (P-16)?
  • Why must the two smallest-frequency symbols be siblings in some optimal tree?
  • How would you transmit the code table so the receiver can decode? (Canonical Huffman codes: send only the code lengths.)

Answers to the Chapter 37 prediction questions

37.3 Q1. Yes: for US coins greedy is optimal (the system is “canonical”). For {1, 3, 4} it is not (DT-45) — canonicity must be checked per coin system.

37.3 Q2. The chosen set must fit before the current deadline. Removing the longest course frees the most time while reducing the count by exactly one, the same as removing any other course; with more free time, every future course is at least as easy to add — an exchange argument.

Chapter 38 — Intervals and Sweep Lines

Goal: handle collections of intervals — merging, inserting, intersecting, covering — and solve geometric-flavoured problems by sweeping a line across sorted events while maintaining a small active structure (a counter, a heap, an ordered multiset).

What you will be able to do after this chapter

  • Merge and insert intervals; intersect two interval lists with two pointers.
  • Turn intervals into +1/−1 events and sweep: maximum overlap, total covered length, free time.
  • Solve covering and stabbing problems greedily (minimum arrows, minimum removals).
  • Compute the skyline of buildings with a sweep and a lazy-deletion heap.
  • Handle the boundary rules — open, closed, half-open — that decide most bugs here.

Topic 38A — Interval lists

Unit 38.1 — Merge, insert, intersect

One-line summary: Merge overlapping intervals: sort by start; extend the last merged interval while the next one starts before (or at) its end. Insert into a sorted disjoint list: copy those entirely before, merge those overlapping, copy those after — O(n). Intersect two sorted disjoint lists: two pointers; the overlap of the current pair is [max(starts), min(ends)] if non-empty; advance the one that ends first.

# file: interval_lists.py
from check import stress

def merge(intervals):                                 # closed intervals [s, e]; touching ones merge
    out = []
    for s, e in sorted(intervals):
        if out and s <= out[-1][1]:
            out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e)
        else:
            out.append([s, e])
    return out

def insert(intervals, new):                           # intervals sorted and disjoint
    s, e = new
    left = [iv for iv in intervals if iv[1] < s]
    right = [iv for iv in intervals if iv[0] > e]
    mid = [iv for iv in intervals if not (iv[1] < s or iv[0] > e)]
    if mid:
        s, e = min(s, mid[0][0]), max(e, mid[-1][1])
    return left + [[s, e]] + right

def intersect(A, B):
    i = j = 0
    out = []
    while i < len(A) and j < len(B):
        lo, hi = max(A[i][0], B[j][0]), min(A[i][1], B[j][1])
        if lo <= hi:
            out.append([lo, hi])
        if A[i][1] < B[j][1]:
            i += 1
        else:
            j += 1
    return out

def to_points(ivs):                                   # brute force on a small integer line (closed intervals)
    return {x for s, e in ivs for x in range(s, e + 1)}

def from_points(pts):
    out = []
    for x in sorted(pts):
        if out and x == out[-1][1] + 1:
            out[-1][1] = x
        else:
            out.append([x, x])
    return out

def rand_ivs(rng, k=5):
    return [[s, s + rng.randint(0, 4)] for s in (rng.randint(0, 20) for _ in range(rng.randint(0, k)))]

print(stress(lambda ivs: to_points(merge(ivs)), to_points, lambda rng: (rand_ivs(rng),)))
print(stress(lambda a, n: to_points(insert(merge(a), n)), lambda a, n: to_points(a) | to_points([n]),
             lambda rng: (rand_ivs(rng), [(s := rng.randint(0, 20)), s + rng.randint(0, 4)])))
print(stress(lambda a, b: to_points(intersect(merge(a), merge(b))), lambda a, b: to_points(a) & to_points(b), lambda rng: (rand_ivs(rng), rand_ivs(rng))))
print(merge([[1, 3], [2, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]]), insert([[1, 2], [3, 5], [6, 7], [8, 10], [12, 16]], [4, 8]))

The brute force converts intervals to sets of integer points — slow, obviously correct, and it sidesteps every boundary question. (Merging adjacent integer intervals like [1, 2] and [3, 4] is a separate question: as point sets they are the same, which is why the checks compare points, not interval lists.)

Deep & Tricky

DT-46. Whether intervals that only touch ([1, 3] and [3, 5]) overlap depends on whether they are closed or half-open, and the sweep must order simultaneous events accordingly: for half-open [s, e), process ends before starts at the same coordinate; for closed [s, e], starts before ends. (Convention; the event order encodes the boundary rule) Meeting rooms (Unit 15.5) are half-open — a meeting ending at 10 frees the room for one starting at 10 — so sorting events as (time, −1 before +1) gives the right count. Sorting as (time, +1 before −1) silently computes the closed-interval answer, one room too many on touching meetings. Decide the convention from the problem statement, then encode it in the sort key.

Topic 38B — Sweeping events

Unit 38.2 — Events: overlap, coverage, free time

One-line summary: Replace each interval by two events, (start, +1) and (end, −1), sort, and sweep while keeping a running count. The maximum count is the maximum overlap; the total length where count > 0 is the covered length; gaps where count = 0 inside the overall span are the free time. O(n log n), independent of coordinate size.

# file: sweep.py
from check import stress

def sweep_stats(intervals):                            # half-open [s, e)
    events = sorted([(s, 1) for s, e in intervals] + [(e, -1) for s, e in intervals])   # -1 sorts before +1
    count = best = covered = 0
    prev = None
    free = []
    for x, d in events:
        if prev is not None and x > prev:
            if count > 0:
                covered += x - prev
            else:
                free.append((prev, x))                 # a gap between busy stretches
        count += d
        best = max(best, count)
        prev = x
    return best, covered, free

def brute(intervals):
    pts = {}
    for s, e in intervals:
        for x in range(s, e):
            pts[x] = pts.get(x, 0) + 1
    best = max(pts.values(), default=0)
    covered = len(pts)
    free = []
    if intervals:
        lo, hi = min(s for s, _ in intervals), max(e for _, e in intervals)
        for x in range(lo, hi):
            if x not in pts:
                if free and free[-1][1] == x:
                    free[-1] = (free[-1][0], x + 1)
                else:
                    free.append((x, x + 1))
    return best, covered, free

gen = lambda rng: ([(s := rng.randint(0, 20), s + rng.randint(1, 5)) for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 6))],)
print(stress(sweep_stats, brute, gen))
print(sweep_stats([(1, 3), (2, 6), (8, 10), (9, 12)]))

Half-open intervals avoid an off-by-one at every boundary

With half-open intervals [start, end), a meeting ending at 10 and one starting at 10 do not overlap, lengths are end − start, and the events at the same time are ordered “end before start” automatically when you sort (time, +1 for start / −1 for end) tuples — because −1 < +1. With closed intervals the same sort counts touching meetings as overlapping. Decide which convention the problem uses before writing the comparison; most room-booking problems are half-open.

Unit 38.3 — Stabbing and covering: minimum arrows, minimum removals

One-line summary: Minimum points that stab every interval (minimum arrows for balloons): sort by end; shoot at the end of the first unstabbed interval; skip all intervals containing that point. Minimum removals to make intervals non-overlapping = n − (maximum non-overlapping set) — Unit 37.1’s earliest-finish greedy. Both are the same exchange argument.

# file: stabbing.py
from itertools import combinations, product
from check import stress

def min_arrows(balloons):                              # closed intervals: an arrow at x bursts [s, e] if s <= x <= e
    arrows, last = 0, float("-inf")
    for s, e in sorted(balloons, key=lambda b: b[1]):
        if s > last:                                   # not yet burst
            arrows, last = arrows + 1, e
    return arrows

def arrows_brute(balloons):
    if not balloons:
        return 0
    candidates = sorted({e for _, e in balloons})      # some optimal solution shoots only at right ends
    for k in range(1, len(balloons) + 1):
        for shots in combinations(candidates, k):
            if all(any(s <= x <= e for x in shots) for s, e in balloons):
                return k

gen = lambda rng: ([(s := rng.randint(0, 15), s + rng.randint(0, 5)) for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 6))],)
print(stress(min_arrows, arrows_brute, gen))
print(min_arrows([(10, 16), (2, 8), (1, 6), (7, 12)]))

One more problem: minimum intervals to remove so the rest do not overlap

Keep as many non-overlapping intervals as possible (Unit 37.1’s activity selection: sort by end, greedily keep each interval that starts after the last kept end); the answer is the number not kept.

# file: erase_overlap.py
from itertools import combinations
from check import stress

def min_removals(intervals):                      # half-open [s, e)
    kept, last_end = 0, float("-inf")
    for s, e in sorted(intervals, key=lambda iv: iv[1]):
        if s >= last_end:
            kept += 1
            last_end = e
    return len(intervals) - kept

def brute(intervals):
    n = len(intervals)
    for keep in range(n, -1, -1):
        for subset in combinations(intervals, keep):
            ivs = sorted(subset)
            if all(a[1] <= b[0] for a, b in zip(ivs, ivs[1:])):
                return n - keep

def gen(rng):
    out = []
    for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 7)):
        s = rng.randint(0, 8)
        out.append((s, s + rng.randint(1, 4)))
    return (out,)

print(min_removals([(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (1, 3)]), min_removals([(1, 2), (1, 2), (1, 2)]))
print(stress(min_removals, brute, gen))

Minimum arrows (this unit) and minimum removals are the same greedy; they differ only in whether touching intervals count as overlapping (closed balloons versus half-open meetings).

Unit 38.4 — Sweep with an active set: the skyline

One-line summary: When the sweep needs more than a count — the maximum height among active buildings, the nearest active segment — keep the active items in a heap (with lazy deletion) or an ordered multiset. Skyline: at each x where a building starts or ends, the skyline height is the maximum active height; output a key point whenever it changes.

# file: skyline.py
import heapq
from check import stress

def skyline(buildings):                                # (left, right, height), half-open [left, right)
    xs = sorted({x for l, r, _ in buildings for x in (l, r)})
    by_left = sorted(buildings)
    active, i, out = [], 0, []                         # active: (-height, right)
    for x in xs:
        while i < len(by_left) and by_left[i][0] <= x:
            l, r, h = by_left[i]
            heapq.heappush(active, (-h, r)); i += 1
        while active and active[0][1] <= x:            # lazy deletion: building ended
            heapq.heappop(active)
        h = -active[0][0] if active else 0
        if not out or out[-1][1] != h:
            out.append([x, h])
    return out

def brute(buildings):
    xs = sorted({x for l, r, _ in buildings for x in (l, r)})
    out = []
    for x in xs:
        h = max((hh for l, r, hh in buildings if l <= x < r), default=0)
        if not out or out[-1][1] != h:
            out.append([x, h])
    return out

gen = lambda rng: ([(l := rng.randint(0, 15), l + rng.randint(1, 6), rng.randint(1, 9)) for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 6))],)
print(stress(skyline, brute, gen))
print(skyline([(2, 9, 10), (3, 7, 15), (5, 12, 12), (15, 20, 10), (19, 24, 8)]))
$ PYTHONPATH=../lib python3 skyline.py
2000 stress tests ok
[[2, 10], [3, 15], [7, 12], [12, 0], [15, 10], [20, 8], [24, 0]]

Lazy deletion is safe because only the top of the heap is read: a building that has ended but is buried under a taller active one does no harm until it surfaces, at which point it is popped. Chapter 18’s project used the same sweep with a segment tree when the active structure had to answer “covered length” rather than “maximum”.

Pattern

P-39. Intervals → sort by start (merging, inserting) or by end (selecting, stabbing). Questions about “at any moment” → events + sweep, with a counter for overlaps, a heap or ordered multiset for the best active item, and a segment tree for aggregates over coordinates. (Practice) Fix the boundary convention first (DT-46) and test with touching intervals. Trade-off: a sweep needs all intervals up front; for online insertions and queries, use an ordered map of boundaries (this chapter’s project) or an interval tree.

  2. Predict. For balloons [(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 5)], how many arrows are needed?

Chapter 38 Project — An online booking calendar

Goal: implement a calendar that accepts bookings [start, end) one at a time (online) and, after each, reports the maximum number of simultaneous bookings so far (the “k-booking” problem), with up to 100,000 bookings over times up to 10⁹. Approach 1: a sorted map of boundary deltas and a full re-sweep per booking — O(n) each. Approach 2: a dynamic segment tree over the time range with range-add and global maximum (lazy propagation, nodes created on demand) — O(log T) each.

# file: calendar/calendar_k.py
import random
import time
from sortedcontainers import SortedDict
from check import stress

class SweepCalendar:
    def __init__(self):
        self.delta = SortedDict()
    def book(self, s, e):
        self.delta[s] = self.delta.get(s, 0) + 1
        self.delta[e] = self.delta.get(e, 0) - 1
        cur = best = 0
        for d in self.delta.values():                   # O(n) re-sweep
            cur += d
            best = max(best, cur)
        return best

class DynamicSegTree:
    """Range add on [l, r), global max, over [0, size). Nodes created lazily in dicts."""
    def __init__(self, size):
        self.size = size
        self.mx, self.tag = {}, {}
    def add(self, l, r, v, node=1, lo=0, hi=None):
        hi = self.size if hi is None else hi
        if r <= lo or hi <= l:
            return
        if l <= lo and hi <= r:
            self.mx[node] = self.mx.get(node, 0) + v
            self.tag[node] = self.tag.get(node, 0) + v
            return
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        self.add(l, r, v, 2 * node, lo, mid)
        self.add(l, r, v, 2 * node + 1, mid, hi)
        # tags are never pushed down: a node's max = its own tag + max of children
        self.mx[node] = self.tag.get(node, 0) + max(self.mx.get(2 * node, 0), self.mx.get(2 * node + 1, 0))
    def global_max(self):
        return self.mx.get(1, 0)

class TreeCalendar:
    def __init__(self, size=10**9):
        self.t = DynamicSegTree(size)
    def book(self, s, e):
        self.t.add(s, e, 1)
        return self.t.global_max()

def run(cls, bookings):
    c = cls()
    return [c.book(s, e) for s, e in bookings]

gen = lambda rng: ([(s := rng.randint(0, 30), s + rng.randint(1, 8)) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 12))],)
print(stress(lambda b: run(TreeCalendar, b), lambda b: run(SweepCalendar, b), gen))

rng = random.Random(31)
for n in (2_000, 20_000, 100_000):
    bookings = [(s := rng.randint(0, 10**9 - 10**6), s + rng.randint(1, 10**6)) for _ in range(n)]
    for name, cls in (("dynamic segment tree", TreeCalendar), ("sorted map + sweep", SweepCalendar)):
        if cls is SweepCalendar and n > 20_000:
            print(f"n={n:>7,}: {name:>20}: skipped (quadratic)")
            continue
        t = time.perf_counter()
        res = run(cls, bookings)
        print(f"n={n:>7,}: {name:>20}: final max overlap {res[-1]} in {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f} s")

The segment tree never pushes tags down: since the only query is the global maximum, a node’s maximum can be defined as its own tag plus the larger child maximum — the same “tags that are never pushed” idea as the rectangle-union project of Chapter 18. Creating nodes on demand keeps memory proportional to n log T instead of T.

Answers to the Chapter 38 prediction questions

38.4 Q1. [[1, 5]]: for closed intervals, touching at 4 counts as overlapping (4 <= 4). For half-open [1, 4) and [4, 5) the point sets are disjoint but adjacent; whether to merge them is a choice (they cover a contiguous range), so state it explicitly.

38.4 Q2. Two: an arrow at 2 bursts (1, 2) and (2, 3); one at 4 bursts (3, 4) and (4, 5).

Chapter 39 — String Algorithms

Goal: match patterns in linear time (KMP prefix function, Z-function), find all palindromic substrings in linear time (Manacher), and build the two great substring indexes — the suffix array with LCP and the suffix automaton — to answer “distinct substrings”, “longest repeated substring”, and “longest common substring” questions efficiently.

What you will be able to do after this chapter

  • Compute the prefix function and use it for matching, periods, and borders.
  • Compute the Z-function and use it for matching and string compression.
  • Find the longest palindromic substring in O(n) with Manacher’s algorithm.
  • Build a suffix array in O(n log n) and its LCP array with Kasai’s algorithm.
  • Build a suffix automaton and count distinct substrings, find the longest common substring.

Topic 39A — Linear-time matching

Unit 39.1 — The prefix function (KMP)

One-line summary: pi[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of s[:i+1] that is also its suffix (a border). Computed in O(n) by falling back along borders: k = pi[k−1] while the next characters mismatch. To find pattern p in text t, compute pi for p + "#" + t; positions with pi == len(p) are matches. The smallest period of s is n − pi[n−1].

# file: kmp.py
from check import stress

def prefix_function(s):
    pi = [0] * len(s)
    for i in range(1, len(s)):
        k = pi[i - 1]
        while k and s[i] != s[k]:
            k = pi[k - 1]                             # fall back to the next shorter border
        if s[i] == s[k]:
            k += 1
        pi[i] = k
    return pi

def find_all(text, pat):                              # start indices of pat in text
    if not pat:
        return list(range(len(text) + 1))
    pi = prefix_function(pat + "\0" + text)           # "\0" never occurs in either string
    m = len(pat)
    return [i - 2 * m for i in range(len(pi)) if pi[i] == m]

def smallest_period(s):
    p = len(s) - prefix_function(s)[-1]
    return p if len(s) % p == 0 else len(s)           # a full repetition, or the string itself

w = lambda rng, k: "".join(rng.choice("ab") for _ in range(rng.randint(0, k)))
print(stress(find_all, lambda t, p: [i for i in range(len(t) - len(p) + 1) if t.startswith(p, i)], lambda rng: (w(rng, 15), w(rng, 3) or "a")))
print(stress(smallest_period, lambda s: next(p for p in range(1, len(s) + 1) if len(s) % p == 0 and s[:p] * (len(s) // p) == s),
             lambda rng: ((w(rng, 3) or "a") * rng.randint(1, 4),)))
print(prefix_function("aabaaab"), find_all("abababab", "abab"), smallest_period("abcabcabc"))

What the prefix function stores, and why the fallback loop is linear

π[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of s[:i + 1] that is also a suffix of it. When the next character does not extend the current border, KMP falls back to the next-longest border, π[k − 1], instead of starting again — the borders of a border are borders too. The while loop looks expensive, but each fallback decreases k, and k increases by at most one per character, so the total number of fallbacks is at most n: O(n) overall. Pattern search is the prefix function of pattern + "#" + text, with # a character that appears in neither.

Unit 39.2 — The Z-function

One-line summary: z[i] = length of the longest common prefix of s and s[i:]. Computed in O(n) by maintaining the rightmost Z-box [l, r) found so far: inside it, z[i] starts from the mirrored value z[i − l] (capped at r − i), then extends by direct comparison. Matching: Z of p + sep + t. It is often simpler than the prefix function for “prefix of s occurs at position i” questions.

# file: zfunc.py
from check import stress

def z_function(s):
    n = len(s)
    z = [0] * n
    if n:
        z[0] = n
    l = r = 0
    for i in range(1, n):
        if i < r:
            z[i] = min(r - i, z[i - l])               # reuse the mirrored value inside the Z-box
        while i + z[i] < n and s[z[i]] == s[i + z[i]]:
            z[i] += 1
        if i + z[i] > r:
            l, r = i, i + z[i]
    return z

def z_brute(s):
    out = []
    for i in range(len(s)):
        k = 0
        while i + k < len(s) and s[k] == s[i + k]:
            k += 1
        out.append(k)
    return out

print(stress(z_function, z_brute, lambda rng: ("".join(rng.choice("ab") for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 15))),)))
print(z_function("aaabaab"))

Deep & Tricky

DT-47. KMP and the Z-function are O(n) because a pointer that only moves forward (the matched length in KMP, the right end r of the Z-box) bounds the total work; Python’s built-in str.find is not guaranteed linear and, on adversarial inputs, older CPython versions could be quadratic. (Knuth, Morris & Pratt, SIAM J. Comput. 6(2), 1977; CPython 3.10 added the Crochemore–Perrin two-way algorithm for long needles in str.find) In practice str.find and in are excellent and should be used for single-pattern search in Python; KMP and Z matter when you need what they compute along the way — borders, periods, all prefix matches — or a guaranteed bound.

Unit 39.3 — Manacher’s algorithm: all palindromes

One-line summary: Transform s into #a#b#a# so every palindrome has odd length; compute p[i] = palindrome radius centred at i. Like the Z-function, keep the rightmost palindrome [c − p[c], c + p[c]]; inside it, p[i] starts from the mirror p[2c − i] (capped), then expands. O(n). The longest palindromic substring and the count of palindromic substrings both follow.

# file: manacher.py
from check import stress

def manacher(s):
    t = "#" + "#".join(s) + "#"
    n = len(t)
    p = [0] * n
    c = r = 0                                         # centre and right edge of the rightmost palindrome
    for i in range(n):
        if i < r:
            p[i] = min(r - i, p[2 * c - i])
        while i - p[i] - 1 >= 0 and i + p[i] + 1 < n and t[i - p[i] - 1] == t[i + p[i] + 1]:
            p[i] += 1
        if i + p[i] > r:
            c, r = i, i + p[i]
    return p

def longest_palindrome(s):
    if not s:
        return ""
    p = manacher(s)
    i = max(range(len(p)), key=p.__getitem__)
    start = (i - p[i]) // 2
    return s[start:start + p[i]]

def count_palindromes(s):
    # a radius r at position i of t covers palindromes of original lengths r, r-2, ...: (r + 1) // 2 of them
    return sum((r + 1) // 2 for r in manacher(s))

def brute_longest(s):
    return max((s[i:j] for i in range(len(s)) for j in range(i + 1, len(s) + 1) if s[i:j] == s[i:j][::-1]), key=len, default="")

def brute_count(s):
    return sum(s[i:j] == s[i:j][::-1] for i in range(len(s)) for j in range(i + 1, len(s) + 1))

w = lambda rng: ("".join(rng.choice("ab") for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 12))),)
print(stress(lambda s: len(longest_palindrome(s)), lambda s: len(brute_longest(s)), w))
print(stress(count_palindromes, brute_count, w))
print(longest_palindrome("forgeeksskeegfor"), count_palindromes("aaa"))

Why Manacher is linear

Manacher keeps the palindrome reaching furthest to the right, [l, r]. For a new centre i inside it, the mirror centre l + r − i has already been computed, and its radius is a guaranteed lower bound for i’s radius (clipped at r). Expansion only happens beyond r, and every successful expansion pushes r to the right — so the total expansion work is O(n). Inserting a separator between characters (#a#b#a#) handles odd and even palindromes with one loop.

Topic 39B — Substring indexes

Unit 39.4 — Suffix array and LCP

One-line summary: The suffix array is the list of suffix start positions in sorted order. Build it in O(n log n) by prefix doubling: sort by the first 2^k characters using the ranks of halves from the previous round. Kasai’s algorithm computes lcp[i] = longest common prefix of the suffixes at sa[i] and sa[i+1] in O(n). Then: number of distinct substrings = n(n+1)/2 − Σ lcp; longest repeated substring = max lcp.

# file: ../lib/suffix_array.py
"""Suffix array by prefix doubling (O(n log^2 n) with Python's sort; simple and fast enough) and Kasai LCP."""

def suffix_array(s):
    n = len(s)
    if n == 0:
        return []
    rank = [ord(c) for c in s]
    sa = list(range(n))
    k = 1
    while True:
        key = lambda i: (rank[i], rank[i + k] if i + k < n else -1)
        sa.sort(key=key)
        new = [0] * n
        for j in range(1, n):
            new[sa[j]] = new[sa[j - 1]] + (key(sa[j]) != key(sa[j - 1]))
        rank = new
        if rank[sa[-1]] == n - 1:                      # all ranks distinct: done
            return sa
        k *= 2

def lcp_array(s, sa):                                  # lcp[i] = LCP(suffix sa[i], suffix sa[i+1])
    n = len(s)
    rank = [0] * n
    for i, p in enumerate(sa):
        rank[p] = i
    lcp, h = [0] * max(0, n - 1), 0
    for p in range(n):                                 # in text order: h drops by at most 1 each step
        if rank[p] + 1 < n:
            q = sa[rank[p] + 1]
            while p + h < n and q + h < n and s[p + h] == s[q + h]:
                h += 1
            lcp[rank[p]] = h
            if h:
                h -= 1
        else:
            h = 0
    return lcp
# file: sa_test.py
from check import stress
from suffix_array import suffix_array, lcp_array

def distinct_substrings(s):
    sa = suffix_array(s)
    return len(s) * (len(s) + 1) // 2 - sum(lcp_array(s, sa))

def longest_repeated(s):
    sa = suffix_array(s)
    lcp = lcp_array(s, sa)
    if not lcp or max(lcp) == 0:
        return ""
    i = max(range(len(lcp)), key=lcp.__getitem__)
    return s[sa[i]:sa[i] + lcp[i]]

Suffix array by sorting — and what the LCP array adds

The simplest construction sorts suffixes by their first 2ᵏ characters for k = 0, 1, 2, …, using the ranks from the previous round as keys: O(n log² n) with comparison sort, O(n log n) with radix sort. The LCP array (Kasai’s algorithm, O(n)) gives the longest common prefix of each pair of neighbouring suffixes. Together they answer: number of distinct substrings (n(n + 1)/2 − Σ lcp), the longest repeated substring (max lcp), and, with a separator between two strings, their longest common substring (the largest LCP between neighbours that come from different strings).

Unit 39.5 — The suffix automaton

One-line summary: The suffix automaton of s is the smallest DFA accepting exactly the substrings of s — at most 2n − 1 states, built online in O(n) by adding one character at a time with suffix links. Each state represents a set of substrings ending at the same positions, with lengths in (len(link), len]; so the number of distinct substrings is Σ (len[v] − len[link[v]]). Walking t through the automaton of s (following links on mismatch) finds the longest common substring in O(|t|).

# file: ../lib/sam.py
"""Suffix automaton (online construction)."""

class SuffixAutomaton:
    def __init__(self, s=""):
        self.next, self.link, self.len = [{}], [-1], [0]
        self.last = 0
        for ch in s:
            self.extend(ch)

    def extend(self, ch):
        cur = len(self.len)
        self.next.append({}); self.link.append(0); self.len.append(self.len[self.last] + 1)
        p = self.last
        while p != -1 and ch not in self.next[p]:
            self.next[p][ch] = cur
            p = self.link[p]
        if p != -1:
            q = self.next[p][ch]
            if self.len[p] + 1 == self.len[q]:
                self.link[cur] = q
            else:                                       # split q: clone with the shorter length
                clone = len(self.len)
                self.next.append(dict(self.next[q])); self.link.append(self.link[q]); self.len.append(self.len[p] + 1)
                while p != -1 and self.next[p].get(ch) == q:
                    self.next[p][ch] = clone
                    p = self.link[p]
                self.link[q] = self.link[cur] = clone
        self.last = cur

    def distinct_substrings(self):
        return sum(self.len[v] - self.len[self.link[v]] for v in range(1, len(self.len)))

    def longest_common_substring(self, t):
        v, l, best, end = 0, 0, 0, 0
        for i, ch in enumerate(t):
            while v and ch not in self.next[v]:
                v = self.link[v]; l = self.len[v]
            if ch in self.next[v]:
                v = self.next[v][ch]; l += 1
            if l > best:
                best, end = l, i + 1
        return t[end - best:end]

Pattern

P-40. Single-pattern search → str.find (or KMP/Z when you need borders, periods, or guarantees); many patterns → Aho–Corasick (Chapter 16); palindromes → Manacher; questions about all substrings (distinct count, repeats, common substrings, k-th substring) → suffix array + LCP or suffix automaton; quick probabilistic answers → rolling hash + binary search (Chapter 3). (Practice) Stress-test every string algorithm on a two- or three-letter alphabet: small alphabets create the repetitions that break incorrect fall-back logic. Trade-off: suffix structures are memory-hungry in Python (dicts per state); for n beyond ~10⁶, use arrays or a compiled library.

Mastery check

  1. Predict. What is the prefix function of “abab”?
  2. Predict. How many distinct non-empty substrings does “aaa” have, and what is Σ lcp of its suffix array?

Chapter 39 Project — Longest repeated substring three ways

Goal: find the longest substring occurring at least twice in a 200,000-character text, three ways — (1) Chapter 3’s binary search + rolling hash, (2) suffix array + LCP, (3) suffix automaton (track, for each state, the first end position and whether it occurs twice) — check that all agree, and time them.

# file: repeated/repeated.py
import random
import time
from sam import SuffixAutomaton
from suffix_array import suffix_array, lcp_array

def lrs_hash(s):
    MOD, B = (1 << 61) - 1, 911382323
    n = len(s)
    pw, h = [1] * (n + 1), [0] * (n + 1)
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        h[i + 1] = (h[i] * B + ord(ch)) % MOD
        pw[i + 1] = pw[i] * B % MOD
    def repeat_of(L):
        seen = {}
        for i in range(n - L + 1):
            x = (h[i + L] - h[i] * pw[L]) % MOD
            if x in seen and s[seen[x]:seen[x] + L] == s[i:i + L]:   # verify: no false positives
                return i
            seen.setdefault(x, i)
        return -1
    lo, hi, best = 1, n - 1, ""
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        i = repeat_of(mid)
        if i >= 0:
            best, lo = s[i:i + mid], mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return best

def lrs_sa(s):
    sa = suffix_array(s)
    lcp = lcp_array(s, sa)
    i = max(range(len(lcp)), key=lcp.__getitem__)
    return s[sa[i]:sa[i] + lcp[i]]

def lrs_sam(s):
    sam = SuffixAutomaton()
    first_end = [0]                                     # some end position of each state's strings
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        sam.extend(ch)
        while len(first_end) < len(sam.len):
            first_end.append(i)                         # strings of a new state (or clone) end at position i
    n_states = len(sam.len)
    cnt = [0] * n_states
    v = 0
    for ch in s:                                        # each prefix's state gets one end position
        v = sam.next[v][ch]
        cnt[v] += 1
    for u in sorted(range(1, n_states), key=lambda u: -sam.len[u]):
        if sam.link[u] > 0:
            cnt[sam.link[u]] += cnt[u]                  # a suffix occurs wherever its extensions occur
    best = max((u for u in range(1, n_states) if cnt[u] >= 2), key=lambda u: sam.len[u], default=None)
    if best is None:
        return ""
    end = first_end[best]
    return s[end - sam.len[best] + 1:end + 1]

rng = random.Random(32)
base = "".join(rng.choice("abcd") for _ in range(200_000))
s = base[:150_000] + base[10_000:10_150] + base[150_150:]          # plant a 150-character repeat
results = {}
for name, f in (("hash + binary search", lrs_hash), ("suffix array + LCP", lrs_sa), ("suffix automaton", lrs_sam)):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    r = f(s)
    results[name] = r
    print(f"{name:>21}: length {len(r)} in {time.perf_counter() - t:.1f} s")
print("all three agree on the length:", len({len(r) for r in results.values()}) == 1,
      "| each result occurs twice:", all(s.find(r) != s.rfind(r) for r in results.values()))

The three methods may return different substrings when several repeats share the maximum length — the check compares lengths and verifies that each answer really occurs twice. The planted 150-character repeat dominates the ~10-character repeats that occur by chance in random text over four letters (about log₄ n² ≈ 17 characters, in fact).

Review checklist

  • Why does the hash version verify candidate matches by comparing the actual substrings?
  • In the suffix automaton, why are occurrence counts propagated along suffix links from longer to shorter states?
  • Which method would you choose for a 10⁸-character genome, and why?
